News.title: Teen, 17, who 'couldn't wait to be mum' dies day after planned gender reveal party
News.content:
Teen, 17, who 'couldn't wait to be mum' dies day after planned gender reveal party

EXCLUSIVE: A 17-year-old who was looking forward to her gender reveal party tragically never got the chance to meet her little baby after she died suddenly earlier this month

View 7 Images Summer Rose Miles couldn't wait to be a mum (Image: Chloe Jade)

A teenage girl tragically died just one day after a planned gender reveal for her unborn baby.

‌



Summer Rose Miles, 17, collapsed at home and suffered a catastrophic brain haemorrhage on Thursday (July 9), before an air ambulance critical care team rushed to the scene before she was driven to hospital.

‌



There, while on life support, on what should have been the day of a gender reveal celebration, she delivered her tiny baby, who was born sleeping.

‌



The mum-to-be had emergency surgery but the damage to her brain stem was too severe. Her loved ones were then forced to say the hardest goodbye of their lives.

Her devastated older sister, Chloe Jade, has now started a GoFundMe page to help heartbroken parents, Mandy and Scott Miles, pay for a funeral they could never have imagined having to organise.

View 7 Images Summer Rose Miles tragically died unexpectedly (Image: Chloe Jade)

‌



She spoke exclusively to The Mirror about how incredible her brave, fearless and bold little sister was.

In an emotional conversation with this reporter, Chloe, 27, who grew up with the family in Top Valley in Nottingham, said: “She couldn’t wait to be a mum. She has said this since I remember her playing with dollies.

“She loves children so much, and although young, and it was a shock for everyone, we know she’d have been the best mummy ever, and everyone was looking forward to the next chapter.”

‌



After school, Summer excelled in college, which is where she met Carson, her boyfriend and best friend.

According to Chloe, getting pregnant changed her massively, and she instantly matured and gained a different outlook on life.

View 7 Images Summer pictured with her mum Mandy (Image: Chloe Jade)

‌



Looking back fondly, she recalled: “She had a different light about her — it was beautiful.”

But in a cruel twist, Summer, who had been 17 weeks pregnant, died on July 12 — and her siblings and parents remain utterly in shock.

Asked about the brain haemorrhage, Chloe told us: “The doctors said it was spontaneous, tragic and rare, especially in her age and pregnancy. Summer was otherwise fit and healthy.”

‌



Chloe said the heartbreak and pain of saying goodbye to Summer was impossible to put into words.

Summer and Carson’s baby gender reveal was due to take place on July 11 — just two days after she collapsed.

Her family and friends had been invited over for the reveal and Summer, who was the most excited, had been convinced it was going to be a girl.

‌



View 7 Images Summer pictured with her dad Scott (Image: Chloe Jade)

Chloe said: “The gender reveal decorations and plans were all prepped by my mum, following a private scan gifted to her from her boyfriend's family who would have also attended.

“Unfortunately the scan never had a chance to happen. One of the last things Summer told my mum was that she was thankful for how nice she had made the garden look for her big day outside.”

‌



Chloe said Summer had a particularly close bond with her mum and she described her little sister as being her mother’s shadow.

Remembering her sibling, she said she was a “whirlwind of chaos and laughter” and hugely popular with friends, as reflected in the many tributes since her untimely death.

Chloe has fond memories of road trips, seaside visits and sibling tattle tails with Summer who she also described as being a “little rebel” with “youngest child syndrome”.

‌



One of their favourite shared hobbies was spending time with horses — and Summer left behind her own pony called Princess, which was the present she got on her seventh birthday.

View 7 Images Summer with her pony called Princess (Image: Chloe Jade)

However, Chloe pointed out: “She would always want to ride my Rosie, because she loved a challenge!”

‌



Growing up, Summer always said she wanted to be like her older brother, Jordan, who was her biggest protector.

Chloe said Summer was a bit of a tomboy when she was younger but this soon changed when she would find her walking around in high heels she had taken from her wardrobe.

She also used to enjoy swimming with her dad as a child and she would cheer him on from the sidelines when he played football.

‌



One of Summer’s favourite things to do was spending time with her niece, Ava, who she shared a beautiful bond with, something Chloe said she will always be grateful for.

During family car journeys, Summer would insist on playing drum and bass, despite everyone else calling it “rubbish music”.

Laughing, Chloe added: “We went to a Coldplay and Oasis tribute a few weeks back and she sang her heart out to Coldplay with us and it was so special.

‌



View 7 Images Summer (middle) with her sister Chloe (right) and her niece Ava (left) (Image: Chloe Jade)

“When she first told me her new favourite song was Yellow, we sent a video singing it together to her dad to show how far she’d come with her music taste.”

Tragically, that fun, bubbly and bright character, who had no filter, is now no longer with us.

‌



And while Chloe reflected on the special memories, she and her family are also going through hell, by having to arrange a final farewell for Summer.

Writing an emotional message on the fundraiser, she said: “My world has fallen apart, and my heart is broken beyond words. I have created this GoFundMe on behalf of my family to offer whatever help and support I can during the most devastating time of our lives.

View 7 Images Mandy, Summer, Chloe and brother-in-law Jake (Image: Chloe Jade)

Article continues below

“No parent should ever have to bury their child, especially a 17-year-old daughter and her baby. We are not asking for anything more than a little help towards easing the financial burden that comes with arranging the beautiful farewell that Summer and her baby deserve.

“We will give them the best send-off we possibly can, no matter what & no matter the cost, but if I can take even a small amount of pressure away from Mum and Dad, it would mean everything and more.”

You can make a donation to the GoFundMe here

News.title: Angry locals tell council 'sort it out' as bin bags pile up in UK city streets
News.content:
Angry locals tell council 'sort it out' as bin bags pile up in UK city streets

Bin bags started piling up under a new fortnightly collection plan - the latest attempt by the council to deal with its collections that have been reduced by an 18 month strike

View 3 Images The bin bags pictured in Sutton Coldfield (Image: Birmingham Live)

There is fury as bin bags have started piling up in the city where workers have been on strike for 18 months.

‌



Councillors have hit out the latest attempt to improve waste collection in Birmingham, where refuse workers started industrial action in early 2025.

‌



The government were forced to bring army planners in to keep some collections going after the council declared a major incident as infestations of maggots and rats 'as big as cats' took hold around uncollected bin bags on the city streets, reports Birmingham Live.

‌



But the latest attempt to improve recycling collections has been met with fury as the council told 50,000 residents an incorrect start date, and missed out some properties.

Conservative Cllr Richard Parkin slammed the council for missing out a block of flats in Sutton Coldfield. In a video, he said: “I am actually really annoyed. The council has introduced this waste pilot scheme without any consultation with councillors.

“They have introduced fortnightly household waste collections and they have also included in the scheme flats.”

‌



View 3 Images Video shows bin bags piling up in Birmingham once again (Image: Birmingham Live)

His video then shows piles of black bags, with split bags with nappies and animal waste spilling out.

He added people in flats generate a lot of waste and lack space to accommodate the wheelie bins needed: “[The council] needs to stop fortnightly waste collections outside flats. It isn’t working. It’s not going to work and they have let everybody down.

‌



“Birmingham City Council sort it out!”

Labour lost control of the council in May, with a new minority coalition of Greens, Liberal Democrats, and independent Better Birmingham councillors now trying to turn the city’s waste problem around.

The councillor with that task is Harris Khaliq, who acknowledged ‘issues’ during the new service’s introduction. He apologised to the 50,000 households given ‘incorrect calendar information’.

‌



Cllr Khaliq said: “We understand one size does not fit all. We have a diverse city with different types of properties, high density properties, low density properties.

“Driveways, no driveways, terraced houses, semi-detached houses, and all sorts that we have got to take into account to make something work.”

View 3 Images Bin bags have piled up in certain areas of Birmingham since last March (Image: PA)

‌



He also acknowledged the issue with the flats, and said it would be ‘captured and co-ordinated’ to make sure wider lessons are learnt and implemented into the wider city’s plan.

The council, Britain’s largest, and trade unions are said to be close to agreeing a pay deal, but remain tight-lipped on ‘sensitive’ negotiations.

Previously, the council explained it was starting the fortnightly pilot so it could improve recycling rates to access new government funding. During the bin strike, recycling bins have not been collected in swathes of Birmingham.

Article continues below

A spokesperson said: “If we continue with low recycling rates, the city could lose out on millions of pounds of government funding that could go back into funding services for residents.

“The new system means people get more collections, more value for money and cleaner streets. We want to work with everyone in the pilot areas to make this a success that can benefit the whole city.”

News.title: New PM Andy Burnham announces VAT cuts on household electricity bills from October
News.content:
New PM Andy Burnham announces VAT cuts on household electricity bills from October

Millions of households across the UK will benefit from immediate action to help with their electricity bills this winter, the Prime Minister has announced as one of his first decisions in office

View 2 Images Britain's new Prime Minister Andy Burnham (Image: James Veysey/Shutterstock)

Andy Burnham has announced VAT on electricity bills will be removed in one of his first acts as Prime Minister.

‌



The new PM, who promised breathing space on the cost of living in his first speech from Downing Street, said the move is expected to knock £45 off the average bill.

‌



Downing Street said the new measure - estimated to cost £850 million in 2026-27 - will be funded by savings from the scrapped digital ID programme.

‌



Mr Burnham said: "Westminster has not been working for people for too long, with families struggling with the cost of living. That needs to change.

"I said I wanted to give people breathing space, and that’s what I’m announcing on my second day as Prime Minister. We’re taking immediate action to cut taxes on energy bills, put more money in people’s pockets and bring back hope.”

The Government said on Tuesday it would remove VAT from domestic electricity bills from October 1, with the next price cap announcement in late August.

‌



Donald Trump shares details of first call with new Prime Minister Andy Burnham READ MORE :

View 2 Images The move is expected to take around £45 off the yearly Ofgem price cap. (Image: Hispanolistic via Getty Images)

The £45 off the average bill is on top of the £150 removed by Keir Starmer's government in the Budget last year - although that ended up being slightly less in practice as other costs contributing to the price cap increased.

Small businesses who qualify for the domestic energy VAT relief, charities, and residential care homes eligible for the reduce rate will also see a cut on their bills.

‌



Newly appointed Chancellor John Healey MP said: "For too long, too many people have struggled with the cost of living. Today’s energy tax cut will give families some breathing room on bills, and provide some reassurance this winter.

"This measure is funded this year from cancelling the Digital ID programme, and it will help bring down inflation while supporting households in every postcode.”

It comes as Mr Burnham prepares to assemble the new-look Cabinet for the first time on Tuesday morning after culling top ministers from the Starmer-era, including Chancellor Rachel Reeves, deputy PM David Lammy and Business Secretary Peter Kyle.

‌



The new PM will also continue with the government’s reshuffle in the ministerial ranks.

Mr Burnham made clear he would act to help cash-strapped Brits with the cost of living during his first days in Downing Street in his first speech to the country on Monday.

The new Labour leader said he would act urgently to give people "breathing space" on the cost of living as he vowed his arrival would be a "circuit breaker" moment with a new political and economic model to sweep away the damage done by Margaret Thatcher that communities have struggled to recover from.

Article continues below

“I know people at home are fed up with politics," he said. "I hear you and I want to be honest with you – we have not been good enough, and we need to be better. We will be."

Downing Street said further long-term measures on the cost of living will be made in the next budget this autumn.

Follow our live blog for the latest politics updates by clicking here.

News.title: Doctor says adding one thing to meals will 'change your health'
News.content:
Doctor says adding one thing to meals will 'change your health'

You likely won't even notice this added to food such as pasta sauce

View 3 Images A doctor encouraged people to add this ingredient to your meals to up your fibre and healthy protein intake (Image: Getty)

A doctor is urging people to add a cheap ingredient to their meals to “change their health”. According to the expert, this simple addition could help lower your cholesterol and weight.

‌



We are all well aware of the importance of eating a healthy, balanced diet. What you eat can directly influence how well your body functions, even raising or lowering your risk of serious problems.

‌



Luckily, there are some simple rules you can follow to ensure you’re giving your body what it needs. In a video uploaded to his TikTok account, Doctor Rajan Karan explained one such rule.

‌



Dr Karan, who is better known as Dr Raj, told his more than five million followers they should be looking to add more beans to their food. By swapping out some meat for beans you could increase your fibre intake, while lowering your intake of saturated fat, he said.

He referenced a study, published in the European Journal of Nutrition in 2025, which saw 52 men swap out 200 grams of red processed meat in their weekly diet for the same amount of peas and faba beans (also known as fava beans or broad beans). Dr Raj said: “If you eat a lot of meat like I used to, this simple swap could change your health.

Content cannot be displayed without consent

‌



“Scientists at the University of Helsinki instructed 51 men to reduce the amount of red meat and ultra-processed meat they were eating to just 200 grams a week, that’s seven ounces, equivalent to five per cent of their total protein intake.

“Meanwhile, the men ate more legumes specifically, peas and faba beans, equivalent to 20 per cent of their total protein intake, and they continued eating chicken, eggs, fish and other protein sources as normal.”

The results were significant. He continued: “Beyond the beans swap, the men were not told to eat any less or restrict any of their calories, but after just six weeks, they lost an average of one kilo or 2.2 pounds of weight and the changes didn't stop there.

‌



“By the end of the study, the men who had eaten legumes had low levels of total and LDL cholesterol [‘bad’ cholesterol], suggesting that the diet swap reduced their risk of heart disease. At the same time, the men's iron levels improved, which is surprising given that red meat is considered to be a good source of dietary iron.”

He therefore encouraged people to top up their diets with more beans. He said: “Let's face it, we collectively eat more saturated fat than we should be and replacing a small portion of meat with beans is something every person could do.

‌



View 3 Images Adding beans to your meals is a good way to up your fibre and polyphenol intake (Image: Getty)

“For example, when you're next making spaghetti bolognese, use half the amount of beef mince and top it up with beans and you’d barely notice it because beans virtually taste of nothing and you're sneaking in fibre, polyphenols and a saturated fat-free protein source.”

One of the study authors, professor of molecular nutrition Anne-Maria Pajari, said: “In a trial setting, participants often monitor their eating more closely, which may contribute to weight loss. But in this study, despite its relatively short duration, the legume group lost significantly more weight than the meat group. We didn’t encourage the participants to lose weight, but asked them to continue eating as before, apart from consuming the foods we provided.”

Article continues below

View 3 Images In a study, men who replaced red meat and processed meat with beans lowered the'r "bad" cholesterol levels (Image: Getty)

She added: “In the short term, critical nutrient intake wasn’t jeopardised in the legume group. This was likely because the participants remained on mixed diets, rather than cutting out any foods entirely. However, research is needed on the effects of switching to plant-based diets on the body’s nutritional status, particularly in vulnerable population groups, such as children and older adults.

“The legume food products we provided were quick to cook, making them easy to use. We also handed out recipes to encourage cooking. Based on our findings, I believe a moderate dietary change towards a more sustainable direction, using peas, beans and lentils, is possible for most of us.”

News.title: Iran-backed group declares another crucial strait closed as Middle East war widens
News.content:
Iran-backed group declares another crucial strait closed as Middle East war widens

The rebel Houthis in Yemen have said they would close the Bab el-Mandeb Strait - a key Saudi waterway out of the Red Sea since the Strait of Hormuz closed

View 3 Images Armed Houthis gather at Sabeen Square to hold a demonstration in support of Houthi leader in Yemen Abdul Malik al-Houthi's statements in Sanaa, Yemen on July 17, 2026 (Image: Mohammed Hamoud/Anadolu via Getty Images)

An Iranian-backed group has threatened to impose a maritime blockade against a US ally as the Middle East conflict widens.

‌



The rebel Houthis in Yemen have said they would close the Bab el-Mandeb Strait - a key Saudi waterway out of the Red Sea since the Strait of Hormuz closed amid the US-Iran war.

‌



The Strait of Hormuz was closed by Iran early into the conflict in retaliation to joint US-Israeli strikes on several key Iranian sites. The critical waterway facilitated the movement of 20% of all global oil traded, but the closure has rocked oil movement and in turn, global markets.

‌



View 3 Images Three boys play in the shallow waters of the Strait of Hormuz, as a plume of smoke rises from an explosion in the background, off Bandar Abbas, Iran, Monday, July 13, 2026 (Image: AP Photo/Razieh Poudat)

The Houthis' armed forces said in a statement that they were declaring "a maritime embargo against the criminal Saudi enemy, based on the equation of 'an eye for an eye', effective immediately". It said that this was for "an unjust and oppressive siege" imposed on Yemen by the Saudis.

Saudi Arabia condemned the Houthi naval blockade announcement and accusations Riyadh of "besieging" the Yemeni people. The internationally recognised Yemen government also condemned the Houthi statement.

‌



The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen have said they would act to protect shipping and respond with force to the Houthis.

"Such threats are a blatant violation of international law and falls under acts of maritime piracy," the coalition said.

View 3 Images Satellite view of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait is a vital trade route linking the Red Sea, Gulf of Aden, Arabian Sea, Suez Canal, and Mediterranean (Image: Gallo Images/Orbital Horizon/Copernicus Sentinel Data 2026)

Article continues below

The full closure of the Bab el-Mandeb strait would reduce global oil supply by 7% as it would leave most of Saudi oil exports unable to leave the region, Sydney Morning Herald reports.

The closure could open a new front against the US in its war with Iran and contribute to a massive drop in oil out of the Gulf.

Oil prices rose briefly after the Houthi statement, but later fell back as traders held out hope of a diplomatic breakthrough.

News.title: Dr Amir Khan warns women 'might not know about' 5 symptoms
News.content:
Dr Amir Khan warns women 'might not know about' 5 symptoms

You might need to speak to your GP if you experience these

View 3 Images Doctor Amir Khan warned that you may not have heard of these possible symptoms (Image: Doctor Amir Khan/Instagram)

A doctor has warned of five symptoms many women “might not know about”. According to the expert, these can hit during the menopause but aren’t widely talked about.

‌



Menopause is a natural life stage that typically affects women between the ages of 45 and 55. It happens when oestrogen levels in the body drop to a point where periods cease completely.

‌



As a consequence of these hormonal shifts, the body can experience a broad range of symptoms that can impact both physical and mental health. Most people are aware of some of the more familiar effects, including hot flushes, mood swings, and brain fog.

‌



However, there are some lesser-known side effects you may not have heard of. In a video uploaded to his Instagram page, Doctor Amir Khan explained more.

He said: “Hey guys, I want to talk about five things falling oestrogen levels around the menopause effects that you might not know about.”

Content cannot be displayed without consent

‌



Gum inflammation and dry mouth

He said: “Number one, your gums and teeth. Falling oestrogen can cause gum inflammation and dry mouth, increasing the risk of gum disease and tooth loss. Some women even notice their teeth feeling more sensitive or loose.”

A change in hearing

He said: “Number two, your hearing. Oestrogen actually helps protect the delicate hair cells in the inner ear.

“So when levels drop, hearing can become less sharp, especially for higher-pitched sounds.”

‌



View 3 Images Menopause can increase the risk of gum disease and tooth loss (Image: Getty)

Coordination and balance

“Now lower oestrogen affects the inner ear and muscle strength, both key to balance,” he continued. “One reason falls become more common after the menopause.”

Reaction to caffeine

Dr Amir said: “With less oestrogen, your liver breaks down caffeine more slowly, so that afternoon coffee can suddenly keep you awake all night.”

‌



View 3 Images You may be prescribed HRT if you are going through the menopause (Image: Getty)

How your skin heals

He added: “Your skin's ability to heal. Oestrogen helps maintain collagen and blood flow to the skin.

“As it drops, cuts and bruises can take longer to heal and skin becomes thinner and more fragile. Knowledge is power, so now you know these things, it might help explain some of your symptoms.”

‌



The NHS lists some of the most common symptoms of menopause as:

Changes to your periods

Hot flushes and night sweats

Sleep problems

Mood changes, poor memory and brain fog

Weigh gain

Vaginal problems

UTIs

Article continues below

If you think you have symptoms of menopause or perimenopause you should speak to your GP.

News.title: Boy, 16, arrested after mum found dead and sister, 12, seriously injured
News.content:
Boy, 16, arrested after mum found dead and sister, 12, seriously injured

Police found a 35-year-old female dead at a property in western Australia and her 12-year-old daughter was found with serious injuries nearby after fleeing the home and managing to call police

View 3 Images Police say a teenage boy is suspected to have stabbed his mother to death and seriously injured his 12-year-old sister (Image: ABC News)

Police say a teenage boy is suspected to have stabbed his mother to death and seriously injured his 12-year-old sister in an alleged family violence homicide.

Officers rushed to a property on Mills Street in Bentley about 6.15am where they found a 35-year-old female dead. The 12-year-old girl was found with serious injuries about 600 metres away along a busy highway in Cannington after fleeing the home and managing to call police.

WA Police Detective Acting Inspector Jessica Securo from the Major Crime Division said both the mother and daughter's injuries were suspected stab wounds.

View 3 Images Two crime scenes have been established (Image: ABC News)

She confirmed the girl managed to escape the residence, on Mills Street, after she was allegedly stabbed by her brother. The 16-year-old boy is in police custody and was arrested this morning at a home in Bentley, in Perth's south east.

Inspector Securo said police will investigate the matter as a suspected family violence homicide and said there was no ongoing risk to the wider community. She said: "A 16-year-old male who is the son of the deceased female and the brother of the injured girl has been taken into police custody.

"While the investigation remains in its early stages, police are investigating this as a suspected family violence homicide and homicide squad have carriage," abc news reports.

Inspector Securo confirmed the 12-year-old girl is receiving treatment in Perth Children's Hospital and said that police would examine any past interactions the family had with police. Inspector Securo said: "That will form part of our investigation, to look at all incidents involving police, support services and what led to this incident occurring."

View 3 Images Police at the Scene (Image: ABC News)

Article continues below

The home remained a cordoned-off crime scene on Tuesday, as detectives doorknocked the neighbourhood.

"As part of this process, investigators will examine all available evidence and speak with relevant witnesses," Det Securo said.

No charges have been made as the police investigation continues.

News.title: Chris Mason: Cull of Starmer allies as new chancellor faces crunching spending choices
News.content:
A government ends and a new government begins, determined to make a splash with its early policy announcements.

We can expect to see and hear plenty from the new Prime Minister Andy Burnham and his senior ministers in the coming days, making arguments, travelling the country and trying to make an impact.

Burnham's new cabinet will meet for the first time at lunchtime.

Its appointment became something of a nocturnal affair.

At gone 22:00 BST on Monday night, there was still a minibus full of ministerial wannabes inside Downing Street waiting for their new positions to be confirmed.

One of the later posts to be filled was that of defence secretary, a role taken by Wes Streeting, whose resignation as health secretary two months ago contributed to the draining of Sir Keir Starmer's authority as prime minister.

The story of the reshuffle can best be summarised as neither of the two ministers most widely talked up as chancellor - Shabana Mahmood and Ed Miliband - getting that job, it instead going to John Healey.

And there being a pretty significant cull of the ministers closest to and most loyal to the now former prime minister: think David Lammy, Darren Jones, Peter Kyle, Lord Hermer, Steve Reed and Rachel Reeves â albeit Reeves, I am told, was offered a cabinet post but turned it down.

News.title: Who's in Andy Burnham's cabinet?
News.content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has started building his new cabinet after taking office following the resignation of Sir Keir Starmer.

Tap or click on a cabinet member in our interactive guide below to learn more about them and their role in government. The guide will be updated as new appointments are made.

News.title: Man, 28, charged with murder of Ann Widdecombe
News.content:
A 28-year-old man has been charged with the murder of Ann Widdecombe, police and prosecutors have said.

Joshua Kerry, from Rotherham in South Yorkshire, is set to appear at Westminster Magistrates' Court on Tuesday.

Counter Terrorism Policing said "determining the motivation, including any possible political motivation" remains "an active avenue" of investigation.

Kerry was initially arrested on suspicion of murder on 11 July, before being additionally arrested on 13 July on suspicion of the commission, preparation or instigation of acts of terrorism.

Widdecombe, 78, a former Conservative minister and Reform UK spokeswoman, was found dead on Thursday 9 July at her home in Haytor, Devon, having sustained serious injuries.

In a statement read outside New Scotland Yard, Laurence Taylor, head of UK Counter Terrorism Policing said: "I want to make it very clear that our investigation into [Kerry], determining his motivations and any wider activity he may have been involved in is continuing."

"As with all murder investigations, understanding the 'why' is a key part of our enquiries," he said, adding that it was "a particularly intensive and complex investigation".

Taylor said it remained the case that investigators were not looking for anyone else in connection with the incident.

He added that counter terrorism teams have gathered "a huge amount of information" over the last week, leading to more than 800 lines of enquiry.

The investigation, which remains ongoing, has been led by Counter Terrorism Policing South East, supported by Devon and Cornwall Police.

Frank Ferguson, of the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS)'s special crime and counter terrorism division, said: "Our prosecutors have worked closely with the police to establish that there is sufficient evidence to bring this case to court, and we will continue working with them as their investigation progresses."

"We remind all concerned that proceedings against the defendant are active and he has the right to a fair trial," Ferguson said.

"It is vital that there should be no reporting, commentary or sharing of information which could in anyway prejudice these proceedings."

News.title: At least 27 dead and 83 missing after passenger ferry capsizes off Guyana
News.content:
At least 27 people have drowned after a passenger ferry capsized off the coast of Guyana on Saturday night local time.

Sixty-nine people aboard the MV Barima had been rescued, Prime Minister Mark Phillips told reporters on Monday, adding 83 more remained missing.

Divers continue to search the site where the vessel capsized and people who believe their loved ones may have been on board the stricken vessel have been asked to contact the authorities.

"Our focus again is on finding people," said Phillips. "We still have hope."

An investigation into the tragedy had been launched, he said earlier.

"Let me be absolutely clear: where negligence, misconduct or criminal wrongdoing is established, those responsible will face the full force of the law," he said.

Guyana's Public Works Minister, Juan Edghill, expressed his anger at a news conference on Sunday, accusing those who operated the ferry of trying to "cheat the system".

The official registry had listed 133 as being on board the ferry, but Phillips said on Monday he was now "confident" there were 179 people.

Edghill also said the ferry's captain and at least one crew member had tested positive for cannabis.

"We have zero tolerance for members of the crew drinking or smoking while at work. And for us to have positive tests from the captain... this is serious," the minister said.

He added the captain and several of his crew had been taken into police custody.

News.title: Watch: 'My flat was turned into a brothel,' landlord tells BBC Panorama
News.content:
A BBC Panorama investigation has uncovered how organised crime gangs are exploiting the UK's private rental market - targeting properties to take over and use for their operations.

Among those featured in a new documentary is landlord and property developer Craig Shepheard, who discovered his flat was being used by a prostitution ring, run by a network in Brazil.

BBC Panorama reporter Hazel Martin also found that criminals are using fake IDs to get rental agreements.

News.title: Russian warship carried out firing exercise off Plymouth coast
News.content:
A Russian warship, shadowed by a Royal Navy vessel, carried out a live-fire artillery exercise just 40 nautical miles south of Plymouth on Monday.

The Royal Navy monitored the exercise and is continuing to "track the vessel's activity closely", a Ministry of Defence (MoD) spokesperson said.

The Russian frigate, Neustrashimy, was also being monitored by a French military aircraft which made radio contact with the warship asking it to clarify its intentions, the BBC has been told.

Prior to opening fire, the BBC was also told that the Russian warship informed the Royal Navy Offshore Patrol Vessel, HMS Tyne, of its intention to conduct gunnery activity.

The Russian warship requested that that HMS Tyne reposition to a safer distance, which it did. The Russian live-fire exercise took place in international waters and lasted for 30 minutes.

The incident will be a reminder for the new prime minister of increased Russian naval activity near UK waters in recent months. UK defence sources would not comment on whether the incident might have been timed to coincide with the start of Andy Burnham's premiership.

Last month, Royal Marine Commandos boarded a Russian "shadow fleet" oil tanker in the English Channel in a six-hour operation which was the first of its kind by UK armed forces.

Also in June, a British couple in international waters in the English Channel came across a Russian warship - Admiral Grigorovich - 23 miles (37km) off the Isle of Wight.

The frigate fired warning shots as Jane and Alan Kelvey sailed their yacht on what Russia's defence ministry said had been a "dangerous approach". However, the couple said they were "not on a collision course".

Russian warships regularly pass through international waters in the Channel, which are separate from UK and French territorial waters.

Additional reporting by Ella Kipling

News.title: Is UK facing drought for second summer in a row?
News.content:
Summer so far has been exceptionally hot and dry across much of the UK, with three widespread heatwaves and the longest run of dry days in central England since 1995.

England, Wales and eastern Scotland have been the driest areas over recent weeks, and this follows a very dry spring in similar regions.

Very little rainfall is forecast through this week for most places, with only a few light showers possible, mainly close to coasts.

As we head through the second half of summer, what are the longer range predictions, and are we heading into drought for the second summer in a row?

News.title: Bumblebees are struggling in UK heatwaves - but you can help them
News.content:
UK bumblebees could suffer sharp falls in their numbers as heatwaves become more frequent and intense, new analysis suggests.

The findings - shared exclusively with the BBC - draw on data from the Bumblebee Conservation Trust's long-running national monitoring scheme, which shows a decline in populations after the record-breaking heat of 2022.

The warning comes as Britain emerges from a third heatwave in as many months, with temperatures in the range where bumblebees can struggle to fly without overheating.

Bumblebees are not just one of the best-loved sights of the British summer, they are also vital pollinators, helping sustain wildflowers and some of the crops we rely on.

News.title: Ofcom launches investigation into Married at First Sight UK
News.content:
Married at First Sight UK is facing renewed pressure after the broadcast regulator launched an official investigation into the hit Channel 4 reality TV show.

In a statement on Monday, Ofcom said it was investigating "a fairness and privacy complaint" about the prime-time show.

In May, a BBC Panorama investigation revealed rape allegations from two female cast members on the show - allegations the men involved deny.

An Ofcom fairness or privacy complaint can be lodged by individuals who participated in TV or radio programmes. Complaints like these usually relate to claims of being treated unfairly or having unwarranted infringements of privacy on programmes.

It is understood the watchdog is considering a complaint of unjust or unfair treatment from a cast member of Married at First Sight UK.

At least one other cast member previously complained to Ofcom about their treatment on the show, but the watchdog dismissed their complaint as it found the broadcaster had no case to answer.

An Ofcom spokesperson said such complaints are considered "on a case-by-case basis through a detailed and careful assessment process".

News.title: South East Water hosepipe ban to affect 2.4 million people
News.content:
A hosepipe ban has been expanded to cover 2.4 million people across the south of England after record-breaking temperatures.

South East Water's ban now includes parts of Sussex, Surrey, Hampshire and Berkshire - an extra 1.5m customers. A ban in parts of Kent has been in force since 3 July.

Douglas Whitfield, SEW's water supply director, said it was "deeply sorry" and "incredibly grateful to everyone helping us protect water supplies" after exceptionally hot and dry weather.

Eastbourne MP Josh Babarinde said he was "appalled", calling it "the direct result of years of underinvestment in upgrading infrastructure and building resilience".

Under the restrictions, households in the affected area will be banned from using a hosepipe in their homes for tasks including cleaning, filling ponds, or watering plants.

The ban will officially come in from 00:01 BST on Saturday, but SEW has asked its customers to abide by the restrictions immediately.

The UK record for the hottest day in June was broken for a third day in a row last month, with temperatures reaching 37.3C, the Met Office said.

News.title: Sara Sharif killer wants inquest with jury
News.content:
The woman who murdered her stepdaughter Sara Sharif has asked for the inquest into her death to be held in front of a jury.

Beinash Batool and Sara's father Urfan Sharif were jailed for life in 2024 after the 10-year-old was found dead at the family home in Woking.

She had been violently abused in a "campaign of torture" lasting two years.

Bite marks, an iron burn and scalding from hot water were among dozens of injuries found on her body in a post-mortem examination.

On Monday, Batool's lawyer Dr Anton van Dellen said jurors would help determine if Sara was failed by people who were scared of being accused of racism.

"This is just the type of judgement where a diverse local jury would provide a helpful perspective," he added.

A review into the 10-year-old's death found that services in Surrey failed to properly investigate why Sara started wearing a hijab - that covered her bruising - for "fear of causing offence".

Neighbours also said they were worried about "being branded as being racist" if they reported concerns.

News.title: Ryanair profits drop as Iran war puts off passengers and lifts fuel costs
News.content:
Ryanair's profits have fallen sharply as war in the Middle East sent jet fuel prices soaring and customers reluctant to book flights.

The Irish airline's pre-tax profits dropped 34% to â¬593m (Â£503m) between April and June while sales were flat as the company was forced to cut fares to stimulate demand.

Ryanair also said it expects summer fares to be slightly lower than last year due to "consumer hesitancy" around air travel.

The price of fuelling a plane has jumped since the US and Israel launched strikes against Iran in February and while Ryanair said it had "hedged" or struck deals for the most future fuel costs, those not included in these arrangements had more than doubled.

Crude oil prices hit $90 (Â£67) a barrel for the first time in a month on Monday, before falling back slightly, after a weekend of intense exchanges of fire between the US and Iran.

Traffic through the Strait of Hormuz â an essential route for global oil and gas supplies â has ground to a halt.

An interim peace deal last month brought some respite to oil and energy prices, but they spiked again as negotiations broke down and fighting resumed.

The airline warned that its results for the year will be "highly sensitive" to external factors such as conflict escalation in the Middle East and Ukraine as well as the price of unhedged jet fuel.

Fares for for the key summer period between July and September are on track to be "modestly" lower than last year, with many passengers booking closer to departure than normal.

The firm's finance chief, Neil Sorahan, said flights on its popular Mediterranean routes were still full. "People [are] as keen to get away as ever, albeit booking just a little bit later," he said.

Between April and June, Ryanair's revenue ticked up 1% to â¬4.4bn.

While passenger numbers rose 6% to 6.1 million- helped by the Easter holiday in April - fares fell by 6% as the airline reduced fares to entice flyers concerned about the Iran war.

Ryanair's share price fell 5% on Monday.

Russ Mould, investment director at AJ Bell, said Ryanair was in a better position than many of its rivals, but nonetheless "visibility is worse than San Francisco airport when the fog sets in".

"The renewed escalation in hostilities in the Middle East is unhelpful and without a lasting resolution, challenging times for the airline and travel space look set to continue."

News.title: Kevin Keegan, Liverpool footballer who managed England and Newcastle United, dies aged 75
News.content:
Former England captain and manager Kevin Keegan has died at the age of 75, seven weeks after he revealed he had been diagnosed with stage four cancer, his family have confirmed.

One of English football's most decorated players, Keegan enjoyed spells at Scunthorpe United, Liverpool, Hamburg, Southampton and Newcastle during an illustrious playing career.

He later went on to manage Newcastle, Fulham, England and Manchester City.

Keegan revealed he had stage four cancer in June, which is the most advanced stage of cancer and means the disease has spread to other parts of the body.

His family initially disclosed he was battling the disease in January, after he had "further evaluation of ongoing abdominal symptoms" in hospital.

A statement on behalf of the Keegan family said he was "surrounded by his wife and daughters in his final moments".

"Kevin, a double Ballon d'Or winner, was a much loved husband, father and grandfather," it continued.

"The family would like to thank Kevin's incredible medical team for all their support. This is a hugely difficult time and they are requesting space and privacy."

Newcastle United paid tribute, describing Keegan as "one of the most iconic, influential and deeply loved figures in our club's history".

The club statement added: "Kevin was more than a legendary footballer and manager. He was the beating heart of Newcastle United for generations of supporters.

"Kevin's impact will not be measured by appearances or results. It will live on in the memories he created with club and country, the dreams he inspired wherever he went, and the generations of supporters around the world who fell in love with football because of him."

Liverpool, for whom Keegan played for between 1971 and 1977, said Keegan's "indomitable spirit and remarkable contribution will be forever etched in our history and his legacy will live on".

Hamburg said football had lost one of its "defining figures" and they would always "cherish" his memory, while Fulham said Keegan "forged a strong connection" with the fans, who would "forever hold wonderful memories" of his short time at the club.

Keegan's first club, Scunthorpe, described him as "one of the best players of his generation", with an "inspirational demeanour" and "brilliant personality".

England and Manchester City both offered their condolences to the Keegan family, with the latter describing him as "one of the most iconic and fondly remembered figures in English football".

The Three Lions will celebrate Keegan's life when they host Spain in a Uefa Nations League match at Wembley on 26 September.

News.title: Ofcom unable to take further legal action against suicide forum
News.content:
Ofcom said it is unable to take further legal action against a pro-suicide forum which campaigners say has been linked to over 130 UK deaths.

The regulator said, external the site had blocked access for the "vast majority" of UK users, and it had "no further legal routes available" under the Online Safety Act.

But it accepted people would still be able to access the forum by using a VPN, which hides your location online.

Andy Burrows, chief executive of the Molly Rose Foundation, said the decision to take no further legal action would "result in more lost lives" and that announcing it on the day a new prime minister was named showed "an utter lack of moral courage".

In response, an Ofcom spokesperson said it had made the decision a "matter of days ago" following "months of work to exhaust all possible legal routes".

They said bereaved families were informed of the decision this morning after being contacted last week.

"In that context, we do not consider it appropriate to delay the announcement further to accommodate today's political developments," they said.

Meanwhile, Ofcom enforcement director Suzanne Cater said the regulator had used its powers "to the fullest extent possible".

"We'll continue to monitor the forum closely to check the geoblock remains in place," she said.

The geoblock means people based in the UK are unable to access the site, unless they mask their location through a VPN or similar means.

Ofcom said it was working with the government to explore whether its enforcement powers should be strengthened.

In particular, this concerns its ability to get a website blocking order through the courts, which would legally mandate internet service providers in the UK to block the website.

The regulator says it has reached the limit of what it can legally do under the Online Safety Act because the forum has implemented the geoblock.

The BBC has approached the government for comment.

News.title: 'Scrutiny' needed over baby's death, court hears
News.content:
Preston had been taken to Blackpool Victoria Hospital three times before his death and seen by a "battery of professionals" including medical staff, social workers and welfare officers from various bodies.

Wilson told the hearing an inquest had initially been opened shortly after Preston's death but was then suspended while police investigated, culminating in the trial and conviction of his adoptive parents.

Wilson said he had to consider whether an inquest should continue, given "relevant issues" had already been heard during the eight-week criminal trial.

However, while he said he would not make a final decision on Monday, subject to submissions from lawyers for other public bodies, it was "highly likely" one would take place, probably in the autumn of next year.

He said: "I feel there's sufficient reason to resume. There are acts and omissions of public authorities that need to be scrutinised in a public hearing in which Preston's family can participate.

"It's clearly going to be a wide-ranging inquiry."

The coroner said he was aware there had been calls for a public inquiry, but his role meant that was not a matter for himself to consider, but to proceed on the basis of whether or not to hold an inquest.

The court heard Oldham Safeguarding Children's Partnership, had resumed a review into Preston's death, following its suspension for the criminal trial to take place.

This review was likely only to be completed by January 2027, and the inquest cannot be held before then, the court heard.

Much of the hearing dealt with which people or public bodies should be legally represented at any inquest.

They included Preston's biological mother and grandmother, Sara and Debbie Davey, neither of whom were present for the hearing but were represented by lawyers in court.

Preston was born while his mother was in custody and a place in a mother and baby unit in prison was refused, the court heard.

Instead, he was taken from her by a court order from Oldham Council and placed with temporary adoptive parents before being adopted by Varley and McGowan.

News.title: Fire crews to remain at Arthur's Seat for days after blaze
News.content:
Firefighters are expected to remain at Arthur's Seat in Edinburgh "for a couple of days" following a large blaze on Sunday evening.

Small plumes of smoke could still be seen on Monday morning along Salisbury Crags and large swathes of vegetation below the cliff face had been burned black.

Six fire engines were sent to tackle the the grassfire on the slope between the Scottish Parliament and St Leonard's, with crews working overnight to douse the flames and dampen hotspots.

The Scottish Fire and Rescue Service (SFRS) said there were "no reported casualties" but Police Scotland said Queen's Drive, the road that encircles the Holyrood Park hills, remained closed to all vehicles.

It is the second fire in the last three months at the landmark, an ancient extinct volcano that offers panoramic views of the Scottish capital.

A Very High risk of wildfire warning for the central Highlands, southern and eastern Scotland has been extended to Friday as warm weather is forecast to continue.

The warning was extended by the SFRS, in conjunction with the Scottish Wildfire Forum (SWF).

With his own sitcom, a thriving stand-up career and various films in the works, Sasha Nezlobin was one of the biggest comedy names in Russia. But in the space of just a few months, he went from writing a new show to fleeing his home country and the wrath of Vladimir Putin.

In February 2022, the comedian found himself frantically packing a suitcase to escape Moscow with his family. He had criticised Russia’s prosecution of those speaking out against the war with Ukraine – and Nezlobin, his wife and their young daughter were headed for the last direct flight to New York before Europe and North America closed their airspace to Russian planes.

“At the airport, the lady at the check-in counter asked me, ‘Are you leaving forever?’” Nezlobin says. “It was a really honest conversation and I told her, ‘I don’t know for now,’ because it was true.”

Four years on, 42-year-old Nezlobin and his family – who now live in Los Angeles – are yet to return to their lives in Russia and most likely never will. He has watched too many of his fellow comedians face jail time for jokes they’ve made. Instead, he’s heading to Edinburgh’s Fringe Festival to tell his story, performing a show for the first-ever time in the English language.

open image in gallery Sasha Nezlobin was a successful comedy star in Russia ( Alexander Nezlobin )

“I started writing about it and it really helped me,” he says. “The best advice I was given was to write stand-up and bring your pain into it – you can release yourself of it.”

Back in Russia, Nezlobin was a certified TV personality – shooting to stardom as a cast member on sketch show Comedy Club. “The closest thing to it is Saturday Night Live in the United States. It was a big, big show,” he explains. The comic later starred in his own sitcom, Nezlob, before moving into writing and directing with the 2016 comedy Groom and supernatural comedy Doomsday in 2022.

Months before Doomsday started airing in Russia, Putin announced plans to invade Ukraine, despite having promised not to attack Russia’s Eastern European neighbour. Thousands of troops began mobilising, European countries introduced sanctions and Moscow descended into panic. Not only was Nezlobin nervous about being unable to leave the country, but just days before, he had signed an anti-war letter addressed to Putin and shared a post on Instagram criticising the invasion along with other comedians. He later edited the post after Russia criminalised the making of anti-war statements. “There is no call to action here,” the post currently reads. “I just want peace. Please.”

Two days after posting on Instagram, Nezlobin took one of the last direct flights out of Russia to New York with his daughter, who was just nine years old at the time. Having flown a few times to the States for gigs, the comedian had his green card ready and had prepared documents for his family beforehand, in case a quick getaway was needed. He managed to sell their Moscow flat extremely quickly, too. Once his wife joined them via several connecting flights to the States, they eventually settled in Los Angeles, jobless and with a limited knowledge of the English language.

“It could be better, but it could be way worse,” he says of his new life in America. “For me, the US is a good country because it was built up by immigrants and there are many here. People are not questioning where you’re from because they understand that even with my limited language, I can be an American citizen. There are many different accents here and I love this country because I grew up watching Hollywood movies and American comedies.”

open image in gallery Nezlobin on ‘Evening Urgant’ – a late night chat show in Russia ( Evening Urgant )

Since relocating, Nezlobin has continued his comedy career by performing stand-up for the Russian-speaking diaspora across North America, gigging in Boston, Las Vegas and Philadelphia among other states – and he hasn’t stopped speaking out about Putin’s censorship laws.

“In my performances, I joke about how posting something like ‘stop the war’ on Instagram – just three words – can put you in prison for seven years in Russia, but cases of sexual assault only get five years,” he says, adding that he also highlights how Trump “trying to control the media and attacking LGBTQ community rights is what Putin did when he came into power”.

Despite being over 6,000 miles away from Moscow, Nezlobin is still facing backlash from pro-Kremlin groups over his comments. “A huge religious community in Russia asked the general prosecutor to investigate my jokes for LGBTQ propaganda as it’s recognised as a terrorist organisation there. It is so stupid,” Nezlobin said. The comic is now considered an “enemy of Russia” by these groups, who’ve leaked his contact details – and those of other anti-war comedians and journalists – online.

“Angry people started to call. They want to ruin our lives,” he sighs. “They are doing it to stop us from doing well.”

The comic fears what might happen to him and his family if they do move back to Russia – particularly after watching fellow comedians go behind bars. In February, stand-up comic Artemy Ostanin was sentenced to five years and nine months in jail for a joke seen by pro-Kremlin activists as mocking a soldier who lost his legs in Ukraine, despite the performer not explicitly mentioning the war.

open image in gallery Sasha Nezlobin is telling his story in a new show at Edinburgh Fringe Festival ( Sasha Nezlobin )

“I think I have to wait a couple more years to see what is happening,” he says. “In the past, during the time of the USSR, we’ve had writers and performers escape Russia but when they’ve returned, they’ve been put in prisons and killed so I’m not sure. I hope for my wife and daughter it will be safe.”

For now, Nezlobin is enjoying the freedoms that come with life in the States – especially for his daughter, who is now 13. “In Russia, there is propaganda about how American schools have a stupid education system but what I see is that it’s good for my daughter,” he says.

“She’s doing really well and she laughs at my English. She asks me to stop talking in public because she thinks my accent is so horrible that we could be deported, which is funny.”

While his story may be extraordinary, he’s hoping that people will relate to the everyday challenges that he’s faced along the way when he performs at the Fringe and across Europe next month.

“All of us go through our own struggles and have lost something in our lives. It could be a friend, a parent or a business,” he says. “I lost my country but I haven’t lost myself.”

Sasha Nezlobin: I’m Fine is on at Edinburgh Fringe Festival’s Pleasance Dome (10 Dome) from 5 until 31 August (but not 15, 16, 17 or 18)

While the attention on Adam Ramsay-Peaty has not wavered, the athlete himself is much changed.

It marks two years since the 31-year-old narrowly missed out on a third consecutive 100m breaststroke Olympic gold at Paris 2024, and while he will be back in the pool at a major championships this summer, his life looks completely different.

Now married and expecting a child due in early December with model Holly Ramsay-Peaty, daughter of chef Gordon, the swimmer has also relocated to London for training and to be nearer the in-laws.

open image in gallery Adam Ramsay-Peaty married Holly in December ( Jordan Pettitt/PA Wire )

With those changes have come their own share of tabloid drama, but this matured version of Ramsay-Peaty would prefer to take any of the expectation that comes with being a big name and do the talking in the pool at Glasgow 2026.

open image in gallery Adam Ramsay-Peaty hopes to do his talking in the pool this summer ( PA Wire )

“Pressure can be given to anyone, but it's probably best in my hands because the more pressure I'm under, the better I perform,” he said.

“At the same time, you need a strategy for managing the noise and we probably haven't done that as well as we could, but I'll make sure the swimming does the talking.

“We can't control every variable in life, but I can stand behind the blocks and not really care about what people's opinions are.

“Being at peace with a 100m or 50m breaststroke race is a beautiful place to be. Nothing else matters in that moment. That's the beauty of sport. If you can find that state of mind, it's an incredible place to be.

open image in gallery Adam Peaty already has four Commonwealth Games gold medals ( Getty )

“That's the Adam people should see – the racer. Everything else is my private life.”

The spotlight will shine brightly for different reasons when he travels up to Glasgow for the first championships since Paris 2024.

With gymnast Max Whitlock ruled out of Team England’s efforts in the Scottish second city, Ramsay-Peaty will likely find himself as the leading face of his nation.

And while it is not a new position for a man who has led British swimming’s efforts for the best part of a decade, his new outlook is also playing its part in shaping his role at a fourth Commonwealth Games.

open image in gallery Adam Ramsay-Peaty remains the face of British swimming ( Getty )

“As one of the older athletes on the team, you've got a chance to share experiences, but you've also got a duty of care towards the younger swimmers,” he said.

“Not everyone is going to race how they want to. Some will swim out of their skin and others will have a few shockers. That's just sport.

“Being a father has enabled me not just to sympathise because I've been through it, but to empathise if someone's experience is different.

“The love and kindness I can show now is very different to the person I was from 2014 onwards.”

Setting aside ego cannot be easy for one of the best athletes of a generation.

open image in gallery Adam Ramsay-Peaty was denied by the barest of margins in the final of the men’s 100 metres breaststroke at the Paris Olympics ( PA Wire )

The three-time Olympic gold medallist was struggling with coronavirus and, self-admittedly, some complacency when he narrowly missed out in the French capital.

But at his first championships since, this new version of Ramsay-Peaty is ready to open the chapter on his end goal of LA 2028 Olympic Games.

“I want these Commonwealth Games to be a springboard and to come away confident in my ability to race the best in the world,” said the 31-year-old.

“Paris 2024 was bittersweet. I'd spent 18 months getting back after the breakdown and a difficult period in 2023. I was in a great place physically, but then I caught COVID-19 just before the championships.

“Now it's about putting that right. Did ego play a part? Did complacency play a part in 2024? Potentially. But now it's about bringing everything back down, focusing on the details and enhancing the performance.

open image in gallery The swimmer’s perspective has changed in recent years ( PA Wire )

“As an athlete, I see the sport completely differently now. I don't see success as medals any more. That's not defeatist, it's probably the opposite.

“Success for me is coming away from Glasgow knowing I've done absolutely everything I possibly could to finish as high as I can. If I look after the process, the outcome will take care of itself.”

By anyone else’s standards, Paris 2024 would not have been a failure. Ramsay-Peaty won Olympic silver, just 0.02 seconds behind Italy’s Nicolo Martinenghi.

But with six Olympic medals, eight world titles, 16 European titles and four Commonwealth Games titles, normal has never been Ramsay-Peaty’s playing field.

And through a decade of success that has seen him break 14 world records, the Commonwealth Games continue to play a formative role in what comes next.

“If my career was a book, the Commonwealth Games would be very definitive chapters,” he explained.

“Now we're towards the back of the book and I know that, so I want to make sure the book is written the way I want it.

open image in gallery Adam Ramsay-Peaty is back at the Commonwealth Games 12 years after announcing his arrival as a force ( Getty )

“I'd like to get to Glasgow as a full-circle moment from my first one in 2014, when I beat Cameron van der Burgh, and see what we can come away with.”

Thanks to National Lottery players, more than £33million is raised every week for good causes. It’s because of you that sport, arts, heritage and community projects, as well as our athletes competing at the Glasgow 2026 Commonwealth Games, are supported across the UK.

The 27th man on the podium had a plan. Donald Trump gatecrashed the pictures of another trophy lift, lingering awkwardly as Spain celebrated their World Cup glory. There was a certain inevitability to it: Trump may have only turned up for one game in the tournament – a relief for the thousands subjected to unacceptable delays because of his unnecessary presence – but his fingerprints were all over it.

Trump was whistled and booed at the MetLife Stadium on Sunday. He nevertheless wants another World Cup final; or, more precisely, another World Cup. “I had a great idea for Gianni [Infantino],” he said. “Announce us again next time. We will be requesting it again immediately.”

Which rather ignores the fact that the next two tournaments are already allocated, neither to the United States. But why let such details get in the way of a half-baked brainwave? Trump had already said, too, that there would be a difference. “This time we would leave Canada and Mexico out,” he stated on Friday. Although if Canada does become the 51st state, perhaps that would change. Given his expansionist schemes, maybe games would also be played in the Trump Dome in Greenland, paid for by a crypto billionaire.

open image in gallery Donald Trump’s presence loomed over this World Cup ( Getty )

But if the reality is that the earliest the US could host another men’s World Cup is 2038, they will stage the women’s tournament in 2031, along with Mexico, Jamaica and Costa Rica. There are suggestions Infantino wants the 2029 Club World Cup to be held in the United States.

There are reasons why none of them should be; not without significant changes in the country. They broadly fall under three categories: the moral, the financial and the logistical.

As Russia and Qatar recognised, hosting World Cups gives legitimacy to dubious regimes. Yet neither of them did so in a year when they were at war with another country in the tournament. The American attack on a school in Iran, resulting in 168 people, mainly children, dying might constitute a war crime.

Even when sticking to football, the Iranian team was treated unfairly when it came to issues as basic as entering and leaving the US. “A disaster World Cup,” their striker Mehdi Taremi called it. Given the fondness for conflict of a president laughably given an invented Fifa peace prize, other countries could be forgiven for wondering if it is them next.

open image in gallery Trump was awarded the concocted ‘Fifa peace prize’ before the tournament even started ( Getty )

There is a sporting element to the immorality, too. When Folarin Balogun’s suspension was lifted so the United States forward could face Belgium – entirely coincidentally, after Trump phoned Infantino – it represented one of the lowest points in Fifa’s history: governmental interference and political pressure, rather than sporting merit, meant the supposed principles of fair play were abandoned.

After it succeeded – in rendering Balogun eligible, though not in the scoreline as the US were walloped 4-1 – it would probably only empower Trump to try something similar again.

There is a further aspect. The Trump administration’s values are the polar opposite of those the World Cup ought to offer, of diversity and inclusiveness, a language that “unites people” and turns “strangers into friends”, as Tom Cruise said in his bizarre speech before the World Cup final.

As many a visitor can testify after the last six weeks, the vast majority of Americans are friendly and helpful; yet 77 million voted for this monstrosity of a government. Giving them major international sporting events rewards them when the actions of the United States, from tariffs to the war in Iran, have made much of the rest of the world poorer.

open image in gallery Tom Cruise’s bizarre speech before the final addressed some of what the World Cup should stand for ( Getty )

There are other financial elements to overlook the US and not merely because the World Cup has probably bolstered a flailing tourist industry, buffeted as millions of foreigners have been repelled from visiting Trump’s United States; it would have had a greater benefit had the US administration actually let more football fans enter the country.

Fifa can trumpet that this has been the most lucrative World Cup ever, aided by more teams (48) and games (104). It has also been the greediest, using the American market to ramp up ticket prices. That has been compounded by the Trump administration and American corporate culture, all looking at football fans and seeing dollar signs as costs got extortionate. A memory is of being a mile or two from the stadium in Foxborough and seeing car-parking spots in yards being advertised for $150 and then $200; that rip-off culture needs to be addressed, not encouraged.

The logistical element relates to the sheer size of the United States; perhaps not as big as Trump would like, but still huge. Some of this tournament would inevitably have been impractical and expensive. It was compounded by bad choices and decision-making which illustrated the US authorities and Fifa, once again, put the fans last; the lack of organisation in many venues was damning.

open image in gallery The organisation at some of the venues was inadequate ( Getty )

The choice of them, and the schedule, showed a lack of consideration. Germany played three group games in Houston, Toronto and New York. Austria went from San Francisco to Dallas to Kansas City. Too few host cities were near each other.

Too few grounds were actually in the cities. Many of the stadia impressed; the locations did not. The aversion to public transport in swathes of the United States rendered some still more unsuitable. Boston was a perfect host city in every respect bar one: the ground was nowhere near Boston...

Priority should have been given to accessible stadia. There were arguably only three near enough to city centres in the United States in this World Cup: Seattle, Atlanta and Philadelphia (Toronto was a Canadian example that worked well).

Chicago opted out in part due to Fifa’s demands; yet Fifa should be looking for the right places, not just the most profitable. With Soldier Field’s central location and Chicago’s rapid-transit system, it would have been a far better Midwestern base than Kansas City, which lacked the infrastructure required.

open image in gallery Kansas City was ill-equipped to host World Cup matches ( Getty )

Fifa may be too arrogant to learn, but it could do worse than study Euro 2024, a tournament with a better ethos and feel, built on the right principles. It was imperfect at times, but the German S-Bahn and U-Bahns worked well in cities such as Berlin and Hamburg. American car culture is far from ideal for such tournaments.

Do Fifa care? Almost certainly not. Perhaps confirmation was not needed that they have lost touch with the game’s roots or its rank and file. It came anyway, partly with every indication they were Americanising the game.

A lesson should be that there are no hydration breaks unless temperatures soar, no half-time shows, no tickets for celebrities that could have gone to genuine fans. And no tournaments in the United States in the foreseeable future; not as things are, anyway.

Four Indian nationals were among 10 people killed in an alleged Russian cruise missile strike on a cargo ship leaving Ukraine's southern port of Odesa over the weekend.

India's foreign ministry said on Monday that the vessel, MV Golden Leo, was attacked on Sunday evening just as it was departing Odesa with 17 crew members, including five Indians.

The surviving Indian crew member was critically injured, the foreign ministry added.

The Ukrainian navy alleged that the vessel, flying the Guinea-Bissau flag and owned by a Turkish company, was targeted by Russian forces with three cruise missiles.

Ten people were killed, including a Ukrainian pilot, Ukraine’s Sea Ports Authority said after launching a search and rescue operation.

The ship was leaving Ukraine's maritime corridor carrying grain when it was struck, the Ukrainian navy said.

open image in gallery Photo shared by the Ukrainian navy shows the damaged cargo vessel Golden Leo after an alleged Russian missile strike in the Black Sea on 19 July 2026 ( @UA_NAVY )

India’s foreign ministry condemned the attack, calling the targeting of civilian crew members "deplorable".

“As per information available, four Indian nationals have tragically lost their lives while one is hospitalised in a critical condition. Our mission in Ukraine is closely monitoring the situation and is making every effort to extend all possible assistance to those affected,” it said in a statement.

“India condemns such attacks,” it added, “and reiterates that targeting commercial shipping and endangering innocent civilian crew members or otherwise impeding freedom of navigation and commerce is deplorable and should be avoided.”

According to the Ukrainian navy, the missiles struck the starboard side of the vessel and sparked a fire.

The ports authority said the rescue operation continued through the night into Monday, the blaze was brought under control, and eight people were rescued.

open image in gallery ( @UA_NAVY )

Ukraine’s acting foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, condemned the attack, noting that it came just hours after Russia's overnight missile and drone assault on Kyiv.

"While the world is still responding to Russia's brutal overnight attack on Kyiv, Moscow continues its campaign of terror throughout the day," Mr Sybiha said on social media.

Akhil Joyan, a 26-year-old seafarer from the southern Indian state of Kerala, was among those killed.

Joyan, who had worked as a mariner for six years, held the world record for the most rope pull-ups in half a minute, according to the Indian Express.

India has more than 300,000 seafarers employed globally, according to government data, making it one of the largest suppliers of merchant shipping workforces in the world.

Indian seafarers have been hit hard by the US-Israeli war on Iran as well as the Russian war against Ukraine. At least 10 Indian crew members have been killed in separate attacks on ships sailing through the Strait of Hormuz and the Gulf of Oman since the war in the Middle East began earlier this year.

Christopher Nolan said it would be at least three years before he made another film as the scale of The Odyssey had pushed him and his crew to “the limits” of their stamina.

The Oscar winner’s latest film, The Odyssey, an adaptation of Homer’s Greek epic, follows Odysseus’s long journey home to Ithaca after the Trojan War as he battles monsters, gods and mythical foes while his wife Penelope fends off suitors and their son Telemachus searches for him.

Matt Damon plays Odysseus, Anne Hathaway Penelope and Tom Holland Telemachus. The ensemble cast also includes Robert Pattinson as the suitor Antinous, Zendaya as Athena, Samantha Morton as Circe, Charlize Theron as Calypso, Lupita Nyong'o as Helen of Troy. Jon Bernthal, Benny Safdie, John Leguizamo, Himesh Patel, Elliot Page, Bill Irwin, and Mia Goth feature as well.

open image in gallery Matt Damon, Christopher Nolan and Anne Hathaway at the The Odyssey premiere in New York ( AP )

In a new interview, the Inception director confirmed that his fans would need to wait “at least” three years before he made a new film. It took Nolan three years to release The Odyssey after his previous film, Oppenheimer.

“I definitely hit the limits of my own stamina and everybody’s stamina, I think,” he told Today’s Kaylee Hartung.

“I mean, it’s The Odyssey, of course it should be difficult. We are not doing the job right making a film of The Odyssey if it doesn’t seem difficult.”

He had spent about two decades considering how to adapt the Greek epic before deciding the time was right, Nolan said.

“Now, I can get something made that I couldn’t otherwise get made. For me to take on Greek mythology on a big modern cinematic canvas is something that hasn’t been done.”

The Odyssey is the first feature film to be shot entirely on IMAX film cameras, made possible after the director worked with IMAX to develop lighter, quieter equipment capable of handling dialogue-heavy scenes.

open image in gallery The Odyssey is Christopher Nolan’s highest-ranked film on review aggregator Rotten Tomatoes ( Universal Pictures )

The Odyssey, released on 17 July, is Nolan’s highest-ranked film on the review aggregator Rotten Tomatoes, beating The Dark Knight, Interstellar, and The Prestige.

The Odyssey boasts a score of 95 per cent on the review aggregator, one per cent more than indie psychological drama Memento, Batman Begins and its sequel The Dark Knight.

In her five-star review of the new movie, The Independent’s Clarisse Loughrey described it as “Nolan’s best work to date”.

Nolan’s “stamp is all over the film – this is intellectual, brutalist, muscular Hollywood fare – yet it never wavers in its commitment to, and comprehension of, its source text,” she wrote. “There is not a single decision here that’s been thoughtlessly made, nor that I imagine Nolan himself couldn’t easily defend, much to the imagined chagrin of certain lawless parts of the internet.”

The Odyssey is enjoying a record-breaking theatrical debut with a $264.1m worldwide opening, including $124.5m in the US and Canada, making it the biggest global opening of Nolan’s career.

The Odyssey is screening in cinemas now.
