News.title: UK borrowing costs rise at fastest pace in G7
News.content:
Britain’s borrowing costs rose at the fastest pace in the G7 after Andy Burnham said he would take a “flexible” approach to the UK’s fiscal rules.

In his maiden speech as prime minister, Mr Burnham on Monday signalled he could bend the rules underpinning Britain’s finances, spooking financial markets fearful of higher government spending.

UK gilts – a benchmark for how much the Government pays on its debt – saw yields rise 0.08 percentage points to an eight-week high of 5.03pc for the 10-year bond. Thirty-year gilts also pushed higher.

The rise was the fastest in the G7, excluding Japan, whose markets are closed for a national holiday.

After markets closed on Monday, Mr Burnham surprised the City by picking John Healey as his next Chancellor.

Mr Healey, who quit over defence funding rising too slowly, will now be tasked with finding billions of pounds in Britain’s stretched public finances.

Shabana Mahmood, the Home Secretary, had widely been expected for the role. Ed Miliband, the former Energy Secretary, was also in contention.

Mr Healey will replace Rachel Reeves, who resigned on Monday.

The appointment of Mr Healey, a veteran of the Blair-Brown government, may calm fears in the City after Mr Burnham pledged to stretch the fiscal rules by using “flexibility” within them.

Speaking in Downing Street, Mr Burnham said: “I’ve said we’ll stick to the fiscal rules, and by that I mean the existing fiscal rules, and use obviously any flexibility within them.”

James Athey, a fund manager at Marlborough, said: “It’s not a good start because bandying around the words fiscal rules seems to be believed within government circles to be a sufficient condition to get financial markets on side, and that just misunderstands an element of the problem.”

He added that investors were watching closely for any signs that the Government will increase borrowing.

Matt Amis, investment director at Aberdeen, said Mr Burnham’s comments had “got the markets’ attention.”

He said “It just shows this week in particular the language from the Burnham administration, the new chancellor, is going to be key here. The gilt market is on edge.”

Mr Burnham, who has become the UK’s seventh prime minister in just a decade, has inherited a troubled economy as businesses grapple with low confidence and strained public finances.

Monday’s comment suggests the new prime minister will use measures to raise borrowing while keeping the additional sums off the Government’s book.

The Resolution Foundation, a think tank, said he could do this by expanding the remit of institutions like the National Wealth Fund, an arms-length government investment vehicle.

His plan to use “flexibility” in the fiscal rules comes after Ms Reeves altered the main indicator of government debt in 2024.

She tweaked the primary measure of the UK’s debt to Public Sector Net Financial Liabilities, meaning that when public financial institutions borrow to invest in a private business it does not count towards the government’s fiscal rules.

However, the think tank warned that boosting the financial capacity of public financial institutions like the National Wealth Fund by £16bn would cost around £400 million a year in debt interest.

Helen Miller, director at the Institute for Fiscal Studies, warned that challenging public finances will mean Mr Burnham will be forced to make tough choices on spending.

She said: “While chancellors come and go, the underlying fiscal constraints remain the same. Public debt, borrowing and debt-interest costs are all high. One in every £12 the government spends currently goes on debt interest.”

Higher borrowing costs threaten to increase the Government’s debt interest bill, which is already forecast to hit £111.2bn for the financial year - equivalent to 8.3pc of public spending.

Mr Burnham said he would announce a set of measures on Tuesday to give households “breathing space” to help with the cost of living.

“I will set out some of those measures starting tomorrow, including how we pay for them,” he said.

“We will help more young people into education... and we will build more council homes. That is the fair and sustainable way to bring the welfare bill down, to meet our fiscal rules and to honour our commitments on defence to our international partners.”

Mr Amis said: “Tomorrow we’re getting some cost of living news. [Burnham] said he was going to state where that funding’s come from. I think that’s key, any unfunded spending from here would get the market’s attention.”

News.title: India approves first dengue vaccine as cases surge in South Asia
News.content:
India has approved its first dengue vaccine as cases of the mosquito-borne disease surge in South Asia.

Japan’s Takeda Pharmaceutical’s dengue vaccine QDENGA has been approved by India’s drug regulator, the Centre Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO).

The global threat posed by dengue has been rising for years, as climate change, urbanisation and international travel aid the spread of the mosquitoes that transmit it.

The approval comes as hospitals across South Asia grapple with a surge in dengue infections.

In Sri Lanka, health authorities reported 2,652 new cases on Sunday alone, taking the total to 76,044 dengue cases so far this year. At least 53 people have died.

Bangladesh is also suffering a major outbreak with over 9,000 cases and 30 deaths that has piled pressure on its health system even as it battles a measles epidemic.

Dengue is transmitted to humans through the bites of infected Aedes mosquitoes.

Its symptoms include fever, severe muscle pain, and in severe cases, shock and internal bleeding that can be fatal.

Although mortality is relatively low, outbreaks place a substantial burden on health systems.

Takeda’s QDENGA jab is a live-attenuated tetravalent vaccine designed to protect against all four dengue virus serotypes. It can be given regardless of previous dengue infections.

“The approval comes at a critical time for public health, as reported dengue cases in India have increased 11-fold in the past two decades,” the company said in a statement.

News.title: Burnham’s plan to restore UK aid spending
News.content:
Andy Burnham is planning to reverse the cuts to Britain’s aid budget made by his predecessors Sir Keir Starmer and Rishi Sunak, according to reports.

A roadmap for returning the UK to spending 0.7 per cent of Gross National Income (GNI) on international aid will be drawn up as part of a major shake-up of the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO), The Independent reported.

Ed Miliband is set to be named Foreign Secretary and put in charge of overhauling Britain’s international development aims, as well as prioritising climate goals, senior Labour sources said.

The aid spending plan was absent from Mr Burnham’s brief first speech as Prime Minister, in which he pledged to end rough sleeping and bring down the welfare bill in order to fund defence and council housing.

But it follows anger within the Labour Party over what was seen as a broken manifesto promise, when Sir Keir and Rachel Reeves, the Chancellor, slashed aid spending to 0.3 per cent of GNI.

Senior Labour MPs have been lobbying for a return to the 0.7 per cent commitment, a target first established by the United Nations in the 1970s.

It has since become a key yardstick for international efforts to reduce poverty and tackle major health issues like the HIV/AIDS epidemic, vaccine access, and maternal mortality in poor countries.

News.title: The best bars and nightlife in Lyon
News.content:
While drinking in this gourmet city remains firmly rooted in the surrounding Rhône Valley’s ancient wine-growing heritage, new-gen addresses have embraced world cocktail culture in style. They’re using Lyon’s long-envied gastronomic know-how and rich bounty of local seasonal produce to create some sensational new drinks and food pairings as only the French can. Artisanal spirits meanwhile are increasingly fashionable: cornichon gin, Mezcal-fuelled soirées at chef Carla Kirsch’s gourmet tacos joint in Croix-Rousse, and the stunning Christian Drouin gin and pine-needle liqueur cocktail with stick of Comté cheese to stir I recently had at Hôtel Dieu’s Le Dôme bar all spring to mind.

Come the warmer days of spring and summer, the city’s fervent café-life spills onto pretty pavement terraces, while floating bars moored along Les Berges du Rhône (the landscaped river banks of the Rhône’s Rive Gauche or Left Bank) hum with after-dark dance parties and festivities. Clubbing remains fairly mainstream.

News.title: How to have the perfect holiday in France’s gastronomic capital
News.content:
Calling all bon vivants. This is your city. Within seconds of tucking into a traditional andouillette (tripe sausage) or modern vegetarian cuisine in a jam-packed bistro, admiring fine art in a Renaissance abbey, or getting delightfully lost in a traboule (secret passageway) used by 19th-century silk weavers, you’ll quickly realise that Lyon is a city that knows how to live well.

Enthralling, cinematic and richly storied, after living here for 10 years, I still find myself being surprised by a walled garden I never knew, a fresque (wall mural) suddenly popping up on a riverfront wall, a new museum or river boat route.

Street-smart Romans first spotted the city’s extraordinary topography, founding Lugdunum (Lyon’s predecessor) in 43BC on the sunny slopes of Fourvière. And to this day, this basilica-crowned hill above Lyon’s quaint Unesco-listed Old Town (Vieux Lyon) is the perfect perch for clocking the mighty Rhône and Saône rivers that wend their way so gracefully through the centre.

The city’s quays, landscaped with peaceful water gardens and floating bars, buzz night and day – while culture lovers can explore a bounty of museums. Then there’s the gastronomy: among France’s finest, thanks to the unfaltering creativity and sass of city chefs, both past and present.

News.title: The 16 best things to do in Lyon
News.content:
Few dedicated foodies make the pilgrimage to Lyon without dining once chez Paul Bocuse, be it at the late chef’s mythical, out-of-town gastronomic temple in Collonges-au-Mont d’Or (which lost one of its three stars in 2020, having held three since 1965) or at the more affordable Comptoir Paul Bocuse inside landmark covered market Halles de Lyon Paul Bocuse. Across the street, admire a larger-than-life portrait of the iconic chef, frescoed onto the side of a building. Inside the market, the moules glacées (cold mussel ‘soup’) at oyster and shellfish specialist Maison Merle and a gooey round of Saint Marcellin cheese from Fromagerie La Mère Richard are other local legends. Avoid buying fruit and veg here unless you have to – weekly outdoor food markets elsewhere in the city are cheaper.

To sample future talent in the Lyonnais kitchen, mingle with students over lunch, dinner or drinks and live music at La Commune – an innovative food court that hosts chefs aspiring to open their own restaurant in Lyon. Resident chefs cook up a storm at La Commune for maximum six months, meaning an ever-changing rollcall of epicurean excitement at this unique culinary incubator.

To extend the experience further afield, consider a road trip along a section of the Vallée de la Gastronomie, stretching 620km (385 miles). In Lyon, the gourmet route delves into the secrets behind chef Joseph Viola’s award-winning duck foie gras and sweetbread pâté en croûte (think French-posh pork pie) and the city’s distinctive offal-based bouchon (Lyonnais bistro) cuisine.

Sports.title: Liverpool can only make ONE specific signing thanks to Premier League rule
Sports.content:
Liverpool can only make ONE specific signing thanks to Premier League rule

Liverpool could find it a tad tough to make new signings in the window this summer

View 3 Images (Image: Andrew Powell, Liverpool FC via Getty Images)

Liverpool's recruitment team is staring down a logistical headache during this summer's transfer window, as current squad limits mean they have space to register just one more senior non-homegrown player. The Premier League strictly mandates that a maximum of 17 spots within a 25-man senior squad can be allocated to overseas talent.

‌



As things currently stand, the Anfield outfit could easily completely max out their 25-man squad, boasting a breakdown of nine homegrown individuals alongside 16 non-homegrown players.

‌



If they wish to bring in multiple international reinforcements, the Reds' front office will have to pull off some highly strategic squad management, and likely facilitate a few departures, in the coming months.

‌



The nine homegrown players currently registered at Liverpool are: Joe Gomez, Curtis Jones, Harvey Elliott, Conor Bradley, Stefan Bajcetic, James McConnell, Vitezslav Jaros, Jeremie Frimpong (who qualifies through his time at Manchester City's academy) and Freddie Woodman.

The club's 16 non-homegrown players comprise: Alisson Becker, Giorgi Mamardashvili, Virgil van Dijk, Kostas Tsimikas, Milos Kerkez, Wataru Endo, Florian Wirtz, Dominik Szoboszlai, Alexis Mac Allister, Ryan Gravenberch, Alexander Isak, Cody Gakpo, Federico Chiesa, Calvin Ramsay, Hugo Ekitike and new arrival Victor Munoz.

All 37 World Cup pundits ranked as BBC vs ITV winner decided and unexpected star emerges READ MORE :

According to the Premier League, a homegrown player is defined as someone who, regardless of nationality or age, has been registered with any club affiliated to The Football Association or the Football Association of Wales for a period, whether continuous or not, of three complete seasons, or 36 months, prior to their 21st birthday, or the conclusion of the season in which they turn 21.

‌



Regulations stipulate that players who will be classified as under-21s for the 2026/27 season are those born on or after January 1 2005.

View 3 Images Rio Ngumoha during the Premier League game between Liverpool and Brentford. (Image: Jack Thomas/Getty Images)

Rio Ngumoha, Trey Nyoni and new recruit Jeremy Jacquet remain on the entirely unrestricted Under-21 list owing to the fact they were born on or after January 1 2005. While it appears challenging for Andoni Iraola to bolster his squad this summer, the Under-21 Loophole serves as a significant get-out clause.

‌



This means Liverpool can still purchase as many foreign players as they wish this summer, provided those players were born on or afterJanuary 2005 1. Under-21 players do not require registration on the senior 25-man squad list and sidestep the 17-player non-homegrown cap.

For instance, should Liverpool sign 19-year-old Yan Diomande from RB Leipzig, born in November 2006, it would have no bearing whatsoever on their remaining slots. The club could additionally still manage to bring in multiple senior foreign players, so long as they sell, loan out, or de-register players currently occupying those 16 slots.

The likes of Federico Chiesa, Wataru Endo, Alisson Becker, Giorgi Mamardashvili and even Cody Gakpo have all been linked with departures from Anfield this summer. Each time a player moves on, a brand new senior non-homegrown slot becomes available.

‌



There is also a common misconception that a club must field eight homegrown players to fill the remaining spots in their squad. This is not the case in the Premier League, though UEFA do stipulate a fixed number of "locally trained players" in the group.

View 3 Images Harvey Elliott in training with Liverpool's U21s ahead of the start of pre-season (Image: Getty Images)

With Elliott, McConnell, Ramsay, Jones and Bajcetic all facing uncertain prospects at Anfield this summer, however, the Reds may also need to bolster their homegrown quota.

‌



A solution does exist, with 21 homegrown-eligible players currently on the club's books. Yet few of those, if any at this point, appear ready to step up to first-team level.

Under Premier League regulations, though, without offloading players or omitting someone from their squad list, Liverpool can only make one further senior signing before hitting the maximum permitted 17 non-homegrown players allowed within their 25-man squad.

Sports.title: 'Wayne Rooney wants Man Utd job – but he's already found the ideal role for himself'
Sports.content:
'Wayne Rooney wants Man Utd job – but he's already found the ideal role for himself'

Ex-Manchester United star Wayne Rooney has hinted at a return to management after spells with Derby and Birmingham City

View 3 Images Wayne Rooney has been a hit on the BBC this summer (Image: BBC)

Wayne Rooney may harbour ambitions of working at Manchester United in the dugout, but it's clear he has found his niche elsewhere: in punditry. United's all-time top scorer has been something of a revelation across the BBC's World Cup coverage this summer.

‌



His no-nonsense approach, coupled with a down-to-earth take on the game, has won him a legion of fans. While Rooney clearly has the know-how should he wish to step back into management, it's perhaps the punditry life that best suits the former Everton striker.

‌



It's fair to say that Rooney's managerial career didn't hit the highs the Liverpudlian would have envisaged for himself. Spells at Derby, Birmingham, DC United and Plymouth Argyle saw him fail to claim any silverware, while he oversaw the Rams' relegation to League One in 2022.

‌



Previously, Rooney said he would only return to coaching if he was offered a position among Michael Carrick's coaching staff at Manchester United.

Rooney told BBC Sport: "Of course, I've never closed doors and never say never, but at the moment – where I am now, where my head space is – I wouldn't."

‌



Gabby Logan escapes wrath of annoyed viewers after BBC makes change for World Cup final READ MORE :

Pressed on if he would join Carrick at United, he added: "Of course I would. It's a no-brainer. I'm not begging a job here by the way. Just so everyone knows, if I was asked to go in of course I would."

Ever since turning to a role in the media in several years ago, he impressed with his savvy takes and bagged a role on Match of the Day in 2025.

Would the ex-England star really wish to trade in life in the media for the stress of the touchline? There are many on social media hoping he doesn't, judging by their reaction to Rooney's role as an analyst.

‌



"Wayne has been spot on on a lot of things lately. This is the best version of him," one fan posted on X. Another added: "Wayne Rooneys [sic] review of the half time show was worth every penny of my licence fee." A third said: "A real revelation of this World Cup has been Wayne Rooney's skill as a pundit."

View 3 Images Wayne Rooney on the BBC's coverage of Mexico vs England (Image: BBC)

The affection for Rooney perhaps stems from his ability to call it as he sees. He's not afraid to say what many are thinking, a virtue in a media landscape that can prioritise its relationship to top stars and managers over dropping some home truths.

‌



Such unfiltered honesty can sometimes manifest itself as being offensive for the sake of it, but this isn't Rooney's style.

Case in point: The former Everton forward won a few more fans on Sunday night during the BBC's coverage of the World Cup with a take that was funny, relatable, but not uncouth.

After the 27-minute long half-time show from the likes of Justin Bieber, Rooney said: "I'll be honest, mine (highlight) was when it finished. I like lot of those artists but I thought it was crap."

‌



There is a desire among football fans to see ex-players who have scaled the heights of the game, such as Rooney, rather than TikTok and YouTube stars on their televisions. While many amateur tacticians have plenty to offer, nothing can quite replicate the thoughts of someone who has battled it out for 90 minutes at the likes of Old Trafford or Anfield.

Former Liverpool midfielder Graeme Souness, an ex-player whose punditry was also praised for its unflinching nature, is a fan.

View 3 Images Wayne Rooney lasted just 15 games with Birmingham City (Image: Getty Images)

‌



"I like listening to Wayne Rooney as a pundit because he talks common sense," Souness told The Daily Mail. "I love Wayne Rooney as a player, and I like to listen to him – he has got authority, so I can listen to him. Some of the other pundits, I turn the sound down."

While the dugout could still hold a place for Rooney, for now, he has found his calling. Speaking to the BBC in August 2025, he gave a truthful appraisal of his skills as a pundit.

As expected, it was harsh but fair. "I think I'm quite fair and honest really - that is the only way to be," he said. "I say this as a player, a manager and now as a pundit - it's the same values.

Article continues below

"The fans aren't stupid. If you expect me to sit there and try and sugar-coat things which fans can see, I don't think I should be doing it."

Sports.title: Man Utd’s failed transfers for five-time Champions League winner and two World Cup heroes
Sports.content:
Man Utd’s failed transfers for five-time Champions League winner and two World Cup heroes

Manchester United are continuing to make moves in the summer transfer window ahead of the upcoming Premier League campaign

View 6 Images Michael Carrick is working hard on transfers (Image: Kirill KUDRYAVTSEV / AFP via Getty Images)

Manchester United notably let a future World Cup winner and one of England's most lethal strikers escape their grasp. The club have overseen some remarkable transfers down the years, attracting many successful players to Old Trafford.

‌



However, United have watched some promising talents choose other Premier League clubs and further afield. Michael Carrick has secured deals for Andrey Santos, Karl Darlow and Youri Tielemans this summer.

‌



Talks with Atalanta's Ederson hit a roadblock after a medical flagged up knee issues. Carrick is determined to prevent any more transfer setbacks as he assembles a squad capable of competing for trophies.

‌



Here, Mirror Football looks at some of the botched transfers at United, including a Ballon d'Or winner and World Cup champion.

FOLLOW OUR MAN UTD FB PAGE! Latest United news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

Lisandro Martinez in floods of tears as Man Utd star suffers World Cup final agony READ MORE :

Ronaldinho

United came within touching distance of a £9million swoop for Ronaldinho from Paris Saint-Germain in 2003. The Brazil star had shone in France, recording 44 goal contributions across 77 outings.

‌



The midfielder was viewed as David Beckham's successor, who appeared destined for a move to Spain. Barcelona had opened discussions with the England skipper over a £30m transfer and Real Madrid were also circling.

View 6 Images Ronaldinho almost joined United (Image: Denis Doyle/Getty Images)

Madrid ultimately secured Beckham for around £25m, yet Barca managed to swoop in and snatch Ronaldinho from under United's noses. United were "99.9% certain" the World Cup winner would sign but the Spanish giants pipped them to his signature for £25.5m.

‌



The Brazilian would go on to claim the Ballon d'Or in recognition of his outstanding performances in Spain.

John Obi Mikel

John Obi Mikel snubbed United in favour of Chelsea, despite holding talks with Sir Alex Ferguson and even penning a pre-contract. Speaking on TNT Sports' What I Wore, the Champions League winner said: "My first trial was with Manchester United. After the Under-17 tournament, I went there for trials. And then United thought, 'Spend two, three months with us, and then go back home, and come back. And when you become 18, you can sign a professional contract.'

"So I went back home and then Chelsea heard about the whole thing, that I was back home. And they sent an agent to Nigeria to come and get me to go to trials at Chelsea. I went to trials at Chelsea and they liked me and wanted me to sign. So they thought, 'Okay, we're not going to make the same mistake as United by sending you back home. We're going to send you to Norway'. United went to find out where I was, and then they sent an agent to come to Oslo.

‌



View 6 Images John Obi Mikel's United move was all but confirmed before the Blues swooped in (Image: ADRIAN DENNIS / AFP via Getty Images)

"That's when the contract came from United, Fergie and his agents. That's when I signed the contract. But of course, Chelsea had sent me to Norway and they said, 'Why would you do that? We've been looking after you for about a year now.' So when they saw that [I'd signed for United] they refused to let it go and said they'd fight. FIFA couldn't sort it out and get either team to back off, the English FA got involved and then I had a one-to-one meeting with Fergie.

"He said he wanted a meeting with me, alone without anybody for 30 minutes, and that he would be able to convince me to come to Manchester United. So I had the meeting, but he couldn't convince me and that's how it was settled."

‌



Toni Kroos

Toni Kroos verbally agreed to join United from Bayern Munich in 2013 as David Moyes stepped into Fergie's shoes at Old Trafford. The Germany international was considered a top target but remained in his home country for a further season before making the switch to Real Madrid.

View 6 Images Toni Kroos became a European giant in his own right (Image: Michael Regan - UEFA/UEFA via Getty Images)

Moyes told talkSPORT in 2018: "Toni Kroos had agreed to come to Manchester United with me. I met him and his wife and we agreed it all when he was at Bayern Munich."

‌



Kroos went on to claim the World Cup with Germany in 2014 and won the Champions League five times at Madrid.

Paulo Dybala

In 2019, United attempted to orchestrate a swap deal with Juventus featuring Paulo Dybala and Romelu Lukaku. Ole Gunnar Solskjaer believed the Belgium international wasn't needed and reports from Italy suggested an agreement had been reached between the sides.

View 6 Images Paulo Dybala was subject to a potential swap deal (Image: Valerio Pennicino/Getty Images)

‌



Dybala eventually decided to stay with Juve and won 11 major honours in Italy. He was also included in the Argentina side that lifted the World Cup in 2022 and currently plays for Roma.

Alan Shearer

Alan Shearer had his choice of Newcastle and Manchester in 1996 following his Premier League triumph with Blackburn Rovers. The division's all-time leading marksman sat down with Sir Alex and his childhood hero, Kevin Keegan, who proved pivotal in the forward's eventual decision.

View 6 Images Alan Shearer could've been a Red Devil (Image: Shaun Botterill/Allsport/Getty Images/Hulton Archive)

‌



He revealed on The Rest is Football podcast in 2023: "I had the choice between Newcastle and Man United. I went to meet Kevin and Sir Alex on the same day, I met Kevin in the morning, Sir Alex in the afternoon. And the first words in the afternoon, Sir Alex came in and said to me, 'Am I meeting you first or am I meeting you second?'

"And I said, 'I've just met Kevin this morning,' and he said, 'That's me f*****, I've got no chance.' I asked why and he said, 'Always first impressions last.' Anyway, a day went over, I went home and I said, 'I'm signing for Man United.'

"Fergie was incredible, we went to Manchester and we went house hunting. Then two days later, I got a call off Kevin to say, 'I would like an hour with you before you go and that's it.' I had talks with him and I rung my Mrs up and said, 'I'm signing for Newcastle, there's a taxi coming in half an hour, you need to pack a bag for me and we're flying to the far east tonight.'"

Sports.title: Liverpool news: Yan Diomande transfer U-turn and club issue statement over arrival
Sports.content:
Liverpool news: Yan Diomande transfer U-turn and club issue statement over arrival

The Liverpool latest focuses on RB Leipzig winger Yan Diomande as the Reds make a statement

View 3 Images Yan Diomande is being linked with various clubs this summer (Image: Joe Prior/Visionhaus via Getty Images)

Liverpool's pre-season has intensified with the club jetting out to the United States on Monday. While not all of his players were on the plane, with some players set to join later on due to their involvement in the World Cup, the next few weeks will give new head coach Andoni Iraola the best look yet at his squad.

‌



The World Cup came to an end on Sunday night. The tournament has dominated the summer, putting transfer business on the back burner for some clubs, including the Reds.

‌



However, with time ticking away until Liverpool face Newcastle United on August 23, the club's transfer business is set to ignite. Today's latest around the Reds sees Iraola confirm a new arrival, while elsewhere, a long-term Reds' target has been at the centre of a possible transfer U-turn.

‌



Liverpool confirm new arrival

Alejandro Rosalen has been confirmed as Liverpool's new first-team goalkeeping coach after the departure of Xavi Valero. The Spaniard has moved to the Reds after five years with Napoli, in which he was part of two Serie A title victories, in 2022/23 and 2024/25.

His career began at Valencia and was followed by one season in Hungary with Videoton. He spent eight years with Fiorentina before he took up the position at Napoli in 2021.

FOLLOW OUR LIVERPOOL FB PAGE! Latest Reds news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

‌



Valero told Liverpool before the end of last season that he wished to leave, just 12 months after rejoining the club from West Ham. As per The Athletic, his exit was unrelated to Arne Slot's dismissal and was believed to be a mutual decision.

View 3 Images Alejandro Rosalen has joined Liverpool (Image: Getty Images)

Valero was part of Rafael Benitez’s backroom staff at Anfield between 2007 and 2010. After spells at Inter, Chelsea, Napoli and Real Madrid, he spent seven years at the Hammers before being hired by Liverpool sporting director Richard Hughes last summer.

‌



In a statement on the club's website announcing the new arrival, Liverpool said: "Alejandro Rosalen has been appointed as Liverpool’s new first-team goalkeeping coach. The 49-year-old Spaniard joins Andoni Iraola’s backroom staff, replacing Xavi Valero, who has now departed the Reds after a second spell with the club in 2025-26.

"Rosalen arrives on Merseyside with a wealth of experience as a goalkeeper coach. His most recent position was at Serie A side Napoli, from 2021 to this summer. While there, Rosalen contributed to Napoli lifting the Scudetto on two occasions (2022-23 and 2024-25).

"He had previously spent eight years with Fiorentina in Italy, a period that followed a single season at Hungarian outfit Videoton. Rosalen’s coaching career had begun in Valencia’s academy, where he stayed for eight years."

‌



Transfer U-turn

Long-time Liverpool target Yan Diomande was reported to have agreed personal terms with Paris Saint-Germain as far back as June. However, crucially, there’s no agreement in place between PSG and the player's club, RB Leipzig, yet, with the German side still hoping to keep the teenager.

View 3 Images Yan Diomande has made his decision (Image: Terence Lewis/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)

Despite making it clear to Leipzig they could afford his apparent £86.8million asking price, the Bundesliga club held firm. Fabrizio Romano has now claimed that several other teams are still trying to muscle in on the deal to take Diomande to PSG as well, which could see the player U-turn on his decision to join the Ligue 1 outfit. However, it's unclear if Liverpool have revisited their interest.

Sports.title: Man Utd news: Marcus Rashford latest as transfer completed with Tottenham for star
Sports.content:
Man Utd news: Marcus Rashford latest as transfer completed with Tottenham for star

Manchester United are busy strengthening their squad in the transfer window while Marcus Rashford's future remains a topic of discussion

View 2 Images Marcus Rashford remains a Manchester United player after his loan spell at Barcelona (Image: Chris Arjoon/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)

Manchester United’s summer recruitment is underway as the club reshape their squad in the transfer market. Michael Carrick has already welcomed several new signings but will want to further strengthen before the start of the new campaign.

‌



United have begun rebuilding their midfield after losing Casemiro at the end of last season. Andrey Santos signed from Chelsea before the club completed a shock move for Aston Villa ’s Youri Tielemans.

‌



Former Leeds goalkeeper Karl Darlow has also arrived as experienced backup to Senne Lammens. However, United have shown a commitment to building for the long-term after sealing a move for highly-rated Tottenham prospect Tynan Thompson.

‌



Meanwhile, Marcus Rashford’s future remains a topic of discussion after his time with England at the World Cup recently came to an end. Here, Mirror Football takes a closer look at some of the stories surrounding United.

FOLLOW OUR MAN UTD FB PAGE! Latest United news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

Marcus Rashford latest

Marcus Rashford is open to rejoining United training at the end of his summer break after collecting a bronze medal at the World Cup. The forward has not played for United since December 2024, though his next steps have seemed uncertain since Barcelona opted not to trigger their £26m buy option at the end of his loan deal this summer.

‌



Stormzy leaks Manchester United's new adidas away kit during World Cup final READ MORE :

A second clause that allowed clubs to sign Rashford for £40m also expired this month. BBC Sport reports that Rashford, who has two years left on his contract, is “relaxed” about the thought of linking back up with the United squad in training.

The 28-year-old is also claimed to have a more positive dynamic with his ex-teammate and new boss Carrick compared to his “confrontational relationship” with former United manager Ruben Amorim. In his latest spell away from Old Trafford, Rashford notched 14 goals and assists apiece for Barcelona last term, winning La Liga.

Upon completing his World Cup duties, Rahford wrote on social media: “Keep believing in us. Our time will come. Now it's time for me to rest, reflect, spend some quality time with family and friends, and come back a better version of myself."

‌



View 2 Images Tynan Thompson has completed a move to Manchester United (Image: Manchester United/Manchester United via Getty Images)

£8m transfer complete

United have completed the signing of Tottenham Hotspur prospect Tynan Thompason. The 18-year-old, who was named in Champions League matchday squads for Spurs last season, has arrived for an initial £4m, plus a further £4m in potential add-ons.

The winger is set to start his United career with the club’s U21s but could force his way into first team plans. The deal with Spurs also includes a 15 per cent sell-on clause.

‌



Announcing the transfer, a United statement said: " Manchester United have agreed the signing of exciting young winger Tynan Thompson, subject to registration. The England youth international has joined from Tottenham Hotspur.

"The 18-year-old scored 13 goals and contributed six assists last season across Under-18s to Under-21s level, including seven goals in seven UEFA Youth League games. His performances earned him opportunities within Spurs’ first-team matchday squads. Everyone at United would like to welcome Tynan to the club and wish him the very best of luck for the future."

Sports.title: Arsenal news: Tottenham beaten to signing as shock short-term transfer to save millions eyed
Sports.content:
Arsenal news: Tottenham beaten to signing as shock short-term transfer to save millions eyed

Mikel Arteta and Arsenal are gearing up for a busy pre-season and some transfer business is now taking centre-stage

View 2 Images Mikel Arteta is braced for more Arsenal arrivals (Image: Arsenal FC via Getty Images)

As Arsenal await the return of their World Cup stars, including newly crowned champions David Raya, Mikel Merino and Martin Zubimendi, attention will soon turn to transfer plans. There has already been some movement but we are expecting plenty more to follow.

‌



Piero Hincapie has now signed permanently for £34.5million after a successful season on loan from Bayer Leverkusen. Illan Meslier became the second new addition, with the goalkeeper joining from Leeds United on a free.

‌



Karl Hein, Jakub Kiwior and Leandro Trossard have all moved on to free up some funds. More could yet follow, with Fabio Vieira and Gabriel Jesus among those linked with summer exits.

‌



Mikel Arteta and his squad begin their pre-season campaign on August 1 and there's plenty of time to get business done before then. Here are our latest lines from the red half of north London.

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

Arsenal to receive millions in FIFA compensation after disastrous World Cup blow READ MORE :

Arsenal beat Spurs to the punch

Arsenal have agreed a deal for youngster Elijah Upson, son of their former defender Matt. The teenager was on Tottenham's books and Roberto De Zerbi's side reportedly offered him a new, pro contract, only for the Gunners to pounce.

‌



The centre-back, who turned 18 in March, played 23 times in all competitions for Spurs' age group teams last season. He started at the heart of the defence in a 4-1 north London derby win in the Under-18 Premier League, with Emerson Nwaneri scoring Arsenal's goal.

Elijah's father Matt, 47, was a Premier League champion with Arsenal in the 2001/02 season. He also played top-flight football for Birmingham, West Ham, Stoke and Leicester and played for England at the 2010 World Cup.

Shock Stones move eyed

View 2 Images John Stones is a free agent after leaving Manchester City (Image: CameraSport via Getty Images)

‌



England and Manchester City defender John Stones is available on a free transfer this summer and Arsenal have emerged as a shock suitor. According to The Sun, the Gunners see him as a potential short-term, cheap fix after losing William Saliba for an extended period through injury.

Stones left City at the end of June after more than a decade at the Etihad Stadium. Mikel Arteta was part of the coaching staff for a section of that spell so he already knows all about the former Everton centre-back.

Arsenal are yet to determine how long they expect to be without Saliba, who aggravated a back injury at the World Cup. However, with French media suggesting he could be out for as long as five months, Stones - also a target for Inter Milan - could help plug a defensive hole.

Sports.title: Argentina fans go wild as pilot tells them they've won World Cup in brutal prank
Sports.content:
Argentina fans go wild as pilot tells them they've won World Cup in brutal prank

Videos of the brutal prank have gone viral as the pilot misled Argentina fans they had left the World Cup final victorious causing the cabin to erupt with cheers

View 3 Images The pilot made the decision to play the cruelest of pranks on some Argentina fans [stock image] (Image: Getty Images)

A Spanish pilot played a brutal prank on Argentina fans on board a flight as he told them their country had won the World Cup, sparking wild celebrations.

‌



A viral video shared online shows a plane full of Argentina fans going wild after the announcement is made over the PA system.

‌



Passengers donning the blue and white stripes jump from their seats and erupt into cheers at the news.

‌



View 3 Images The moment this pilot pranked all the Argentinians on board stating they had won the World Cup

Many would have been left heartbroken as they were unable to watch the game live due to being in the air. News of the final result was left to the pilot to break, and he did so in a very cruel way.

He announced over the intercom that Argentina had taken the victory, with the cabin filling with excitement.

‌



The passengers had no idea how the game had panned out, with the domination of their team, a red card and a last minute goal from Spain.

The wild celebrations were cut short by the pilot as he revealed it was a joke and that Spain had won the World Cup.

View 3 Images The Argentina team were left gutted after their defeat (Image: Maja Hitij - FIFA/FIFA via Getty Images)

Article continues below

The cheers were quickly replaced by a stark silence as Argentina fans on board were left devastated.

The joke was a risky move from the pilot as the result led to chaos on and off the pitch, with players scrapping and Argentinians protesting on the streets.

It is believed, however, that there was no disorder on the plane.

Sports.title: World Cup final: FIFA investigation launched after disgraceful Argentina throw punches at Spain stars
Sports.content:
Spain have been crowned world champions but the behaviour of Argentina at the final whistle has led to calls for Fifa to ban several players - follow all the reaction

Spain are world champions, beating a bad-tempered Argentina 1-0 in New Jersey in the final.

Ferran Torres's extra time winner came after nearly two hours of goalless football at MetLife Stadium and with Argentina reduced to 10 men by Chelsea's Enzo Fernandez getting sent off for two bookable offences.

At the final whistle, a huge brawl kicked off, triggered by Leandro Paredes attacking a number of Spain players including Rodri, Eric Garci and Gavi - with Paredes sent-off for throwing punches and kicking out.

There have been calls for Fifa to "throw the book" at Argentina, who also turned their backs on Spain receiving their medals and lifting the trophy in another poor act of sportsmanship.

Sports.title: Ombudsman's half-sister makes debut at Wolverhampton
Sports.content:
The Sky Sports Racing cameras head to the Midlands today, with evening racing from Wolverhampton on the agenda.

7.00 Wolverhampton - Ombudsman's half-sister debuts at Dunstall Park

Ombudsman's half-sister Syndicale makes her racecourse debut in Dunstall Park's Tips For Every Race At raceday-ready.com EBF Restricted Maiden Fillies' Stakes.

Karl Burke's filly, who is by Ten Sovereigns, will have all eyes upon her as she tackles the seven-furlong trip on the tapeta. The Spigot Lodge team have sent three two-year-olds into battle at the track thus far in 2026, with two emerging victorious.

The Cheveley Park-owned Consultation comes here off the back of a decent run at Yarmouth at the end of last month, which has worked out very nicely. The winner that day Zigazig Ah subsequently took out Newbury's Super Sprint, which gives the form an enormous boost given Consultation was beaten less than three lengths at Yarmouth. Any progression here would likely see her go close.

Perfect Love - who was bought by the Basher Watts Syndicate for 30,000gns as a yearling - could attract attention. The daughter of Palace Pier will be ridden by Alistair Rawlinson for Mick Appleby, who is closing in on 200 career winners at Dunstall Park.

2.28 Vichy - Horizon Dore and Zarraf lock horns in Listed company

Horizon Dore and Zarraf lock horns in today's Listed Prix Hubert Baguenault de Puchesse at Vichy.

At his peak, Patrice Cottier's charge was rated 120 after finishing third in the 2023 Champion Stakes but the six-year-old gelding has slowly regressed in the years since. However, it's clear some ability remains with the most recent of his nine wins coming in the Listed Le Vase d'Argent in April.

Image: Horizon Dore returns to action this afternoon. (Photo: Zuzanna Lupa)

Younger and more progressive is four-year-old Zarraf - who is trained by Alicja Karkosa. This lad beat Arabian Force and most notably Wolferton winner Map Of Stars in the Prix Lord Seymour at ParisLongchamp in April before struggling in Group 2 company. The aforementioned form line is the best recent form in the race and on that showing, he should take all the beating.

New Ground finished fourth in last year's Derby and arrives here after finishing fifth in a conditions race at Chantilly in March. That was his first run after being gelded and if he retains his form from last term, he can challenge.

8.00 Wolverhampton - Oh So Perfect chases hat-trick

Also owned by Basher Watts and company is Oh So Perfect, who comes here chasing her hat-trick after over four months on the sidelines.

Having been an eight-race maiden when going to post at Chelmsford in February, she has since hit form - rising from a rating of 46 to a mark of 56 today. It remains to be seen whether the handicapper has got to grips with her, but don't rule out a third successive victory.

Based is a course and distance winner and has been dropped 1lb after disappointing under a 6lb penalty when a 4/1 joint-favourite at Newcastle recently.

Musical Soldier has been very unlucky of late, having been denied the last twice by under a length. Retaining his mark of 55 here, today could be the day for Ollie Sangster's charge with Jack Callan's 3lb claim potentially being the difference.

Sports.title: Menzies shocks world No 2 Humphries in World Matchplay thriller
Sports.content:
Cameron Menzies produced a massive upset to defeat 2024 champion Luke Humphries 10-7 at the World Matchplay on Monday night.

World No 2 Humphries took centre stage against one of the most entertaining and unpredictable players in the game in Menzies.

And it was the Scot who raised the Empress Ballroom roof with an inspired 170 checkout to stun the former world champion and seal his first win on the Winter Gardens stage.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Cameron Menzies lands 'The Big Fish' to stun Luke Humphries at the World Matchplay

Betfred World Matchplay - Monday's results

Round Two

Ross Smith 10-6 Kevin Doets Gerwyn Price 11-9 Martin Schindler Cameron Menzies 10-7 Luke Humphries Rob Cross 10-3 Danny Noppert

Menzies produced a brilliant double-double 129 finish to lead Humphries 3-2, but 'Cool Hand' made it six consecutive breaks of throw with a magnificent 167 checkout to level straight after the first interval.

Menzies then went on a blistering four-leg burst to race into a 7-3 lead but could only win one out of the next five legs as Humphries went on a charge.

However, Menzies landed an inspired 170 checkout to cause a mighty shock as he set up a second-round clash with Ross Smith.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Humphries pinned this stunning 167 on the bull

"No one gave me hope! I didn't give myself hope but I finally won a game at the Winter Gardens," said a delighted Menzies.

"Luke Humphries is a great guy, a great player. At 7-3 I was just trying not to think of that finishing line but the nerves kicked in. To beat Humphries, I know he will be disappointed. He gave me a lot of stress at doubles but that's my biggest win.

"I show a lot of emotion and I hate that I do that. I'm trying to keep myself intact. Try to keep myself composed because I know he was going to have a spell and batter me and he had a little spell but lucky enough I had that lead.

"I know that's not Humphries but I'll take it any day of the week."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Menzies hits this HUGE double-double finish against Humphries

Mardle: Menzies' greatest moment - he knows he can handle anything now

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Hear from Menzies and Wayne Mardle after the Scotsman claimed a famous win over Humphries

"It's his best ever win, and he mentioned that," said Wayne Mardle, speaking to Sky Sports.

"With Cameron Menzies, everyone mentions his emotions, but it's the way he had to win that game.

"Nothing went according to plan. He was broken back early twice, that's up-and-down emotions. The high of breaking to being broken back.

"Then he went on a run, and got pegged back. There was a lot happening in that game, but he held it all together beautifully.

"Humphries had an amazing spell of four legs, but then Menzies found a level again, and that's something we don't see enough.

"What he should take away from tonight was the way he handled this situation. It was like he was there a million times before.

"He knows he can handle anything now."

Humphries vs Menzies: Tale of the Tape

Menzies to face 'Smudger' next

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player It was very nearly a debut to forget for Kevin Doets as he came close to taking a tumble on the stage

Ross Smith came through a fantastic encounter as he defied a 104.19 average from debutant Kevin Doets - taking out 160 and a match-winning 120 - to reach the second round.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Doets hiit this 161 finish on the bullseye - just in time to save the match!

'Hawkeye' saved the match with a stunning 161 checkout but Smith held the Dutchman at arm's length.

After storming out of the gates to a 5-0 lead 'Smudger' kept his composure through a mid-session scrap before sealing victory - signing off with a spectacular 120 Shanghai finish.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Smith nailed this magnificent 160 checkout on his way to victory

Price wins in extra time to set up Cross showdown

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Gerwyn Price nails the ton checkout to sink Martin Schindler

Former World Matchplay finalist Gerwyn Price survived a huge scare against German No 1 Martin Schindler to book his spot in the second round.

'The Iceman' trailed 4-0 and 6-2 before roaring back and punishing Schindler for errors on the outer ring to win 11-9.

"It doesn't usually happen. Without the crowd, I would have lost today," admitted Price. "That was the worst I've played all season.

"It goes to show, throwing sheep about instead of darts about, it doesn't help! It was a tough one for me. I've got no confidence at the minute because I haven't played a lot.

"To battle through it. Martin was just as rubbish as me, thankfully.

"That was one I should have lost, but I've won and I'm still in the tournament - I can't be any worse!"

Price will take on Rob Cross next after 'Voltage' kicked off his campaign with a convincing 10-3 win over Danny Noppert.

The 2019 champion led 5-0 at the break and never relented, averaging 97.41, pinning a 128 checkout, and ending with an impressive 52.6 per cent on the doubles.

What's happening at the World Matchplay on Tuesday?

Image: Luke Littler and Michael van Gerwen headline the World Matchplay action on Tuesday

The 2026 Betfred World Matchplay continues at the iconic Winter Gardens from July 18-26, as a 32-player field compete for the prestigious Phil Taylor Trophy.

Two-time world champion Luke Littler takes on Nathan Aspinall in a blockbuster clash after opening his defence of the Phil Taylor Trophy with a sensational 10-6 win over Niko Springer on Day One in Blackpool.

Betfred World Matchplay - Tuesday's fixtures [first to 11 legs]

Round Two - Evening 7pm

Jonny Clayton vs Gary Anderson Michael van Gerwen vs Dirk van Duijvenbode Luke Littler vs Nathan Aspinall Josh Rock vs Stephen Bunting

Stephen Bunting takes on Josh Rock after winning through a Winter Gardens classic against debutant Niels Zonneveld, surviving three match darts to edge past the Dutchman 13-12.

Sports.title: Palace seek £55m-plus for Lacroix as talks with Chelsea begin
Sports.content:
Chelsea are in talks with Crystal Palace over the signing of defender Maxence Lacroix.

Sky Sports News understands Palace are seeking more than the £55m Tottenham paid for Jan Paul van Hecke from Brighton to sanction Lacroix's sale.

Palace and Chelsea enjoy good relations at the highest levels and they have done deals for players such as Trevoh Chalobah and Ben Chilwell.

Chelsea want to sign a centre-back and ideally any new arrival would be physically imposing and bring Premier League experience.

Chelsea have raised around £130m from sales in this window and more players are set to leave.

In defence, players who could move on include Chalobah, Benoit Badiashile, Malo Gusto and Axel Disasi.

Rogers arrives for medical ahead of record-breaking move

Morgan Rogers arrived for a medical with Chelsea on Monday morning, which you can exclusively watch below, ahead of completing a British-record £117m move from Aston Villa.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Morgan Rogers has been spotted arriving for his Chelsea medical after the Blues agreed a £117m deal with Aston Villa.

All being well, Rogers is then expected to sign a six-year contract at Chelsea with the option of another year until 2033.

Rogers returned from the USA on Sunday following England's third-place finish at the World Cup, via a bronze-final victory over France.

Chelsea moved quickly to secure the deal ahead of Arsenal, who were unwilling to match the asking price despite Rogers being their top forward target.

Image: Morgan Rogers will become Chelsea's most expensive player

Rogers will become the most expensive British player of all time when he completes his move from Aston Villa, with the fee eclipsing the £116m fee paid by Manchester City for his England team-mate Elliot Anderson.

Rogers is also set to become Chelsea's record signing, overtaking the £115m the Blues paid Brighton for Moises Caicedo in 2023.

Sports.title: A pioneer and a superstar, Kevin Keegan’s achievements were extraordinary
Sports.content:
Kevin Keegan, who has died aged 75, is the only British player to win the Ballon d’Or twice, was the star of Liverpool’s first European Cup-winning team, a messianic figure at Newcastle United as a player and coach, forging a team so memorable that Fifa’s president wrote to commend him, and was the captain and then manager of the England men’s national team. And yet, as Keegan would ruefully reflect, he will principally be remembered by many for an emotional outburst that precipitated Newcastle’s historic failure in a Premier League title race, a TV interview which presaged the coming era of the modern game.

Keegan’s “I’d love it” rant of April 1996, directed at Alex Ferguson, became a meme before the modern meaning of the word and social media even existed, repeatedly played on Sky Sports and becoming indelibly marked in the minds of multiple generations, many not even born when it occurred. It frequently tops polls as the most memorable moment in Premier League history and foreshadowed an era where digital clips and personality narratives would dominate football coverage.

There is a danger, however, of reducing Keegan’s life to a series of ever-more emotional explosions, of which there were many, such as his punch-up with Leeds United’s Billy Bremner in the 1974 Charity Shield. For that would obscure the extraordinary nature of his achievements and the fact he was arguably the most charismatic modern English footballer; more eloquent than David Beckham and Paul Gascoigne and more passionate than Bobby Moore. He had a rare gift for inspiring players and almost everyone who interacted with him at his best came away uplifted.

Still, Keegan’s meltdown on TV, where he took issue with Ferguson’s supposed “mind games” in suggesting Leeds players would go easy on Newcastle during a tight title run-in with Manchester United, became a defining moment. “Strangers shout ‘love it’ to me from car windows,” wrote Keegan in his autobiography. “Autograph hunters tell me they would ‘love it’ if I could sign their pieces of paper. When I go to charity events I am often asked to sign photographs showing me in that classic pose: headphones on, finger jabbing, blazing eyes. Those pictures tend to be auctioned for a lot more money than the ones where I am playing for England or any of my clubs.”

Keegan claimed to be relaxed about the characterisation, skewed though it was, perhaps because more than any English footballer before he had maximised football’s commercial and media opportunities and accepted the respective bouquets and brickbats that ensued. Even before that meltdown, he would be best remembered by many in the 1970s for his excruciating bike crash on Superstars, a TV show which pitted athletes from different sports against each other in unfamiliar disciplines. Sprawled across the cycle track, Keegan’s bare flesh was ripped red raw by the gravel. Most remember the drama but few recall that, showing characteristic pig-headed determination, he got back on the bike, bloodied and bandaged, for a rematch, which he won before winning the entire contest.

Keegan was born in Armthorpe, Doncaster, to Doris and Joe, a war veteran Durham miner who had migrated south in search of work at Markham colliery. His upbringing echoed Monty Python’s Yorkshiremen sketch, only his memories were authentic, a throwback to a different century. Their terrace house “had a detached outhouse where we washed. Our bath was an old zinc tub and the toilet was at the foot of the garden and we never had electricity until I was 10 and we moved into a council house in Balby.”

View image in fullscreen Kevin Keegan shares a joke with Alex Ferguson after the rollercoaster 1995-96 season. Photograph: Adam Butler/PA

Keegan’s ascent to the peak of the game’s elite was unforeseen, few recognising his talent early on, most dismissing him as too small. He always credited Sister Mary Oliver, the nun who ran his Catholic primary school football team and who refereed with a crucifix around her neck, as being as important to him as a mentor as Bill Shankly was. “Kevin’s football must be encouraged,” she wrote in a school report, which gave him immense self-belief.

Doncaster Rovers rejected him and he started work at Peglers Brass Works at 16, playing for their football team but only in the reserves and also for a pub team on Sundays, where he fortuitously played against a Scunthorpe scout, Bob Nellis, who got him a trial at the struggling Third Division club. Keegan referred to himself as a “mongrel” and “weasel” and the “least-talented” Ballon d’Or winner, and despite impressing at Scunthorpe it was still a major shock when Shankly, the man he regarded as a second father and progenitor of his success, took him to Liverpool. Shankly told him: “You’re not just a great player – you’re one of the great players!” It seemed an unlikely boast but Keegan scored on his Liverpool debut and was never dropped thereafter. He would inherit from Shankly comparable motivational skills.

Quick Guide The Keegan years: from player to manager Show 1951 Kevin Keegan is born on 14 February in Armthorpe, near Doncaster. 1968 Begins playing career at Scunthorpe United. 1971 Signed by Bill Shankly for Liverpool at age of 20, initially as a midfielder. 1972 Makes England debut against Wales in November. 1973 Liverpool win the league; Keegan scores twice in Uefa Cup final win over Borussia Mönchengladbach. 1974 Scores twice as Liverpool beat Newcastle 3-0 in the FA Cup final. His first England goal comes against Wales. 1976 Liverpool win the league title and Keegan scores in each leg of Uefa Cup final win against Club Brugge. His celebrity is such he appears on the TV show Superstars, and famously crashes his bike during one of the races. 1977 Another league title for Liverpool, who also win their first European Cup, a 3-1 victory over Mönchengladbach. Keegan moves to Hamburg for £500,000, nearly double the German transfer record. 1978 Wins Ballon d’Or. 1979 Wins Ballon d’Or again as Hamburg secure their first German ‌championship title in 19 years, and first in the Bundesliga era. 1980 Captains England at Euros but they are knocked out in the group stage. Leaves Hamburg to join Southampton for two seasons. 1982 Transfers to Newcastle in the Second Division. Plays final match for England, after 63 caps (31 as captain) and 21 goals. 1984 Helps Newcastle secure promotion in his second season, then retires from playing. Across his club career, he scores 204 goals in 592 ‌appearances. 1992 Takes first coaching role as manager of struggling Newcastle in February. Danger of relegation to the Third Division is averted. 1993 Leads them to the First Division title and promotion to the Premier League in his first full season in charge. 1994 Newcastle finish third in Premier League. 1996 Newcastle finish second in the Premier League, ​despite leading for most ​of campaign – by 12 points at one stage. Season includes famous “I would love it if we beat them” comments when discussing rivals Manchester United on Sky Sports. 1997 Leaves Newcastle and takes over at Fulham for two seasons. 1999 Takes charge ​of England national ‌team in February. 2000 Coaches England at Euro 2000 where they beat Germany but still go out in the group stage. Resigns in ​October after a 1–0 loss to Germany in World Cup qualifying. 2001 Takes over at Manchester City. 2008 Returns to Newcastle but lasts eight months after tensions with the board and owner Mike Ashley. Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

Though reclusive, Keegan also had a streak of extrovertism, embracing every aspect of the game’s growing commercial opportunities, from his famous Brut advert to appearances on Top of the Pops, where his single Head Over Heels in Love reached the top 40. Though he enjoyed standing out, he admitted he would never have got away with his trademark bubble perm in the old-school Liverpool dressing room. His wife, Jean, whom he met on the waltzers at the Doncaster St Leger horse racing meeting when she was 16 and he was 19 and to whom he remained married for life, burst into fits of laughter when she first saw it. He had the last laugh, the hairstyle inspiring alarming copycat versions across the football world.

Keegan remained true to what he considered to be his working-class, mining roots, declaring himself a Labour man, annoyed that a staged photo of him feigning to kiss then prime minister Margaret Thatcher on the cheek was interpreted as support for economic policies which had ravaged heavy industry. He was more at home playing head tennis with a later PM, Tony Blair, to whom he was close enough to host at his home for dinner.

View image in fullscreen The then Newcastle manager Keegan chats to the Labour leader Tony Blair in the summer of 1996. Photograph: Adam Butler/PA

Keegan inherited two mantles from Britain’s greatest players of the 1960s. As George Best, the original footballer sex symbol of the modern era, lapsed into alcoholism and increasing unreliability, Keegan became the more wholesome and dependable commercial face of the superstar footballer in Britain, inundated with deals. For England he effectively became Moore’s successor as captain but at a time when the national team was in decline from his predecessor’s World Cup-winning heights. For Keegan, as the sole outfield world-class player, it was a heavy burden to bear as they missed out on successive World Cup finals.

His first major tournament for his country was the ill-fated 1980 European Championship and his World Cup career amounted to 20 minutes in 1982, a campaign which was disrupted by a back injury and where “my only contribution was a dreadful miss against the host nation to send us home. That moment is probably the only moment of my England career that people remember now.” It would prove to be his last game for England at the age of just 31.

More notable features of Keegan’s England career were his courage in defying IRA death threats to play against Northern Ireland in Belfast, then walking out on the team when Don Revie dropped him shortly afterwards and being arbitrarily beaten up by Yugoslav custom officials prior to a game in Belgrade, a horrific and wholly underserved ordeal that sparked an international incident. His frustration was best summed up in a story he told about the great Dutch player Johnny Rep. Surveying an England team at Wembley in 1977, Rep turned to Keegan and said: “Kevvy, you have problems here: this is the worst England side I have seen.” The Netherlands won 2-0 and, as Keegan recalled, could have scored at will.

Keegan was a pioneering player, negotiating release clauses, unheard of at the time in England, at Liverpool and Hamburg, allowing him to leave if a club met a £500,000 fee, thereby controlling his moves. Leaving Liverpool at what was assumed to be their peak – he had just helped them win their first European Cup in 1977 – to join a team sixth in the Bundesliga was demonstrative of both Keegan’s single-mindedness and capacity to challenge himself. He also quadrupled his salary, reflecting the economic state of English football at the time.

View image in fullscreen Keegan with the ball at his feet for Hamburg in the 1977-78 Bundesliga season. Photograph: Colorsport/Shutterstock

Hamburg was not an initial success. Jealous teammates held meetings to get him kicked out of the club and, according to Keegan, refused to pass to him. His nadir came at Christmas 1977 when, in a festive-season friendly, unhappy at his plight and frustrated with over-physical treatment from the Lübeck defender Erhard Press, Keegan punched him on the jaw and subsequently knocked him out, receiving an eight-week ban as punishment. Yet, a year later, he won his first Ballon d’Or and went on to lead Hamburg to their first Bundesliga title since 1960.

Keegan embraced Germany, learning the language and was nicknamed “Mighty Mouse”, a tribute to his astonishing strength given his diminutive size. His first daughter, Laura, was born there but his finale, a European Cup final that would have sealed Hamburg’s place in history, was a sad one, ending as it did in defeat to Nottingham Forest. Having won three league titles, two Uefa Cups, an FA Cup and European Cup at Liverpool, the Bundesliga title would be the last trophy Keegan ever won. He was just 29 years old.

Keegan made a typically unconventional choice in joining Southampton, a promising yet small-market team under a talented, persuasive manager in Lawrie McMenemy. Keegan propelled them to a top-six finish and qualification for Europe, but they faded to seventh in the second season and Keegan, disillusioned, made a decision that would define the second half of his professional life.

Newcastle were in one of their periodic financial and footballing crises and in the old Second Division when, with money from brewers Scottish & Newcastle, they persuaded him to join in 1982. His father’s links to the north-east and reverence for Newcastle players such as Jackie Milburn were an emotional pull on Keegan, but one that cost him his England career. The manager, Bobby Robson, didn’t feel it appropriate to pick a second-tier player for England and Keegan, still captain and by far the most iconic national team player, learned from the press he had been “dumped”. He felt “betrayed, hurt and humiliated”.

Crowds doubled at St James’ Park with Keegan’s arrival and Newcastle were promoted as champions in Keegan’s second season, 1983-84, by which point he had already decided to quit playing at the age of 33. Typically impulsive, it was when Mark Lawrenson outsprinted Keegan to dispossess him during an FA Cup tie at Liverpool that he decided he would finish his career at the end of the season.

View image in fullscreen Keegan in action for England in May 1979. His international playing career ended in acrimonious fashion. Photograph: Peter Robinson/Empics Sport/PA

Keegan and family, which now included his second daughter, Sarah, born in 1982, decamped to his Marbella villa and, other than periodic business deals and discussions about a long-held dream to launch a Soccer Circus, he embraced retirement. Yet endless rounds of golf failed to satisfy. The family had moved back to his Hampshire home when Sir John Hall, a dynamic north-east businessman, called in 1992, begging Keegan to help Newcastle avoid relegation to the third tier and potential liquidation. Despite having watched no football for years, Keegan accepted. He threatened to quit after a few games but stayed to keep Newcastle up and promptly announced that he wanted to build a dynasty to rival Liverpool and challenge for the Premier League title.

Most considered that quixotic and yet Newcastle won promotion to the Premier League as champions and with judicious youthful signings such as Andy Cole and Rob Lee, and veteran players such as Peter Beardsley, they came third and sixth in the top flight. So great was his authority, Keegan could even placate angry fans on the steps of St James’ Park when the club sold Cole to Manchester United.

With that money the club signed David Ginola and Les Ferdinand and won nine of their first 10 games in 1995-96, often in thrilling fashion, establishing a seemingly unassailable 12-point lead by January. But a crucial defeat at home to Ferguson’s United in March 1996 and the Scot’s repeated use of psychological barbs seemed to weigh heavy on Keegan as his team’s form disintegrated. A dramatic yet debilitating 4-3 defeat at Liverpool led Sepp Blatter to write to Keegan but the sight of him slumped over advertising hoardings as Liverpool scored a last-minute winner suggested the toll was too much.

Keegan eventually cracked, denouncing Ferguson in his famous TV interview. “You can tell him now, we’re still fighting for this title and I’ll tell you, honestly, I will love it if we beat them. Love it!” United won the title with four points to spare.

View image in fullscreen Keegan (left) during a Fulham training session at Roehampton in 1999. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

Keegan initially seemed determined to rebuild as the club signed Alan Shearer for a world-record £15m and they beat United 5-0 at St James’ Park that autumn, but Keegan quit soon after, outraged that a city banker preparing the club for flotation had issued him an ultimatum to sign a contract. Football’s new era seemed untethered from the idealistic foundational values imbued in him by Shankly.

Keegan seemed done with football until the now-disgraced Harrods owner Mohamed Al Fayed used speculative talks about his much-vaunted Soccer Circus to persuade him to become chief operating officer and eventually manager of Fulham in the third tier. He almost seemed at his happiest as the club accelerated to promotion, but his time was interrupted by a national crisis when Glenn Hoddle was sacked as England manager for making offensive comments about disabled people. The clamour for Keegan to take over was indicative of his popularity with ordinary fans. However, it proved a decision he came to greatly regret, taking in a humiliating Euro 2000 group-stage exit and ending with him resigning in the toilets after an ignominious defeat against Germany in England’s last game at the old Wembley Stadium. It was, he conceded, a job beyond his abilities.

That said, Keegan was happy to take on Manchester City in the old First Division, getting them promoted to the Premier League as champions with 99 points. He remained at the club for four years, an almost unprecedented period of stability at the club at that time. When he finally left City he seemed to be done with coaching and finally launched his Soccer Circus in Glasgow, though it closed after a few years. Yet there was to be one last comeback at Newcastle under the ill-starred ownership of Mike Ashley, which proved a disaster and lasted just eight months.

The idea that a high-minded, old-fashioned football manager schooled by Shankly could coexist with a modern businessman as ruthless as Ashley and his cast of minions running the club always seemed improbable. When he walked away from the job, eventually winning a lengthy and bitter constructive dismissal claim, it was to be Keegan’s last act in football. So acrimonious was the departure that he was only able to return in disguise to attend a function at the club.

The current regime made clear Keegan was always welcome back at St James’ Park. That was after his stage four cancer had been revealed in a series of speaking engagements in May 2026, one of which in Newcastle was, in retrospect, a heartfelt farewell to the fans to whom he had always felt closest. After that draining but exhilarating evening Keegan’s associates reported that he was in high spirits, energised by the reconnection with the fans who loved him most.

It was to prove Keegan’s final goodbye. Football, as he observed, had given him everything except for a happy ending.

Sports.title: A big red speaker, Louis Vuitton trophy trunks and a tattoo bet – how Spain celebrated World Cup win
Sports.content:
On the night that Spain won their first World Cup in 2010, Rodrigo Hernández was on camp somewhere lost in the woods of Connecticut. He had been canoeing when the selección beat Germany in the semi-final, upset to have missed it, and for the final he convinced one of the supervisors to let him watch, alone, on a mini-laptop in the hut where the staff slept. When Andrés Iniesta scored the winning goal in the 116th minute, he ran off screaming, doing laps of the lake. He was 14.

On the night that Spain won their second World Cup 16 years later, Rodrigo Hernández was back in the US, not so far from there. When Ferran Torres scored the winning goal in the 106th minute, he ran off screaming in a straighter line and accompanied this time: towards the corner where his other family were. And then, when it ended, when the fighting finished too, he collected the trophy, pausing just long enough for Donald Trump to leave centre stage before lifting it, his timing perfect even here.

It wasn’t the only trophy he had, but those could be handed over and this could not. By the time Rodri departed at 9.38pm eastern time, the last man out of the dressing room at the New Jersey New York Stadium, he couldn’t carry them all: walking with him, just ahead, Ladis had to lend a hand. A football team is never just the players, nor even just the coaches. When he departed the dressing room nine minutes earlier, the same happened for Pau Cubarsí. Nuria helped him, their boy: just 19, looking like a kid down here in the stadium in real life but not on the pitch where he’s a leader. Luis de la Fuente was accompanied by Paloma.

Rodri came with the trophy for the tournament’s best player too. Cubarsí had the young player award, Unai Simón the Golden Glove. They also had two World Cups, every Spain player did: a replica of their own in a black Louis Vuitton trophy trunk, not easy to fit under an arm, and another in Lego. Rodri had three: both of those and the cup. They departed laden down, great big plastic bags full, pieces of the history they made. Shirts, in red and yellow and blue and white. Balls, boots. They had cut the net and taken pieces of that too. They had been given rings, NBA style.

View image in fullscreen Mikel Merino holds a replica of the trophy in the dressing room after Spain’s triumph. Photograph: Alex Pantling/Fifa/Getty Images

Before the final began, Marc Cucurella had sneaked off towards the touchline and buried a coin in the pitch, like that other left-back Joan Capdevila had done in 2010. Iniesta had been out there, his name chanted, as he showed the cup to the stands. After it, Sergio Ramos brought it back again. Dashing out, excitedly kissing it, he placed it on the plinth for this new generation, achieving the impossible in emulating them, to go and collect. One by one they passed, Borja Iglesias and Lamine Yamal among the most evasive in shaking Trump’s hand, until Rodri took the trophy and lifted it to the sky.

Nico Williams went to find his mum in the front row and handed over his medal. Lamine Yamal had made his way across to Lionel Messi, who was sitting but who stood for him, embracing the boy in the bath, the successor: a rite of passage, an image that will be for ever. The actor Javier Bardem was hugging Iglesias, his new friend and idol. Ferran Torres was talking about a “great liberation”: he had suffered, felt how cruel this game could be, how people could be too, but he said: “Destiny is written: God gives to those who deserve.” And Keyne was, well, Keyne. In the dressing room – the same one, Cucurella noted, where he had been at last year’s Club World Cup – the champagne was cracked open.

It was brief – the flight to Spain was scheduled for 11pm and they wanted to get back – and soon they were on their way again. Behind the screen, along the corridor they came, way down in the depths and the half-light of the stadium. The president, the staff, all the players; the many, many people who made this so. Iglesias carried a bag so big it was like he was a student taking his washing home, and he was struggling to stop that box slipping. In the other hand he wheeled a big red speaker. Now playing: Dirty Cash (Money Talks) by PAWSA & Adventures of Stevie V. Lamine Yamal came, via the anti-doping room, in orange sunglasses, four chains, black cap on backwards. He didn’t wear his medal, but most did, thick discs round their necks. And commemorative shirts, ordered up in case.

View image in fullscreen Spain’s Lamine Yamal and Argentina’s Lionel Messi embrace after the match. Photograph: Jeenah Moon/Reuters

Back in Dallas, at a celebration after the semi-final victory, someone had joked to the federation president, Rafael Louzán, that the shirts should say world champions on one side and Finalissima winners on the other, two trophies in one. Tempting, but these bore just the one trophy, “Spain 26” on the back. The war in the Middle East had prevented the Finalissima from going ahead in Doha as scheduled in March and every time another option was offered, Argentina said no, the impression that of a team, a federation, running scared. “Good job we didn’t play,” Emi Martínez had said then, after they scraped past Mauritania in a hastily arranged friendly that filled the hole. “If we had played [Spain] like this …”

Something like this might have happened. Not just because Argentina played like this but because Spain made them play like this. “We gave them a battering,” came the verdict from one of those heading out of the dressing room. This wasn’t just a win; this was more. Has a 1-0 ever been as dominant? There was a moment late in the game, still at 0-0, when the Spain fans chanted: “Look at them! Look at them! How they shit themselves!” and they weren’t wrong. Argentina could not get out all game; as Spain turned the screw, still less, the goal seemingly inevitable; the surprise was that it hadn’t come yet, that there would be just one. When it did it came as a liberation but also an act of irresistible logic.

View image in fullscreen Ferran Torres scores the only goal of the World Cup final. Photograph: Jewel Samad/AFP/Getty Images

Torres’s shot was Spain’s 20th. Argentina didn’t manage one until the 115th minute. They didn’t manage any on target, all game. Across 900 World Cup games for which Opta has the stats, it is only the third time that a team has failed to shoot. And this in the final. They had done to Argentina what they did to France and to everyone, choking them. For the whole tournament Spain had an xG against of 0.3 per game. “If my gloves could talk, they would say they didn’t have much work to do,” Simón said. “Many teams depend too much on the back line,” Aymeric Laporte said, but not Spain.

This was the triumph of a collective, of a group; it ended in New York, but it was built in Chattanooga and beyond, over 51 days. It is the triumph of an idea, a conviction and of a coach too: a victory for De la Fuente and the system he leads and the system that made him. He began his coaching career at Deportivo Alavés in the third tier, where he lasted just 11 games. It was November 2011 when he left and he has not had a club job since.
