World.title: Chel Diokno: Legal expertise in the impeachment spotlight
World.content:
Prosecution counsel Rep. Chel Diokno makes a manifestation during day six of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte on July 15, 2026.

'I've been in practice for almost 36 years, I am used to court proceedings,' Chel Diokno says a day after his impeachment court performance that led to an approved request for Duterte's financial records

Congressman Jose Manuel “Chel” Diokno was calm, cool, and collected amid persistent questioning from senator-siblings Alan Peter and Pia Cayetano on Tuesday, July 21, during the seventh day of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.

Diokno articulated the importance of the prosecution’s motions to subpoena Duterte’s financial records and rebutted claims that their request amounted to a fishing expedition. At the end of the proceedings, the court ruled in their favor.

“This is a big step forward insofar as the presentation of Article 2 (unexplained wealth) is concerned,” Diokno said on Wednesday, July 22.

Play Video

The impeachment court is a familiar ground for Diokno, who also served as one of the private prosecutors in the unfinished impeachment trial of then-president Joseph Estrada from 2000 to 2001. That proceeding was aborted after the second People Power uprising forced Estrada out of Malacañang.

Today, Diokno is one of the 11 public prosecutors in Duterte’s trial. It’s a role that became increasingly likely as early as May 2025, after the victory of his party-list group, Akbayan, became certain. That trial, though, did not push through after the Supreme Court declared the House’s impeachment of Duterte as unconstitutional.

Since then, he has expressed readiness to prosecute Vice President Duterte.

“We have long called for accountability of our top officials. We all know that impeachment is the only way we can hold an incumbent high-ranking official accountable,” he said in a Rappler interview in July last year.

He was elected to the same prosecutor role in May this year, after the House impeached Duterte for a second time.

Diokno carries forward a family legacy rooted in law and public service. He is the son of the late statesman Jose Diokno, widely regarded as the father of human rights advocacy in the Philippines, and the grandson of former Supreme Court justice Ramon Diokno.

A philosophy graduate from the University of the Philippines, he pursued his law degree in Northern Illinois University and qualified for the Illinois Bar in 1986. His father’s death later brought him back to the Philippines, where he went on to pass the Philippine Bar in 1988.

Early in his legal career, he practiced at the Diokno Law Office and later took on the role of litigation head and partner at Moncupa, Diokno & De Los Reyes Law Firm.

In 2003, Diokno became chairman of the Free Legal Assistance Group (FLAG), the Philippines’ oldest network of human rights lawyers. Six years later, he served as the founding dean of the De La Salle University College of Law, now called the Tañada-Diokno School of Law.

Diokno dedicated much of his legal work to providing free legal representation to marginalized sectors and victims of state abuses. These include:

MV Doña Paz disaster: Diokno was one of the lawyers who fought for justice for more than 4,000 lives claimed after the passenger ferry collided with oil tanker MT Vector, making it the biggest maritime disaster in the Philippines. Together with US counterparts, they pursued a class-action civil suit that took nearly three decades to resolve.

Manalo brothers: He successfully petitioned the Supreme Court to issue a landmark Writ of Amparo for Raymond and Reynaldo Manalo, who were abducted in Bulacan for being suspected members of the New People’s Army.

Maria Ressa cyber libel case: He served as counsel of the Nobel Peace Prize laureate. He argued that the case posed a threat to press freedom and the country’s justice system.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, Diokno had also established his Free Legal Helpdesk which sought to provide pro-bono legal assistance to those who could not afford them. He was also elected chairperson of the Bantayog ng mga Bayani Foundation in 2022.

He held advisory positions in the government. He was part of the Presidential Human Rights Committee under presidents Corazon Aquino and Fidel Ramos, and was presidential adviser on human rights to the Integrated Bar of the Philippines from 2017 to 2019.

Diokno has drawn the ire of the Vice President’s father, former president Rodrigo Duterte, who in 2020 mocked his appearance and accused him and the opposition of spreading black propaganda amid the COVID-19 pandemic.

Third time’s the charm for Diokno in elective politics. He mounted unsuccessful Senate campaigns in 2019 and 2022, before finally winning a House seat in 2025, representing party-list race topnotcher Akbayan.

His advocacies include labor and economic rights, gender equality, youth education, and anti-corruption. He has been opposed to the death penalty and political dynasties.

On days 6 and 7 of the trial, Diokno spoke on behalf of the prosecution and asserted that the impeachment court has the constitutional authority over the Vice President’s bank and tax records.

Diokno didn’t fluster, even when Senator Pia Cayetano invoked a 1967 Supreme Court ruling on a case whose respondent was his father. Diokno said a subpoena is not intrusive, as opposed to a search warrant, which was the subject of that landmark decision.

Play Video

Diokno, after the crucial win, said his years of litigation experience proved to be beneficial in the impeachment court.

“That’s a big challenge. It’s tiring to stand (at the court) for hours. But I can say I have some experience arguing in front of the Supreme Court and other courts. That probably helps me a lot,” Diokno said.

“I’ve been in practice for almost 36 years, I am used to court proceedings,” he added. – Rappler.com

Patricia Fontilar is a journalism student at the University of the Philippines Diliman and the managing editor of Tinig ng Plaridel, the official student publication of the UP College of Media and Communication. She is currently a Rappler intern.

World.title: LIVE UPDATES: Impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte
World.content:
WHAT YOU NEED TO KNOW

The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte — the first Philippine public official to be impeached twice by the House of Representatives — began at 2 pm on Monday, July 6.

There are four articles of impeachment against Duterte involving alleged misuse of confidential funds, unexplained wealth, bribery of Department of Education officials, and grave threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and his family.

For the first three weeks, the trial will be held from Monday to Wednesday, and starting July 28, from Tuesday to Thursday. The prosecution will have 62 trial dates, while the defense will have 30 trial dates.

Only 21 out of 24 senator-judges are physically present. Senator Bato dela Rosa remains in hiding as he faces an International Criminal Court arrest warrant over Rodrigo Duterte’s drug war, Senator Jinggoy Estrada has been detained and suspended in connection with a plunder case, and Senator Rodante Marcoleta surrendered to authorities as he also faces a plunder case.

On this page, we bring you the latest updates, analyses, videos, and photos as the trial of the Vice President unfolds.

World.title: [Ask the Tax Whiz] An open letter to the Philippine Senate
World.content:
IMPEACHMENT COURT. Senators wear crimson robes as the upper chamber convenes as an impeachment court for the trial of Vice President Sara Duterte on May 18, 2026.

We deserve leaders who inspire trust instead of division, confidence instead of exhaustion, and hope instead of cynicism

Dear Senate President Gatchalian and Honorable Members of the Senate,

I write this letter not as a tax expert, but simply as a Filipino citizen and taxpayer who still believes in the dignity of public service.

Many of us grew up believing that the Senate is the highest deliberative body in the country—a place where wisdom, civility, and statesmanship rise above anger, pride, and political theater. Sadly, many Filipinos no longer see it that way.

Over the past several weeks, I have traveled from Australia to Canada, the United States, and now Europe, promoting the Philippines as an investment destination. Yet almost everywhere I go—even in China—the same question comes up: “What is happening in your Senate?” Instead of talking about our economic reforms, investment opportunities, and the potential of the Filipino people, I often find myself explaining the political turmoil back home. That is a burden no Filipino should have to carry while representing our country abroad.

While our people struggle with rising prices, recover from natural disasters, and endure one corruption controversy after another, many have watched—some even entertained—by the endless livestreams, public feuds, grandstanding, and political drama that increasingly define our national discourse. The Senate should never become a stage for performance when the nation is crying out for leadership.

Regardless of political affiliation, majority or minority, every senator has the solemn duty to protect not only the Constitution but also the dignity and credibility of the Senate itself. Passion is welcome. Accountability is essential. But respect, humility, professionalism, and self-restraint must never be sacrificed.

The world is watching. Investors, development partners, and millions of Filipinos around the globe look to the Philippine Senate as a reflection of our democracy. Let us give them a reason to admire our institutions—not question them.

The Filipino people deserve a Senate that spends more time solving national problems than creating political spectacles. We deserve leaders who inspire trust instead of division, confidence instead of exhaustion, and hope instead of cynicism.

We expect more from our senators because the Philippines deserves better.

Respectfully,

Mon Abrea

A Filipino citizen and taxpayer

Mon Abrea is a Global Tax Policy Expert and Chief Tax Advisor of the Asian Consulting Group (ACGlobal), the Philippines’ premier international tax advisory and investment consulting tirm. A graduate of Harvard, with executive education at Oxford and advanced tax policy studies at Duke, he is known as “The Philippine Tax Whiz” and a leading advocate of genuine tax reform, advising multinational corporations, foreign investors, and policymakers. Follow him @askthetaxwhiz

World.title: For experts, blanket phone ban in schools is not the way to go
World.content:
Currently, the Department of Education prohibits the use of phones and other electronic gadgets during class time, except for academic purposes and emergencies. Students can still use their devices during recess or breaks.

MANILA, Philippines – Instead of an outright ban on mobile phones and other gadgets in schools, local medical experts are recommending age-based regulation.

The Philippine Mental Health Association (PMHA) and the Philippine Psychiatric Association (PPA) raised the suggeston as the House committees on basic education and health held a joint hearing on six bills seeking to either ban or regulate on-campus gadget usage on Monday, July 20.

Dr. Carolina Uno-Rayco, PMHA national executive director, laid out what’s at stake: “Excessive screen time is fueling a youth mental health crisis. More than three hours of social media daily doubles depression and anxiety risks, while more than four hours links to ADHD (attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder) symptoms, sleep loss, and reduced focus.”

According to the 2022 Programme for International Student Assessment, around 41% of Filipino students said they get distracted using digital devices, which has affected learning of mathematics lessons. (READ: PH still among lowest in math, science, reading in global student assessment)

Currently, the Department of Education (DepEd) prohibits the use of phones and other electronic gadgets during class time, except for academic purposes and emergencies. Students can still use their devices during recess or breaks.

Pasig City Representative Roman Romulo, chairman of the House basic education panel, described the DepEd’s policy on gadgets as unclear and ineffective, urging education officials to rethink the protocol.

Romulo said he wants to ensure that students would be more focused on lessons, following the DepEd’s assessment that around 87% of Grade 11 students were non-independent readers.

For the PMHA, the policy requires stronger legislation for uniform enforcement across schools.

Play Video

Rayco also explained that it is crucial to provide alternative activities to students instead of just enforcing a gadget ban. These activities include sports, physical and social interactions, and other group activities that hone social skills.

While aiming to primarily address the health effects of gadget use, the renewed push for a ban or regulation came following the deadly school shooting in Tacloban City.

Authorities have been looking into the influence of online extremism on two minors who carried out the June 22 shooting, where three students were killed and 20 others injured.

On June 29, the municipal government of Dumanjug in Cebu province enforced a total ban on mobile phones in schools to encourage students to read and interact with their classmates, SunStar Cebu reported.

What experts propose

PMHA’s Rayco suggested the prohibition of gadget use for children aged zero to two years old, then a one-hour cap for children two to five years old. She said this is in line with the recommendation of the World Health Organization.

Meanwhile, the PPA recommended “developmentally-tiered regulation,” which would entail prohibiting gadgets during class time for kindergarten to Grade 3 students, then a shift to “supervised, graduated, and increasingly self-directed use” for older students.

Play Video

Dr. Joan Mae Perez-Rifareal, the PPA’s immediate past president, said the age group of kindergarten to Grade 3 has “the least capacity for self-regulation and the most to lose developmentally from gadget displaced learning and play.”

“Adolescence in particular is the stage in which digital literacy and self-regulation must be actively practiced under guidance and not simply deferred until adulthood,” Rifareal said.

“So, clearly defined exceptions for instructional, health, and emergency use together with due process safeguards such as parental notification and chain of custody protection in cases of gadget confiscation are consistent with clinical evidence…and therefore, visible, supervised, rule-governed use is safer for a child’s development than use driven underground by blanket bans,” she added.

For its part, the Second Congressional Commission on Education (EDCOM 2) also backs having a “differentiated model” that is determined by age and key stage.

EDCOM 2 Executive Director Karol Mark Yee recommended a “strict no personal device in school policy” for kindergarten to Grade 6, as well as a “managed access policy” for Grades 7 to 12, where devices are used only for purposes of instruction.

Yee said schools must set guidelines on how to store gadgets outside class hours.

The Teachers’ Dignity Coalition told lawmakers that it supports regulation of gadget use, and not an outright ban, as teachers and students alike have to use devices amid a shortage of textbooks.

What House bills say

Two out of the six bills being tackled have the same framework as the experts’ recommendations. However, the measure filed by Asenso Pinoy Representative Henry Oaminal Jr. seeks to regulate screen time of children even outside school premises.

Under House Bill No. 7887, Oaminal proposed prohibiting screen time for children two years old and younger, a one-hour cap for kids two to five years old, and a two-hour cap for those six to 12 years old.

For those 13 years old and above, the bill emphasizes regulation focusing on digital literacy, responsible use, and supervised independence, including measures to discourage excessive or unsupervised gadget use, particularly during nighttime.

Oaminal suggested tapping barangay health workers to help in regulating gadget use of children in home and community settings. In schools, devices would only be allowed for academic purposes during class hours, or in cases where students have health conditions that require the use of gadgets.

EDCOM 2’s Yee said other aspects of the proposals also need to be further studied, including the role of various government agencies in regulation of children’s gadget usage and parallel legislation to protect children from online harms. – Rappler.com

World.title: [Vantage Point] Pax Silica: America’s blueprint for the AI economy
World.content:
It’s an invitation to the high table of 21st-century industrial power. And the table is set in Clark.

This analysis draws from an hour-long interview with former Philippine National Railways chairperson Michael Ted Macapagal and the documents he shared with Vantage Point, as well as public statements made by Finance Secretary Frederick Go.

Before entering public service, Macapagal worked as a corporate executive in the US and later held key roles involving the Clark and Subic corridors. His insights into Pax Silica combine private-sector experience with a firsthand understanding of the infrastructure and regulatory hurdles facing the country’s key investment hubs. Although recent reports link him to the leadership of the Bases Conversion and Development Authority, no official appointment has been made.

The announcement that Taiwanese manufacturing giant Foxconn, which produces an estimated 40% of the world’s consumer electronics globally, intends to anchor the first US-led Pax Silica technology hub in New Clark City was met with the standard fanfare reserved for massive foreign direct investment victories.

Yet looking at Foxconn merely as another corporate tenant misses a vital systemic shift. The global economy is quietly but permanently reorganizing its architecture around artificial intelligence, semiconductor fabrication, and trusted technology supply chains.

By stepping into this framework, the Philippines has unexpectedly found itself thrust into one of the most momentous industrial realignments since the end of the Cold War. Whether this historic invitation fundamentally transforms the country’s economic future or simply reinforces its legacy role as a low-cost, back-end assembly line will depend entirely on the strategic choices Manila executes over the coming decade.

Finance Secretary Frederick Go has said that the government hopes to sign the formal framework agreement which will establish this hub before the end of the year.

To appreciate the gravity of the Pax Silica framework, one must understand the macroeconomic and geopolitical anxieties that birthed it. Conceived inside the US Department of State by Undersecretary of State for Economic Affairs Jacob Helberg, the initiative serves as Washington’s premier economic security strategy in the AI era. (READ: US Pax Silica initiative: Good or bad?)

The etymology of the name itself is highly deliberate: Pax, the Latin word for peace, evokes a stable international order, while Silica refers to the compound refined into silicon, the absolute bedrock of modern computing hardware. If oil dictated the geopolitical chessboard and energy security paradigms of the 20th century, silicon will indisputably govern the 21st.

Rather than continuing to rely on hyper-globalized but highly vulnerable supply chains, Washington is assembling a robust coalition of trusted allies to secure semiconductors, advanced manufacturing, critical minerals, and AI infrastructure from geopolitical coercion.

Luzon Economic Corridor

Since its initial launch in December 2025, Pax Silica has scaled with remarkable speed, growing into a formidable 24-member coalition following its mid-2026 Washington summit, which incorporated key partners across Europe, Asia, and Latin America. The Philippines formally aligned itself with this vision in April 2026, positioning itself as a vital, strategic node within Southeast Asia.

Geography explains a portion of Washington’s sudden, intense focus on Manila. Positioned adjacent to Taiwan — the world’s undisputed semiconductor powerhouse — and flanking critical global shipping corridors, the Philippines is an ideal physical logistics anchor.

However, its institutional advantages are what truly caught the attention of American policymakers, including a steadfast treaty alliance with the US, vast unmined reserves of critical “green tech” minerals like nickel and copper, and a young, English-fluent technical workforce.

As traditional regional manufacturing hubs like Vietnam and Malaysia become increasingly enmeshed with Chinese capital, the Philippines offers an uncompromised “trusted node” capable of supporting sensitive Western aerospace, defense, and advanced AI hardware stacks.

At the center of this execution is the Luzon Economic Corridor, a trilateral infrastructure network backed aggressively by the US and Japan. Under a master plan managed by the Bases Conversion and Development Authority, approximately 1,618 hectares of New Clark City are being transformed into an AI-native industrial zone.

This blueprint integrates advanced semiconductor fabrication, hyperscale AI data centers, and a permanent regional Pax Silica Coordination Office to synchronize private enterprise with allied regulatory frameworks, all the while linking Subic Bay’s deepwater capacities through Manila to Batangas via planned high-capacity rail links.

Play Video

This institutional backing explains why Foxconn’s pending arrival carries significance that stretches far beyond a typical corporate expansion. While globally recognized for assembling consumer electronics, Foxconn has transformed itself into a dominant force in the global AI universe.

It is by no means a giant in the server hardware market, manufacturing the complex computing chassis and advanced components that power the world’s largest hyperscale data centers. In the realm of industrial policy, anchor investors possess the unique ability to create self-sustaining ecosystems.

Taiwan’s own semiconductor hegemony did not emerge from isolated factories, but rather from the dense, deliberate clustering of complementary industries.

If Foxconn finalizes its commitment to New Clark City as its priority locator for electronics component manufacturing, it will serve as a global validator for the hub, inevitably drawing in upstream suppliers, logistics providers, precision engineering firms, and specialized chemical companies.

Domestic realities

This presents the Philippines with a rare generational window to move past low-margin, back-end operations and capture highly lucrative segments of advanced electronics and hardware engineering.

Yet, capital injection alone does not guarantee structural transformation because moving up the technology ladder requires confronting stark domestic realities.

Semiconductor fabrication and AI operations are notoriously resource-intensive industries: a single advanced sub-7 nanometer fabrication plant can consume upward of 100 megawatts of continuous power alongside millions of gallons of ultra-pure water daily, while hyperscale AI data centers require similarly massive, unblinking energy loads.

These requirements will severely stress the Philippine power grid, water infrastructure, and local utilities long before the first components roll off the line in Clark. Furthermore, policymakers must fight the historical tendency of the Philippines to attract export-oriented multinational corporations via specialized economic zones while capturing very little of the actual value created.

The country’s historical semiconductor footprint remains limited to low-margin Assembly, Testing, and Packaging, while intellectual property, design, patents, and high-value research remain securely offshore.

Without active government intervention, New Clark City risks becoming just another tax-sheltered manufacturing enclave. Philippine agencies must aggressively use the CREATE MORE Act — which lowers corporate taxes and enhances investment incentives — alongside bilateral agreements to enforce technology transfers, train local engineers, and build joint research pipelines.

There is also a distinct geopolitical premium to calculate, as entering America’s trusted tech network firmly aligns Manila with Washington’s broader tech-containment strategy against Beijing.

While the commercial and defense incentives are potent, deep integration carries profound diplomatic friction with China — the Philippines’ largest trading partner — and leaves Philippine industrial health completely vulnerable to the unpredictable shifts of American domestic politics and future trade policies.

Ultimately, Pax Silica is an invitation to the high table of 21st-century industrial power. Taiwan and South Korea have achieved economic indispensability by mastering the top tiers of the technological stack. Now, the table is set in Clark.

I welcome your views on these and other issues where decisions made in power shape the country’s economic future.

World.title: Sara Duterte impeachment trial: Chel Diokno arguments please the ‘cheldren’
World.content:
LIKE FATHER. Counsel for the prosecution Rep. Chel Diokno makes a manifestation during day six of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte on July 15, 2026.

Incidentally, the defense team of the late ex-chief justice Renato Corona also used the same Stonehill vs Diokno case to show he was being unjustly prosecuted

Day 7 of the Sara Duterte impeachment trial on Monday, July 20, showed what a court veteran is made of: quick to the draw, armed with depth and decorum, poised for balls thrown from left field.

Many forget that Akbayan Representative Chel Diokno spent decades defending the prosecuted, thus priming him for the roadblocks that a well-oiled defense team will throw his way. The “cheldren” — his youth base when he ran — must have been pleased.

The Senate courtroom on Monday looked and sounded different, the sing-song cadence of Diokno and defense counsel Michael Poa filling the air. Here were two opposing lawyers standing their ground without flipping their heads or clenching their fists, telling us in clear language what the laws on bank and tax records mean to privacy and public accountability.

Even the Cayetano siblings tried to temper their tone.

“I recognize that you’re a brilliant man, learned in law,” Senator-judge Alan Peter Cayetano told Diokno, before he grilled the former human rights lawyer with questions not about Ms. Duterte, but about President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.

If the assets records of the Vice President that span decades could be opened for this trial, why did the House committee that looked into the Marcos impeachment complaint not impose the same on him? For a moment there, Diokno appeared surprised by the curveball query, but with clasped hands he brought Cayetano down to earth. Watch it here.

The Cayetanos — two lawyers whose father was also a senator and lawyer — were given the floor to puncture the prosecution’s plea for the impeachment court to subpoena Duterte’s bank and tax records, as well as that of her husband, lawyer Mans Carpio. They zeroed in on two doctrines on why this should not be granted: the “fruit of the poisonous tree” and “fishing expedition.”

On both topics, they gave Diokno a nasty jab by citing a landmark 1967 Supreme Court case that ruled against his venerable father, then-justice minister Jose Wright Diokno. What Senator Pia Cayetano was trying to say, in effect, was, didn’t your father lose that case because he searched and seized items of American businessman Harry Stonehill on the basis of a “general warrant” that the High Tribunal eventually declared unconstitutional?

One could not have asked a better man to address the difference between a subpoena and a search warrant; he had spent a lifetime in the trenches questioning illegal raids and searches committed against his impoverished clients. Chel Diokno would not be baited into defending a father who did not need defending, and gave a quick lecture on why a subpoena is “not a license,” while a search warrant is “invasive” and open to abuse — and that they are governed by different sets of rules. Watch it here.

Stonehill and Corona

Incidentally, the defense team of the late dismissed chief justice Renato Corona also used the same Stonehill argument in its opening statement during his 2012 impeachment trial.

Corona’s lead defense counsel then, Eduardo delos Angeles, cited the case to explain how then-president Noynoy Aquino was using his power to bring down Corona. “The Stonehill case is strikingly similar to the crusade of President Aquino. In both, there are crusading officials who want to eliminate corruption. In both, the public overwhelmingly support these officials. In both, the officials unfortunately transgressed the Constitution,” he said.

Duterte’s defense team is adamant in its stand that to subpoena the bank and tax records of its client from years even before she became vice president was tantamount to a “fishing expedition.” Counsel Poa also cited the “absolute prohibition” in the anti-money laundering law regarding the public release of bank transactions. What’s the point of the prosecution in asking for them, asked Poa? “Transactions do not equate to wealth or net worth.” Watch it here.

The fishing expedition is “baka sakali, on the off-chance,” countered Diokno, an argument that is “untenable,” given the amount of public records that the prosecution has submitted to bolster their case before the court. Watch it here.

At stake on Monday was the very foundation — in the form of government records — of the House prosecution’s charge that the Vice President had amassed unexplained wealth. The court ruled in favor of issuing subpoenas to the critical agencies holding such records: the Bureau of Internal Revenue and the Anti-Money Laundering Council.

Play Video

It’s a long way to go, as we spelled out in this story, but a big win nonetheless because, in the words of former Erap Estrada impeachment prosecutor Oscar Moreno, bank records do not lie.

Before the court went to the business of the day, Senator Erwin Tulfo made an impassioned plea for the senator-judges to avoid raising issues not related to the case. The senators seem to have heeded it.

But Day 8, Tuesday, July 21, promises to raise the temperature again, because of the man of the house: prosecution witness Melvin Matibag, director of the National Bureau of Investigation, whose team attempted to arrest the now fugitive Senator Bato dela Rosa during the May chaos in the Senate and who has started a probe into Alan Cayetano’s alleged questionable acts as government lead in the 2019 Southeast Asian Games held here. – Rappler.com

World.title: US judge approves Anthropic’s $1.5-billion settlement of copyright lawsuit
World.content:
ANTHROPIC. The Anthropic logo, a keyboard, and a robotic hand are shown in this illustration created on June 5, 2026.

US District Judge Araceli Martinez-Olguin grants final approval of the settlement, the largest known settlement of a US copyright case, rejecting arguments that it was too small

A federal judge in San Francisco on Monday, July 20, signed off on artificial intelligence company Anthropic’s landmark $1.5-billion settlement of a class action lawsuit brought by a group of authors who accused it of misusing their books to train its AI chatbot Claude.

US District Judge Araceli Martinez-Olguin granted final approval of the settlement, the largest known settlement of a US copyright case, rejecting arguments that it was too small.

The case is one of dozens brought by copyright owners including authors and news outlets against tech companies over the training of their large language models, and the first major US case to settle.

Now-retired Judge William Alsup initially approved the deal last September.

“We reached this settlement in 2025, after the court’s landmark ruling that training AI on books is fair use under copyright law — which remains the law today,” Anthropic deputy general counsel Aparna Sridhar said in a statement.

“We are pleased that more than 91% of authors and publishers covered by the settlement have claimed their share of the payment, and we’re looking forward to bringing this matter to a close.”

The authors’ lead attorney, Justin Nelson, welcomed what he called a “historic settlement.”

“It is the largest known copyright recovery in history. We look forward to making distributions to the Class as promptly as possible,” Nelson said in a statement, referring to payments to authors covered by the settlement.

The writers sued Anthropic in 2024, arguing that the company, which is backed by ⁠Amazon and Alphabet, used pirated versions of their books without permission to teach Claude to respond to human prompts.

Alsup ruled last June ​that Anthropic made fair ⁠use of the authors’ work to train Claude, but found that the company violated their rights by saving more than 7 million pirated books to a “central library” ​that would not necessarily be used for AI training.

A trial was scheduled to begin last December ⁠to determine how much Anthropic owed for the alleged piracy, with potential damages running into the hundreds of billions of dollars.

The settlement spurred objections from some authors who argued it ​was not large enough, overcompensated the plaintiffs’ attorneys or wrongly excluded some copyright owners.

Judge Martinez-Olguin overruled those objections in her ruling on Monday. The judge said that complaints about the settlement’s size were “not grounded in a realistic assessment of the overall risks and rewards of a trial,” and awarded the attorneys more than $101 million of the $187.5 million they requested in fees.

Some authors and publishers opted out of the settlement and have filed separate lawsuits against Anthropic that are still ongoing. – Rappler.com

World.title: Bukidnon seniors receive P3,000 social pension payout
World.content:
Senior citizens in San Fernando, Bukidnon, line up to receive their P3,000 cash assistance under the national government’s Social Pension Program during the payout that began on July 20, 2026. Photo courtesy of Mckiey Paparon

SAN FERNANDO, Bukidnon — Around 3,000 senior citizens in this town began receiving on Monday P3,000 each under the national government’s Social Pension Program, local officials said.The first payout was held at the Kalagangan Multipurpose Gym, where about 640 beneficiaries from barangays Matupi, Durian, Tabuling, Kalagangan, Payaga, San Jose, Sto. Domingo, and Bunacao received their cash assistance, said Jenevieve Trigo, Office of the Senior Citizens Affairs (OSCA) focal person.The second payout was conducted at the Halapitan gym for 1,514 beneficiaries from the barangays of Tugop, Nakabuklad, Little Baguio, Mabayanan, Sacramento Valley, Mabuhay, and Candelaria.

READ: DSWD social pension program to prioritize oldest indigent FilipinosMayor Rogelio Yeke urged senior citizens to use the cash assistance for food, medicines, and vitamins, instead of spending it on non-essential items or giving it to relatives.The final payout is scheduled on Wednesday, July 22, at the Namnam covered court for 733 beneficiaries from the barangays of Magkalungay, Dao, Bulalang, Iglusad, Kibungkog, Palacpacan, and Kawayan.Trigo also said two residents—one Lumad and one non-Lumad—are expected to qualify as centenarians next year and will each receive the P100,000 centenarian incentive under the Expanded Centenarians Act./coa

World.title: Kapatid to Cayetano: ‘Political prisoner’ label cannot sanitize corruption
World.content:
A composite image of the Kapatid statement and Sens. Rodante Marcoleta and Jinggoy Estrada from INQUIRER FILE

MANILA, Philippines — A support group for families and friends of political prisoners rejected Sen. Alan Peter Cayetano’s description of jailed politicians Rodante Marcoleta, Jinggoy Estrada and Mike Defensor as “political prisoners,” saying the term cannot be used to “sanitize corruption.”

Kapatid spokesperson Fides Lim said political prisoners are detained because of political persecution or for exercising fundamental rights — not merely because they are politicians who claim their prosecution is politically motivated.

“A political prisoner is defined not by any official status but by the reason for their detention,” Lim said in a statement Tuesday, July 21.

Article continues after this 

Over the weekend, Cayetano said in a Facebook Live video that the Department of Justice and the Office of the Ombudsman were being “weaponized” to advance political interests. He also said he believed Marcoleta, Estrada and Defensor would regain their freedom.

“I consider Sen. Jinggoy, Sen. Marcoleta, former congressman Mike Defensor, they are political prisoners,” Cayetano said Saturday, July 18.

Two days later, during the seventh day of the Senate impeachment proceedings against Vice President Sara Duterte, Cayetano repeated the assertion, saying Marcoleta and Estrada were “political prisoners” and that the Blue Ribbon Committee had been “weaponized.”

Lim countered that “the defining characteristic of political imprisonment is political persecution.”

“In these cases, the state routinely fabricates or manipulates criminal charges against dissidents and activists to hide the purely political nature of their arrest,” she said.

Article continues after this 

Lim cited Resolution 1900 (2012) of the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe and other international human rights standards, under which a political prisoner is someone deprived of liberty through politically motivated state action or for exercising fundamental rights such as freedom of expression, assembly and association.

The principle is also reflected in Article III, Section 18(1) of the 1987 Philippine Constitution: “No person shall be detained solely by reason of his political beliefs and aspirations.”

Article continues after this 

“As an organization composed of the families of political prisoners, Kapatid knows this reality firsthand,” Lim said.

She said most of the country’s estimated 675 political prisoners come from poor and working-class communities.

Lim said they “were arrested for organizing and protesting against state actions and instrumentalities that oppress marginalized sectors, violate human rights, and undermine national sovereignty and patrimony.”

“Many have been subjected to systematic red-tagging, trumped-up criminal offenses, planted evidence, and prolonged detention,” she said.

“We know what political persecution looks like, and the cases of these politicians and their den of thieves do not fit the definition,” Lim said.

She said their detention arose from allegations of election offenses for receiving and providing undeclared campaign contributions, and collecting illegal kickbacks from government-funded public infrastructure projects.

These were serious offenses involving the abuse of public office and betrayal of public trust, she said.

READ: Marcoleta, 3 others arrested for plunder

Estrada was arrested on plunder and graft charges, while Marcoleta was charged with plunder and violation of Presidential Decree No. 46.

Defensor’s case was related to the complaint against Marcoleta, who received millions in campaign donations from him.

READ: Jinggoy Estrada to be committed to Payatas jail

“They are not political prisoners simply because they are politicians nor because they claim their prosecutions are politically motivated,” Lim said.

She said Kapatid harbors no illusions about the “deeply flawed” Philippine justice system, which has long been marked by political influence, selective prosecution and double standards.

“Those systemic defects do not convert accountability for corruption into political martyrdom,” she said.

“To describe those charged with corruption as ‘political prisoners’ distorts both law and history,” Lim said.

She said the term “political prisoner” is not a rhetorical device to sanitize corruption.

“It is reserved exclusively for those deprived of liberty for exercising their fundamental rights in the struggle for genuine social justice — a path defined not by self-interest but by selflessness, sacrifice, and a commitment to the collective good,” she said. /dm

World.title: PNP on alert for possible cyber threats ahead of Sona 2026
World.content:
File photo. The Congress plenary during President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s fourth State of the Nation Address. INQUIRER/ MARIANNE BERMUDEZ

MANILA, Philippines — The Philippine National Police (PNP) is on alert for possible cyber threats ahead of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s fifth State of the Nation Address (Sona) this coming Monday, July 27.

“Our primary concerns are cyberattacks against critical information infrastructure, the spread of misinformation and coordinated influence operations, and online scams that exploit public interest in the Sona,” PNP chief Gen. Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. said in a statement Tuesday.

“We are closely monitoring the cyber landscape and are prepared to respond to threats in coordination with our partner agencies,” he maintained.

Article continues after this 

READ: Marcos’ 5th Sona to be ‘simple yet dignified’, says Palace

The annual Sona gathers many top government officials for the president’s annual address to a joint session of Congress, serving as the chief executive’s report on the country’s situation.

Around 20,000 personnel will be deployed for security measures during the 2026 Sona, the PNP previously said.

At least four groups are expected to stage rallies ahead of the Sona, according to the National Capital Region Police Office.

“Cybersecurity is now as important as physical security during major national events,” Nartatez said.

“Protecting digital systems, ensuring the integrity of information, and safeguarding the public from online threats are essential to maintaining public order and confidence throughout the Sona,” he added. /mr

World.title: Marcos unveils upgraded Lucena port terminal, boosting regional travel
World.content:
Photos courtesy of Malacañang Press Corps pool

MANILA, Philippines — President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. on Tuesday said the newly upgraded Passenger Terminal Building (PTB) at the Port of Lucena in Quezon would make travel more convenient for around 500,000 passengers annually.

The port serves as Southern Luzon’s primary roll-on/roll-off gateway, linking mainland Luzon to Marinduque and neighboring island provinces.

READ: Lucena City launches river rehab drive, collects 105 sacks of waste

Article continues after this 

Designed to meet the growing demand for passenger travel, the new PTB features a spacious, fully air-conditioned waiting area with a seating capacity of approximately 1,000 passengers.

Photos courtesy of Malacañang Press Corps pool

Photos courtesy of Malacañang Press Corps pool

It also has automated ticketing counters, modern comfort rooms, improved passenger amenities, enhanced ventilation systems, and solar panels that promote energy-efficient and sustainable port operations.

In a brief statement after inspecting the facility, Marcos said the project is expected to boost tourism, trade, and local economic activity across the Calabarzon and Mimaropa regions while supporting transport operators, shipping lines, restaurants, retail establishments, and other local businesses.

“Good for the farmers of the region, good for Lucena, good for all the surrounding parts,” he said.

“We also have facilities in place in case there are stranded individuals. As we know, typhoons are becoming more frequent nowadays,” he also said.

Article continues after this 

Aside from inspecting the upgraded port terminal, Marcos also awarded Certificates of Entitlement (COEs) to 100 additional beneficiaries in Lucena City under the expanded Pambansang Pabahay para sa Pilipino Program.

The COEs represent an important step toward the processing of land titles and the formal recognition of beneficiaries’ rights to the land allocated to them.

Article continues after this 

A total of 185 beneficiaries had previously received their COEs last year and in March. The program aims to award COEs to a total of 1,119 beneficiaries in Lucena City. /mr

World.title: PNP orders review of cases involving minors to better cater to youth
World.content:
Philippine National Police chief Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. — Photo from Office of the Chief PNP/Facebook

MANILA, Philippines — Philippine National Police (PNP) chief, Gen. Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. ordered the agency to review its recorded cases of minors violating the law as part of an effort to better cater to the youth.

“The Philippine National Police honors and supports the wisdom behind the juvenile justice and welfare law and its genuine intent of reforms and rehabilitation to become better citizens that contribute to nation building,” Nartatez said in a statement on Tuesday.

“As one of the frontliners in dealing with children in conflict with the law, we in the PNP need to review and analyze everything to come up with a better police approach that is responsive to their life’s changes as youth, and that also adapts to the constantly evolving modern society,” he maintained.

Article continues after this 

READ: PNP logs 1,275 school-related incidents from 2022 to 2025

Public interest in Republic Act No. 9344 or the Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act was renewed over the past month when a 14-year-old and a 15-year-old allegedly shot up a Tacloban City school, killing three students and injuring 20 more.

In the wake of the incident, the PNP said it advocated for a lowering of the minimum age of criminal responsibility, after the 14-year-old suspect in the Tacloban case was turned over to social workers in accordance with RA No. 9344.

The PNP also expressed support for the Department of Education’s push to increase counselling in schools, following reports that the two suspects had been bullied, which supposedly motivated the shooting.

“Such interactions and counselling could also lead to a better approach in dealing with school bullying and even students who are engaged in school bomb hoaxes,” Nartatez said.

“The Philippine National Police is not only about law enforcement and anti-crime operations. Your PNP also wants to do its share in a comprehensive and holistic approach to make every community a safe and better place to live in,” he added. /mr

World.title: Tipsters receive over P9M for arrest of 21 wanted persons
World.content:
In a ceremony in Camp Crame, Quezon City on Tuesday, July 21, 2026, Philippine National Police (PNP) chief Gen. Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. (center) leads the turnover of P9,725,000 monetary reward to confidential informants, whose tips led to the arrest of 21 wanted persons across the country. (Photo courtesy of PNP Press Corps pool)

MANILA, Philippines — The Philippine National Police (PNP) on Tuesday awarded a total of P9.275 million in monetary rewards to confidential informants whose tips led to the arrest of 21 wanted persons across the country.

The rewards were presented during a ceremony at Camp Crame in Quezon City, with the informants wearing black clothing and face coverings to conceal their identities.

Article continues after this 

READ: Tipsters get P10.6-M reward for arrest of 30 wanted persons

According to an information sheet by the PNP, the rewards included:

P2.995 million for the arrest of seven persons wanted for murder;

P840,000 for the arrest of six persons wanted for rape;

P1.35 million for the arrest of two persons wanted for syndicated estafa;

P245,000 for the arrest of two persons wanted for violation of Republic Act No. 7610 or the Special Protection of Children Against Abuse, Exploitation and Discrimination Act;

P765,000 for the arrest of a person wanted for violation of RA No. 9516, which pertains to the illegal trade of explosives, and RA No. 10591 or the Firearms and Ammunition Regulation Act; and

P250,000 for the arrest of a person wanted for robbery with multiple homicide

The PNP explained that the reward for the arrest of 19 wanted persons came through a Department of Interior and Local Government (DILG) memorandum circular.

Meanwhile, a joint order issued by the Department of National Defense (DND) and the DILG authorized a P2.83-million reward for information leading to the arrest of two other suspects, who were allegedly members of a communist terrorist group and are wanted for murder.

“This will greatly help our organization,” PNP chief Gen. Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. said in an interview following the turnover ceremony.

“We’re helping each other to account for and arrest all our fugitives. There are 500,000 people, if I’m not mistaken, who are covered by a warrant of arrest and we will go after them one-by-one.”/dp

World.title: Prosecution awaits ‘whale’s worth’ of evidence vs Duterte – Ridon
World.content:
Rep. Terry Ridon —File photo by Grig C. Montegrande | INQUIRER

MANILA, Philippines — The House prosecution panel is awaiting what it described as a “whale’s worth of evidence” against Vice President Sara Duterte after the Senate Impeachment Court granted its request to subpoena her financial records, Bicol Saro party-list Rep. Terry Ridon said on Tuesday.

In a statement, Ridon said that the prosecution is not aiming for small fish or even a shark, but a whale in terms of the weight of evidence that may be used against the vice president.

“From today up to July 30, the prosecution will monitor to catch, not a fish nor a shark, but a whale’s worth of evidence — P6.7 Billion in total transactions. P4.4 Billion in inflows,” he said.

Article continues after this 

According to the lawmaker, the total transactions flagged by the Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) can be used for the following purposes:

aid for 1.6 million families

fuel subsidies for 1.3 million public transport drivers

hospital expenses of 1.9 million patients

college scholarships for 893,000 students

“In other words — for almost 20 years, the movements that passed through the bank accounts of the Duterte-Carpio couple, were as big as government transactions. But who are they? Government officials, lawyers, people who have losing businesses, but they have transactions as big as the government,” he said, adding that such will be the summary of the article on unexplained wealth.

The AMLC’s report on transactions involving Duterte and her husband, lawyer Manases Carpio, first surfaced during the April 22 hearing of the House Committee on Justice.

This was when the committee on justice was discussing the two impeachment complaints against Duterte, particularly on allegations of unexplained wealth and alleged non-disclosure of assets in her Statement of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALN).

During the said hearing, AMLC Executive Director Ronel Buenaventura admitted that they found covered and suspicious transactions made by the Duterte-Carpio couple.

Article continues after this 

Buenaventura made the disclosure after Deputy Speaker Ferjenel Biron asked whether the AMLC had identified suspicious transactions involving Duterte and her relatives.

The AMLC official later clarified that covered transactions are bank transactions over P500,000, which banks report to the council, while suspicious transactions refer to those whose amounts are not determined, but were reported by banks because there is something questionable in terms of how funds were sourced.

Article continues after this 

READ: AMLC confirms suspicious transactions made by Sara Duterte, kin

Later that day, Mamamayang Liberal party-list Rep. Leila de Lima randomly picked 19 financial transactions mentioned in the sworn affidavit of former Senator Antonio Trillanes IV — a staunch Duterte critic who claimed to have obtained files pointing to the Vice President’s bank accounts that supposedly stored her unexplained wealth.

Eventually, Buenaventura confirmed that the 19 transactions randomly picked by de Lima from the affidavit appeared in the AMLC reports — lending support to Trillanes’ claims regarding the transactions.

READ: Trillanes vindicated: AMLC confirms Sara Duterte’s 18 transactions

The Senate Impeachment Court on Monday afternoon granted the House prosecution panel’s request to subpoena Duterte’s financial records.

The prosecution sought the records in connection with Article II of the Articles of Impeachment.

Ridon is the team leader for Article II.

Presiding Officer and Senator-judge Francis Escudero read the ruling, where the Senate Impeachment Court allowed the subpoena, save for a few companies where no immediate links to the Vice President were seen.

“The request for subpoenas directed to the concerned banking institutions, covering the accounts of the Respondent, Atty. Manases Carpio, separately or jointly, the partnership of Carpio Lawyers, and the nineteen listed corporate entities, is granted,” Escudero said.

“The banks are ordered to submit to the Clerk of Court the documents on July 30, 2026 at 9:00 AM with the attendance of the parties’ counsels,” he added.

The court said the records are prima facie relevant and material to Article II (unexplained wealth) and are not a “fishing expedition” because they are intended to establish a factual baseline for assessing whether Duterte’s assets and financial transactions during her term are disproportionate to her lawful income.

READ: Impeachment court grants subpoena for Duterte’s financial records

Furthermore, the court decided that the defense’s argument — that the Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) is not protected from a court’s compulsory processes — is misplaced.

READ: Duterte impeachment trial: Senate junks bid vs AMLC report

After the trial, House prosecutor and Akbayan party-list Rep. Chel Diokno, who represented the prosecution panel during the oral arguments on the request for subpoena, said that the court’s decision is a victory for the Filipino people.
