World.title: How this Champions League winner aims to ignite Stingers
World.content:
Australia's women's water polo team, the Stingers, are no strangers to success.

Winning a silver medal at the Paris Olympics, the best performance by any Australian team at those Games, put the Stingers right in the upper echelons of their field.

It's what makes the World Aquatics Water Polo World Cup finals, being hosted in Australia from July 22-26 at the Sydney Aquatics Centre at Homebush, so exciting.

But the fact the Stingers are challenging at the top of the world rankings is no accident.

The entire team is packed with genuine superstars, playing in some of Europe's biggest clubs in the biggest competitions in the world.

Abby Andrews has proven herself to be one of the very best.

Abby Andrews's first major trophy was the biggest in club water polo. (Supplied: Instagram)

The 25-year-old left-handed shooter won the LEN European Champions League title with Greek giants Olympiacos earlier this year.

Not only that, but the Brisbane native was named the most valuable player in the Final Four tournament, scoring four goals in the semifinal and a fabulous five in the final.

"It was definitely an out-of-body experience," the 25-year-old told ABC Sport ahead of this week's World Aquatics Water Polo World Cup event in Sydney.

"I mean, as an Australian, we always look and we watch the Champions League finals every year and we always think, 'Oh, how cool would it be to be in that, let alone win?'

"I said to some of my [Stingers] teammates here in Australia when I got back, I don't think I've ever won anything.

"Actually being able to lift a cup and just the feeling of euphoria with that, and the celebrations and our massive fan base in Europe is insane …

"That was probably one of the coolest moments of my life. It was awesome."

Abby Andrews scored nine goals across the semifinal and final. (Supplied: LEN European Aquatics)

Andrews's Olympiacos side beat Barcelona-based CN Mataró, featuring Stingers teammate Tilly Kearns, 14-12 in the semifinal, before downing Hungarian giants Ferencvárosi TC in the final by a score of 17-14.

"As the season went on, our team was really gaining strength," Andrews said.

"The semifinal was tough, but I think it was a great stepping stone for us.

"And then the final was brutal. We had lots of momentum swings but honestly, until the very end, we just completely stuck together."

The Final Four, held on the Mediterranean island of Malta, was an enormous occasion, the first time the men's and women's competitions were held at the same venue at the same time.

That allowed the women's teams to truly benefit from the enormous and fanatical support of their ultras.

Loading Instagram content

"It's insane," Andrews admitted of the enormous support.

"I mean, certain games that we play will have flares. They'll have this massive police presence and you just never know like what the crowd's going to do; when they're going to start chanting, if they'll go quiet for a bit.

"It's just something we don't experience here.

"I think what's so cool about the European multi-sport organisations is that they're just fanatics, like, they are absolutely mad, but ultimately their presence is so lifting and we love playing in front of them.

"It's just such a different experience.

"And for women's water polo to get that kind of attention as well, both our men's and women's teams were in the Final Four and the men unfortunately lost the semi, so all the attention shifted to us and the fans just went, 'you know what, let's give [the support] to the women'."

Abby Andrews has been a mainstay in the Stingers team. (Getty Images: James Worsfold)

Andrews joined Olympiacos, the enormous multi-sport club based in the Piraeus region of Athens better known for its football team, soon after winning Olympic silver in 2024.

Having already played overseas in the American college system and in Italy, Andrews has been exposed to the very best of the best for her entire career.

Being able to cap her second season by winning the biggest prize in club water polo underlines the fact that she is on the right track personally.

"I think each experience teaches you something different," Andrews said.

"Having that exposure against the European powerhouses and just playing them regularly, having camps with them is honestly so invaluable and it's been a huge addition to my game.

"I love bringing the new techniques that they have, because obviously some Europeans are different in size, strength, skill and you kind of just adopt new methods as you see them. So it's really fun.

"I think my latest one in Olympiacos, it being my second year, I was able to establish myself more in the systems that the Greek teams play and really settle into that, as well as just realising that I can also step up and have a really big attacking presence.

"It's just such a cool environment to be in and I love like learning about myself in those environments and how I can step up."

Abby Andrews is expecting pressure at her first-ever home World Cup finals. (Getty Images: DeFodi Images/Marcel ter Bals)

Andrews did accept that playing at such a huge club comes with enormous pressure, but that it was "kind of a good extra pressure to have".

Extra pressure is something that Andrews is hoping to embrace over the next week, as the Stingers look to show off their status as genuine world challengers in the World Aquatics Water Polo World Cup, starting in Sydney on Wednesday.

The world's top eight men's and women's national water polo teams will all compete at the event at the Sydney Aquatic Centre, the first time the city has hosted a major global water polo competition since the 2000 Olympics.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Sydney has twice hosted the World Cup finals before: the men's edition in 1999, won by Hungary; and the women's in 1995, won by the Aussies.

The Women's World Cup has also been hosted in Brisbane (1981) and Perth (2002).

But as much as the overall goal is to win the title in Sydney, emulating the Australian women's water polo team that won gold in the same Sydney Olympic Pool at the Sydney Games of 2000, filling the stands and inspiring others to follow in the Stingers' wake is just as important.

"I think this new generation coming through is so eager, I've never seen this kind of excitement from the younger kids coming through," Andrews said.

"I think it's already got such a good momentum and I think if we can really build on that and just fill the stands, get everyone there.

"You're going to be seeing some high-quality water polo from every team around the world, and being able to have this at home, who knows when we'll have this again, maybe not until Brisbane [2032].

"So while we've got this, let's use it. Everyone come down. I just think it's going to be such a spectacle."

World.title: Kids do feel the cold. So why won't they wear a jumper?
World.content:
It happens just when you need to leave. Bags are packed. Shoes are on. Then your child decides a jumper is impossible.

You say: "Put your jumper on."

They say: "I'm not cold."

Do kids really not feel the cold like adults do? Or are they just expressing their independence? And when should you insist?

A clue from pain research

I study how children experience pain, and pain research offers one clue about this jumper battle.

A child may scrape their knee during a game and barely notice until the game stops. The scrape was there throughout, but chasing a friend or reaching the next base kept winning their attention.

The cold can slip into the background in a similar way. A child's fingers may be cooling while the playground remains far more compelling. Then the game ends.

Their attention returns to their hands around the same time their moving muscles stop producing so much heat. Suddenly, the jumper may seem like a better idea.

So "I'm not cold" can mean "I can feel it and I'm comfortable".

It can also mean "the jumper feels worse" or "I want to keep playing". Sometimes it means, "I am four years old and this has become a matter of principle".

Similarly, when parents ask, "But aren't you cold?" we're often asking several questions at once.

Will you still be warm when you stop running? What if the wind picks up? How about later, when we're standing still on the sideline at the soccer field?

Children report the present moment, and parents factor in the forecast.

What cold actually feels like

Your skin contains sensory nerve endings that respond as its temperature changes.

One cool-sensitive channel, called TRPM8, helps convert cooling at the skin into electrical activity in sensory nerves.

This is the same channel that menthol activates, which is why mint can make your mouth feel cool even when there's no real temperature change.

Why it's OK if your child won't wear warm clothing While it can be frustrating for parents and caregivers at times, experts say kids' innate urge to explore independence — like choosing their own clothes — is healthy.

And as you know with mint, a strong cooling sensation can sometimes become uncomfortable or even painful. Other factors such as wind, wetness, contact with cold surfaces, movement, and how much time we're outside can all influence how we experience temperature.

For example, a parent who is standing still in a playground, clutching a coffee, may be acutely aware of the gap in their coat where the icy wind is sneaking in.

But children tend to run, climb and jump in bursts — and moving muscles produce heat.

Children also differ from adults in body size, body composition, metabolism and how their circulation responds to cold.

One 2024 laboratory study, done indoors, looked at children aged six to nine. It found their sedentary metabolic rates (how much energy you're burning when you're resting) were about 39 per cent higher compared to adults in the study.

Their skin was also warmer over parts of their torso, and the skin on their hands recovered temperature and blood flow faster than adults after being exposed to the cold.

So it's not that kids don't feel the cold at all, but they may have quite a different experience from an adult standing in the same air.

Bodies prepare for what comes next

We often learn about thermoregulation — how the body maintains its core temperature — as though the body were simply a thermostat. The body detects a temperature change, then blood flow changes, and sweating or shivering bring it back towards the middle.

But our movement and behaviour also play an important role in maintaining this balance. When we're cold we may walk into sunshine, curl up, or add a layer; when we're hot we take one off. A child who keeps running may already be generating the warmth they need.

Bodies also prepare for expected demands. Researchers use the term allostasis to describe this wider process of how the body maintains stability through change.

Some adjustments happen automatically. For example, before we exercise, our heart rate and breathing begin adjusting for the work ahead. Others involve choices, such as moving into the sun, seeking shelter or reaching for warmer clothing.

But young children outsource some of this forecasting to adults.

Kids supply the live report from inside their body. We add the weather forecast and the schedule. We pack snacks for hunger that has yet to arrive, spare clothes for puddles yet to be found, and jumpers too.

What the jumper itself feels like

A jumper creates its own sensations. It may feel scratchy, bulky or restrictive. It can make climbing harder, then become hot and sweaty as soon as the child starts running.

Tags, seams and some fabrics can feel intensely unpleasant, especially for children with tactile sensitivities. Clothing tags and light touch, for example, can cause marked discomfort for some autistic children.

A child may genuinely prefer mildly cold skin to an irritating texture.

So it's worth asking whether "aren't you cold?" is the right question. Others may work better:

Are you comfortable? Will you be running or sitting still? Would you rather wear the jumper or carry it?

These questions help children connect what they feel now with what they may need later.

When should parents insist?

Parents should be firmer when a child is very young, wet, unwell, exposed to strong wind or likely to remain outside for a long time.

Persistent shivering or numbness means it is time to get warm. Increasing clumsiness, unusual drowsiness, confusion or reduced responsiveness can indicate hypothermia, where the body's core temperature has fallen dangerously low. Hypothermia is a medical emergency.

But for ordinary winter outings, flexible layers allow the plan to change. A jumper can be carried, added when activity slows, and removed when the child warms up again.

Your child reports the weather inside their body. You keep an eye on the weather outside it. A jumper in the bag lets your child feel heard, lets you keep the forecast in view, and lets everyone finally get out the door.

Joshua Pate is associate professor of physiotherapy, University of Technology Sydney. This piece first appeared on The Conversation.

World.title: China, Philippines blame each other over South China Sea clash
World.content:
The Philippines and China are blaming one another for initiating a tense, physical confrontation in the South China Sea.

Vision posted online by the Philippines Coast Guard shows Filipino and Chinese personnel briefly engaging each other from inflatable boats, with the Philippines accusing China of assaulting one of its navy staff.

China's Coast Guard said Philippines personnel initiated "malicious attacks".

In a statement, the Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) said a China Coast Guard inflatable boat had unlawfully approached one of its outposts at sea at the Second Thomas Shoal, circling and taking photos.

"[It] prompted two AFP rubber boats to calmly and non-confrontationally drive it away.

"The Chinese Coast Guard Vessel (CCGV) personnel reacted violently and aggressively by striking a Philippine Navy personnel on the head with a wooden baton, causing injury," the AFP said in a statement.

"These latest aggressive actions and assault by the CCGV demonstrate a blatant disregard for safety, endanger the lives of our personnel and escalates tensions."

Loading...

But China's Coast Guard (CCG) have offered a completely different account, accusing the Philippines of "deliberately distorting facts" and making "false accusations".

In a statement, CCG said during a "routine patrol", two Philippines rubber boats "rapidly approached, encircled, and rammed into the Chinese patrol boat in a dangerous manner".

"The Philippine personnel initiated malicious attacks against the Chinese law enforcement personnel by using oars, long sticks, and other tools," it said.

"The Chinese side, in accordance with laws and regulations, took measures including verbal warnings, collision-avoiding manoeuvrers, and proportional countermeasures to control the situation on the spot, while exercising maximum rationality and restraint."

Beijing said it had summoned the Philippine ambassador to China on Tuesday to lodge solemn representation over the encounter, according to a statement.

Rear Admiral Jay Tarriela from the Philippines Coast Guard posted a photo on social media of the head a Filipino navy personnel with a bleeding gash.

The Philippines Coast Guard and military have had several dangerous encounters with the Chinese Coast Guard in the disputed waters of the South China Sea in recent years.

Chinese state media warns Philippines against 'wrong path'

This incident took place at the Second Thomas Shoal, known by the Philippines as Ayungin Shoal and by China as Ren'ai Reef.

The Philippines grounded the BRP Sierra Madre at the shoal in 1999, which serves as an outpost for its armed forces.

The shoal sits within the Philippines Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ), which stretches 200 nautical miles (370 kilometres) from the Philippines coastline.

China claims the shoal and most of the South China Sea through its "nine-dash line" claim, but a tribunal at The Hague ruled a decade ago that claim had little basis under international maritime law.

China Coast Guard personnel in orange clash with Philippine Navy personnel at Second Thomas Shoal. (CNC Photo via Reuters)

In a statement, the United States State Department said it "condemns China's dangerous and aggressive actions against Philippine navy personnel".

"[We] call on China to immediately cease its destabilising conduct.

"China's troubling pattern of provocation against lawful Philippine maritime operations undermines regional peace and stability and directly contradicts China's repeated commitments to resolve disputes peacefully."

An opinion piece published by Chinese state media argued China was justified in its actions.

And it warned of potential escalation.

"Manila is deliberately creating the impression of a 'small versus big' confrontation at sea, using it as a pretext to spread false narratives of China 'bullying the weak' and 'intimidating its neighbors'," the article said.

"Manila must have a clear understanding of this: Every provocation it makes in the South China Sea will come at a cost and will be met with China's firm countermeasures. If it continues down the wrong path, it will only pay an even higher price."

Australia gifts Philippines drones

The escalation takes place as South-East Asian foreign ministers, including foreign ministers from China, the US and Australia meet in the Philippines.

China's Foreign Minister Wang Yi will be attending these meetings, hosted by Philippines Foreign Secretary Theresa Lazaro.

Before the incident took place, a spokesperson for China's Ministry of Foreign Affairs said China "looked forward to expanding consensus on development and cooperation, making new progress in jointly fostering a peaceful, safe and secure, prosperous, beautiful and amicable home, and striving to forge a closer China-ASEAN community with a shared future".

Australia's Foreign Minister Penny Wong is also at these meetings and visited the Philippines Coast Guard in Manila on Tuesday morning, to announce further Australian support.

Australia handed over sophisticated underwater and long-range drones to the Philippines Coast Guard, part of a broader drone assistance package worth almost $10 million.

Loading Facebook content

The package will also include specialist training on how to operate the new technology.

It's not the first time Australia has made a contribution like this, with the government handing over 35 drones to the Philippines Coast Guard earlier this year.

During her visit to the Philippines Coast Guard, Senator Wong said Australia would "continue to stand up for the rules and norms that underpin our shared security".

"We remain concerned about destabilising and dangerous conduct in the South China Sea, some of which the Philippines Coast Guard knows too well, including the actions by Chinese vessels towards Philippines vessels we witnessed yesterday morning," she said.

"Friends, we do understand the breadth of the challenges you face, including illegal fishing, maritime pollution, environmental damage and climate change."

At these ASEAN meetings, discussions are expected to be held over an ASEAN-led South China Sea Code of Conduct, to manage the overlapping claims in the region and prevent escalation of conflict.

The proposed Code of Conduct has been long delayed, with the Philippines hoping to finalise it by the end of the year.

"I think is one of the most important deliverables for the Philippine chairship," Philippines Foreign Secretary Theresa Lazaro told the ABC.

"I'm an optimist and yet I'm a pragmatist. So, we cross our fingers and I continuously talk to our negotiators."

World.title: Queensland government advertising costs taxpayers almost $50 million
World.content:
The Queensland government splashed almost $50 million in taxpayer funds on advertising last financial year.

Parliamentary budget estimates revealed the LNP administration spent more than $5 million on a statewide campaign on what it is delivering for Queensland.

The blue coloured scheme material has been prominently featured across online platforms, television, radio, and in letterboxes via pamphlets.

The statewide media campaign plugged measures including the number of frontline health staff and local infrastructure spending.

A Queensland government billboard, pictured in June, promoting the number of doctors at the Royal Brisbane and Women's Hospital. (ABC News: Jack McKay)

It's drawn criticism from the opposition for both the prevalence and colour scheme, accusing the government of blue-washing Queensland's traditional maroon.

The government also spent almost $9 million on its road safety campaign, after the 2025 road toll reached a 16-year high, with the current year trending to surpass that.

That was well above the spending on road safety in the previous three financial years, which averaged about $4.7 million.

There was $1.2 million spent on preventative health campaigns, including for flu vaccinations.

Queensland's vaccination rates have languished in recent years as some of the worst nationally.

Premier David Crisafulli told budget estimates the advertising expenditure was in line with previous governments.

Premier David Crisafulli told budget estimates his government had introduced a cap on advertising spending. (ABC News)

"We have introduced a cap on advertising spending," he said.

"So, to be clear that cap is approximately $50 million, which is less than the last financial year of the former government."

An estimated $48.8 million was spent on advertising last financial year in total, compared to $50.7 million spent in the 2023/24 financial year by Labor.

Payouts costing taxpayers

The hearings also revealed taxpayers forked out hundreds of thousands of dollars in payouts to public servants.

Termination payments for ministerial staff totalled more than $410,000 last financial year.

There were 66 employees who were either sacked or resigned, more than a quarter of the total ministerial workforce of 264 staff.

However, payments only went to 16 of them, meaning the average payout was more than $25,000.

Youth justice minister Laura Gerber has been under particular scrutiny for churn in her office, after going through three chiefs of staff.

Bickering erupted between Labor MP Bisma Asif and government member Michael Crandon, when the former attempted to prosecute the issue and was asked to clarify her question.

"She nearly got the question right," Mr Crandon said.

"It would be really helpful if the chair could stop making sexist comments towards me, he's been doing it for the last two days," Ms Asif said.

Both were admonished by the parliamentary speaker.

World.title: Mother of identical quadruplets calls them her 'miracle babies'
World.content:
Jenitar Na'amoana, the mother of four identical quadruplets says the pregnancy has all been "one giant miracle".

"Every day our miracle babies grow strong is another answered prayer," Ms Na'amoana posted on social media, with a photo of one of the baby's tiny hands gripping her finger.

"We love you more than words can ever say, my miracle babies."

Jenitar Na'amoana's four babies were delivered by caesarean at 28 weeks and four days gestation last week at the Royal Brisbane and Women's Hospital. (Supplied: GoFundMe)

Ms Na'amoana gave birth to the extremely rare quads by caesarean section at the Royal Brisbane and Women's Hospital (RBWH) on July 14.

Emily, Harriet, Alexa and Catherine, who were naturally conceived, were delivered at 28 weeks and four days' gestation.

Their birth doubled Jenitar and Jortham Na'aomoana's brood from four to eight.

They are sisters to siblings Denessa 10, Karl, 8, Selina, 3, and Clohi 1.

The delivery comes 76 years after Australia's first surviving set of quadruplets, Alison, Philip, Judith, and Mark Sara, were born in 1950.

But the Na'amoana girls are the first known case of identical quadruplets being born in Australia.

Identical quadruplets Emily, Harriet, Alexa and Catherine were born at the Royal Brisbane and Women's Hospital last week. (Supplied: Metro Health North)

Cathy Scott, president of the Multiple Births Association Brisbane Northside branch, met with Ms Na'amoana in the lead-up to the quadruplets' delivery.

"It was a surprise pregnancy, it was not planned," she told ABC Radio Brisbane.

"So, a very big surprise for the family to discover that it was quads and identical quads. It is such a phenomenon.

Jenitar Na'amoana and Cathy Scott. (Supplied)

"Jenitar is doing amazing. The fact that she had had the four children previously really did help her body prepare for what it was about to go through. But a really big space issue at the end of the pregnancy with four beautiful growing and developing girls on board."

RBWH maternal foetal medicine specialist Alexa Bendall admitted to being "a little nervous" after first meeting the Na'amoanas 10 weeks into the pregnancy, given the high risk.

"Not only are there the four babies with one mum, but also four babies with one placenta," Dr Bendall told News Channel.

Dr Alexa Bendall has been caring for Ms Na'amoana since early in her pregnancy. (Supplied: Metro Health North)

"That comes along with significant risks that can be quite severe but somehow this beautiful little family managed to dodge all of those and end up with four healthy beautiful little girls.

"To be able to … go through the pregnancy missing most of the risks except prematurity is just amazing."

Complications can include growth restriction and unbalanced blood flow between the babies in the womb.

Brisbane woman births identical quadruplets A Queensland family has grown by four after an extremely rare pregnancy where identical quadruplets all shared the one placenta.

'A bit mind-blowing'

Quadruplets are estimated to occur in about one in 700,000 births.

Identical quads are much rarer, happening in about one in 15 million pregnancies.

But maternal foetal medicine expert Nick Fisk believes the Na'amoana quads may be even rarer still, given they were "monochorionic" — the medical term for sharing a placenta.

"Although one can't be precise, I think this type of placental-sharing quads could be rarer than one in 15 million," he wrote on social media.

The babies were born at 28 weeks and four days and delivered by caesarean. (Supplied: Metro North Health)

Ms Scott, herself a mother of twins, said the Multiple Births Association would "help the family any way we can with the capacity that we have".

She said that when she found out about Jenitar expecting quads, her reaction was "just how, how, how, how".

"It's a bit mind-blowing," Ms Scott said.

"It's really important to remember that there are the four other children as well that need the support. It's not just about the multiples. It's about the family as a whole."

Monozygotic quadruplets are estimated at "one in every 15 million pregnancies". (Supplied: Metro Health North)

Ms Scott said Ms Na'amoana was discharged from hospital three days after giving birth to the quads.

"Now we have a situation where mum's at home with her bigger babies and she has four beautiful babies in the hospital," she said.

"We've got children that are at school, children that are at home needing care but then we also have the babies in the hospital that they're trying to get in to visit, to take breast milk in, too, so that the girls can be fed.

"It's a lot of running around for somebody, especially who's still recovering from a caesarean."

Jenitar Na'amoana has described her identical quadruplets as her "miracle babies". (Supplied)

The Na'amoanas have grown from a family of six to a family of 10.

Their biggest challenge may be logistics once the babies are well enough to go home.

"We're talking about a family of 10 that needs a car with six harness points in it," Ms Scott said.

"If anybody out there could help with information or even better, a car for them, that would be amazing because this family is doing it tough."

World.title: Killer high on ketamine stabbed mother at front door, court told
World.content:
On November 14, 2024, Vicky Van Aken baked cupcakes for her next door neighbour Milorad "Mick" Zaric.

That night he texted her, describing the baked goods as "amazing".

Two days later, Zaric stabbed Ms Van Aken to death at her front door in a drug-fuelled rage.

Details of the shocking murder were aired in Victoria's Supreme Court on Tuesday, as the victim's supporters paid tribute to a loving, devoted mother with a heart of gold.

"She was one in a million," her heartbroken sister Mary Kadis said.

The court heard Zaric had lived next door to Ms Van Aken for two decades in Bayswater, in Melbourne's outer east.

He was a regular cannabis user but had taken ketamine for the first time in the days leading up to the killing on the morning of November 16, 2024.

Prosecutor Erin Ramsay said Zaric's son and girlfriend had become concerned by Zaric's strange behaviour after taking ketamine.

She said Zaric pushed his son down the stairs, killed a pet turtle and smashed a television.

Later, once Zaric's girlfriend and son thought he had calmed down, Zaric tried to attack the boy with a knife, the court heard.

Ms Ramsay said Zaric's son fled to Ms Van Aken's home.

Graphic details of the murder were aired in Victoria's Supreme Court on Tuesday, as the victim's supporters paid tribute to the devoted mother. (ABC News: Shane Willner-Browne)

The prosecutor said Ms Van Aken's son witnessed her opening the door to Zaric.

He said, "Welcome home Vicky", and then repeatedly stabbed her, the court heard.

Ms Van Aken's son fought off Zaric and put him in a headlock, enabling his younger brother to flee.

When Zaric was arrested, he told police: "I've had a bunch of ket[amine]."

"Where's the knife?" an officer asked.

"In her neck," he replied.

Zaric later said he had been "microdosing" on ketamine and snorting the drug every 40 minutes.

"It was like I was possessed or something," he said.

On Tuesday, Zaric sat expressionless in the court dock, surrounded by more than 50 of Ms Van Aken's loved ones in the public gallery.

Her photo was displayed in the courtroom as victim impact statements were read out, describing how the murder had brought on heartbreak, shock, anger and a profound sense of loss.

Defence lawyers successfully challenged some sections being read in open court, where Zaric was to be described as a "murderous monster" who was "eternally condemned to hell".

"A courtroom is a place where respect is shown to all before it — victims, witnesses and the person in the dock," defence barrister Ruth Shann SC said.

Sofia Apostolopoulos, Ms Van Aken's mother, said that her daughter's life mattered and she deserved to watch her children grow up.

"I wish this was all just a bad nightmare," she said.

Ms Van Aken was described as the kind of person who would help anyone in need by her sister, Ms Kadis.

"She was all about family and full of love for everyone," Ms Kadis said.

Ms Kadis said the killer had made "excuses" for his actions, but the blame ultimately lay with him because he chose to take drugs.

"This was a result of the life he chose," she said.

Zaric's son also submitted a statement and said Ms Van Aken's death was "devastating".

He described the murder as an act of betrayal carried out by his father.

"The person I needed most was the person who hurt me the most. That is something I will never forget," he said.

Zaric, who has pleaded guilty to murder, is yet to be sentenced.

The hearing, before Justice Jacinta Forbes, continues.

World.title: Retired police officers lambast minister for trauma support delay
World.content:
Retired police officers have made a plea to Tasmania's police minister urging him to meet with them to implement a much-anticipated mental health support pilot program.

The 12-month trial, which would have given six retired police officers access to 12 psychology sessions each, is yet to be implemented, despite Felix Ellis having told parliament last year it would commence this year.

The Retired Police Association of Tasmania (RPAT) also said it has been unable to secure a meeting with Mr Ellis on the issue, despite him telling a parliamentary committee last month he would do so by the end of June.

In November, Felix Ellis told a parliamentary committee that a pilot program had been formed. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

"Don't wrap yourself in the blue and then turn around and do nothing for us," RPAT president David Plumpton said.

" Don't stand in front of all the police gear with all the police members and say 'I'm with you' when, in actual fact, you don't carry through on your words. "

The RPAT said support was needed for retired officers, many of whom were struggling to deal with the lasting effects of trauma from the job.

"[Mr Ellis] says that he cares for us and so forth. He certainly doesn't show it in any way at all," RPAT volunteer wellbeing officer John Mikulski said.

David Plumpton (left) and John Mikulski from RPAT said the association has been unable to secure a meeting with Mr Ellis on the issue. (ABC News: Andrew Cunningham)

"This pilot will be co-designed, including with retired officers, and invitations will be distributed in the coming weeks to commence the co-design sessions," the statement read.

Independent MP Kristie Johnston has urged Mr Ellis to meet with RPAT to immediately implement the program, calling the minister's actions "despicable".

"It's quite clear that Minister Ellis does not care about police officers, and particularly once they have retired," she said.

"Minister Ellis likes to pose for photos with serving police officers but forgets all about them the moment they retire."

Minister Ellis knocked back an on-camera interview, and refused to answer written questions about snubbing former officers.

Instead, a government spokesperson issued a statement, saying the Department of Health was now developing a First Responders Mental Health Support Service Pilot.

'Unique trauma' to police needs specialist approach

RPAT provides some wellbeing services to its members, but they are volunteer-led.

Spike in number of Tasmanian police on mental health leave More than 100 Tasmanian police officers are currently off duty due to mental health compensation claims, a number that has doubled in five years.

"We have people who are almost falling off the edge, who need to see someone fairly quickly. We cannot get them before someone or a psychologist," Mr Mikulski said.

He said that specialist psychologists were needed due to the unique trauma that former officers experienced.

"We're talking about lots of people who have done 30-plus years of service, who have gone to incidents that most of us wouldn't want to go to,"Mr Mikulski said.

" They struggle quite badly, and being police officers, they don't want to throw their hands up and say that they're struggling. "

Mr Plumpton said while Tasmania Police looked after serving officers well, it had a responsibility to assist former officers.

"Our whole mantra is very simple. That is, if they break you, they fix you," he said.

Minister points to state budget in trial delay

The issue of support for retired officers was first raised in parliament in March 2025, when the lower house passed a motion from former Jacqui Lambie Network MP Andrew Jenner.

The motion called on the state government to "immediately establish and fund ongoing mental health support services".

Mr Ellis attempted to amend the motion to instead ask the government to consult on supports, but that change was not supported and the government did not oppose the final motion.

In November, Mr Ellis told a parliamentary committee that a pilot program had been formed.

"The pilot support program is to be trialled for 12 months and a client services manager appointed to facilitate the pilot research and evaluation," he said.

That trial has not begun.

On June 4, Ms Johnston asked for an update on the trial. In response, Mr Ellis pointed to "tough" decisions "in the context of the state's budget".

"We remain committed to seeing a wellbeing support pilot for retired police officers to proceed. We're currently working through the options available to deliver such a program in a sustainable way."

Kristie Johnston called Mr Ellis' actions "despicable". (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

Asked why he had not yet met with retired officers, he replied, "I'm happy to meet within a month".

That meeting has not occurred.

World.title: Randa Abdel-Fattah appears to abandon threatened defamation case against SA Premier
World.content:
Palestinian-Australian author Randa Abdel-Fattah appears not to be pursuing defamation proceedings against South Australia's premier, despite her lawyers previously threatening legal action.

In January, Abdel-Fattah said she had sent two concerns notices to Premier Peter Malinauskas over comments made around the time of her controversial removal from the line-up of this year's Adelaide Writers' Week, which was subsequently cancelled amid a mass boycott.

In a social media post, Abdel-Fattah referred to "many public statements" that she said Mr Malinauskas — who backed her removal from the festival — had made "about me and my character".

At the time, Mr Malinauskas strongly defended his public comments, saying his remarks had been "founded in a desire for compassion and people treating each other civilly".

Days later, Abdel-Fattah said she had "no choice" but to send a second concerns notice, which her lawyers told the ABC related to comments Mr Malinauskas had made on radio station FiveAA.

Previous Adelaide Writers' Week crowd numbers have exceeded 100,000. (Supplied: Adelaide Festival)

This week, Abdel-Fattah confirmed she had launched separate legal action against the organisers of the 2025 Bendigo Writers Festival, from which she withdrew participation amid a censorship row similar to the one that surrounded Adelaide Writers' Week.

But in the same social media video in which she revealed she had launched that action, Abdel-Fattah indicated she was no longer pursuing proceedings against the SA premier.

"I wanted to bring a defamation case but pursuing defamation against a sitting premier has proven to carry prohibitive cost and risk," she said.

"But those of us who are committed to the decolonial recognise not all victories are won in courts."

The ABC asked Abdel-Fattah's lawyer to confirm she was no longer intending to pursue defamatory action against the SA Premier.

In response, the lawyer said they do not have any further comment at this time.

Premier Peter Malinaukas backed the removal of Dr Abdel-Fattah from the Adelaide Writers' Week line-up. (ABC News)

SA Premier Peter Malinauskas today told 891 ABC Radio Adelaide he welcomed the apparent decision not to pursue the proceedings.

"I welcome the fact that it appears as though this court action against me has been dropped," he said.

"I will just maintain my position that I think people should be entitled to debate these issues at writers' weeks and other events, just as long as they respect other people's ability to be able to make a contribution from the alternate case," he said.

Last night, a spokesperson for the SA premier said Mr Malinauskas had "no comment to make regarding Abdel-Fattah's remarks".

The spokesperson added: "At all times the Premier's only involvement in this matter has been to advocate for a civil, respectful and inclusive public debate which presents an opportunity for all reasonable people to have their perspectives heard without fear or intimidation."

A tearful premier and 'Moscow on the Torrens' The removal and subsequent handling of Randa Abdel-Fattah's rescinded invitation to Adelaide Writers' Week has seen the event cancelled, with more than 180 authors pulling out and its own director issuing a pointed and very public resignation. Where does the festival go from here?

In January, the Adelaide Festival board decided to remove Abdel-Fattah from the 2026 Adelaide Writers' Week program, citing her "past statements", but did not specify which ones.

"Whilst we do not suggest in any way that Dr Randa Abdel-Fattah's or her writings have any connection with the tragedy at Bondi, given her past statements we have formed the view that it would not be culturally sensitive to continue to program her at this unprecedented time so soon after Bondi," the board's statement read.

At the time, Abdel-Fattah has said it was "outrageous" to be linked to the incident at Bondi in December last year.

The decision to remove Abdel-Fattah triggered a mass boycott by authors, the resignation of the festival's director Louise Adler, the cancellation of the event and the Adelaide Festival board stepping down.

SA Premier Peter Malinauskas had supported the removal of Abdel-Fattah from the line-up.

World.title: Queensland university shortchanges staff $1.3m in wages
World.content:
NationalQueenslandUniversity Queensland university shortchanges staff $1.3m in wages Catherine Strohfeldt July 21, 2026 — 4:05pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A Queensland university has shortchanged current and former employees by almost $1.3 million, blaming widespread issues in its payment systems. The Fair Work Ombudsman identified 1038 staff members who were shortchanged by CQ University, including academic and professional staff, vocational education and training educators, and student residential advisers. Errors were found in base salary rates, overtime, minimum shift times for casual employees, promotion and progression entitlements for academic staff, and leave entitlements and loading, including for public holidays. CQ University has campuses in Brisbane (pictured), Bundaberg, and Townsville, with its largest in Rockhampton. Catherine Strohfeldt The largest amount missing from any one employee’s pay cheque was $63,350, excluding interest and superannuation.



CQU blamed an incorrect configuration of its payroll system, alongside staff errors, turnovers, and an over-reliance on manual processes. Related Article University Queensland university finalises nearly $2m to underpaid staff While the university had campuses across Queensland and Australia – including Rockhampton, Brisbane, Townsville, and Sydney – most underpaid staff were located at its Rockhampton North campus, a Fair Work Ombudsman spokesperson told this masthead. National Tertiary Education Union Queensland branch secretary Michael McNally said the errors leading to the underpayments were “completely foreseeable”. “The university had every opportunity – from members, as individuals in the union, raising issues about payments to casual staff – to actually invest in the systems that they needed to to pay these people properly,” he said.



“It certainly looks like they’re putting some effort in now ... but they should have been doing that from the start.” McNally said many universities would fix underpayments on a case-by-case basis, but said in most instances, it was evidence of a systemic problem. “We have counted up the underpayments [since 2020], and in Queensland, it’s running at $29.4 million, with about 26,000 staff affected,” he said. The university was ordered to pay $30,000 to the Fair Work Ombudsman as an initial fine. This would be followed by a second fine determined by the number of additional underpayments identified by the office of the Ombudsman, up to a maximum penalty of $100,000.



By May this year, CQU had repaid 875 current and former staff and owed the remaining 163 just over $96,000. Vice-Chancellor Professor Nick Klomp said the university was committed to repaying every current and former staff member who was underpaid. Professor Nick Klomp is the vice-chancellor and president of CQ University. “Whilst all underpayments were unintentional, CQ University takes full responsibility,” he said. He pointed to the fact the university had begun repaying staff and reported itself to the Fair Work Ombudsman in 2023, after it “proactively commenced a comprehensive wage integrity review”.



“Since then, we have established a dedicated wage integrity project team to rectify underpayments and strengthen our systems, processes, and staff awareness to prevent this from happening in the future,” Klomp said. The vice-chancellor said an agreement with the Ombudsman would also ensure the university met commitments to independently audit, issue transparent reporting, and continue to improve compliance. Fair Work Ombudsman Anna Booth said the university deserved credit for engaging with her office. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: ‘We should never allow this to become normal’: School leaders tell of armed guards and threats
World.content:
NationalAntisemitism royal commission ‘We should never allow this to become normal’: School leaders tell of armed guards and threats Michael Bachelard July 21, 2026 — 3:59pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The head of the Australian Council of Jewish Schools and two prominent school leaders have suggested government should carry more of the cost of protecting Jewish schools and students, not parents. Appearing at the Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion on Tuesday, Stephen Rothman said the council’s position was that “at least the recurrent expenditure on guards and other operational recurrent expenditures should be funded by the federal government”. In a hearing block focused on the security needs of the Jewish community, the leaders of Mount Scopus College and Bialik College in Melbourne told the commission the security bills for their respective campuses had increased in recent years, with about 70 per cent of the cost going to armed guards – an expense non-Jewish schools do not require, they said. Following the Bondi Beach terror attack, Mount Scopus College in Burwood had an increased security presence which included police. Joe Armao The evidence came as three rabbis from three different synagogues – including Adass Israel, which was burned down in 2024 in an alleged terror attack – spoke of the burden of security on Jewish communal life in Australia.



Dan Sztrajt, the principal of Mount Scopus in Burwood, in Melbourne’s east, spoke of his shock when the words “Jew Die” were painted on the school’s gates in 2024. Quickly, he said, he was contacted by parents “who told me personally that they would not be sending their children to school” because the graffiti suggested “the school might be targeted, or that this demonstrates that the school doesn’t have sufficient security”. Related Article Antisemitism royal commission Violence a legitimate tactic in freedom movements, pro-Palestine student leader tells royal commission Sztrajt told Commissioner Virginia Bell that a number of schools, including his own, began employing armed guards in 2015 following an antisemitic attack in Europe, and charged parents a levy to cover the cost. Following the Hamas incursion into Israel on October 7, 2023, and Israel’s subsequent war on Gaza, the cost of maintaining security had escalated dramatically, he said. Last year, Mount Scopus parents paid a levy of $1130 per student – up from $500 in 2022, which still fell short of covering the $3000 per student security cost, Sztrajt said, noting that while state and federal governments contributed funding, it was not available to spend on guards.



“The idea that government grants should not be used towards providing that level of much-needed protection has been problematic,” he said. Tyson Wodak, board president of Bialik College in Hawthorn East, told the commission parents at the school paid a security levy of $840 per student – up 230 per cent in recent years. The college also receives government funding, but like Sztrajt, he said it did not cover the full cost of security. “In my view, a well-functioning society ought to provide security to its people as a core part of its orderly function,” Wodak said. He said his school was one of three in the area, but the only one with such a high level of security.



“The other schools, you can walk in at the weekend and play basketball or do whatever you like. We have high fences. We have security everywhere – it’s a secure environment. I just can’t understand why we live in a country where one aspect of our community is expected to live under heavy security which it has to pay for in large part itself.” Another witness, Rabbi Levi Wolff of the Central Synagogue in Sydney’s Bondi Junction, told the royal commission: “Our children, as all Jewish children in this country, are growing up attending schools where they have armed guards in front of their schools and the houses of worship, and that’s normal. Rabbi Levi Wolff, chief rabbi of the Central Synagogue in Sydney, arrives for Tuesday’s royal commission hearing in Melbourne. AAP “That’s normal. But that is not normal, and we should never allow this to become Australia’s normal. “And when any Australian feels that they must hide who they are … by covering their kippah with a cap, or ensuring that they have an armed guard in front of their homes of worship, something has gone wrong for all Australians, not just for the Jewish community.”



Wolff spoke of being struck by the difference when standing outside St Mary’s Catholic Cathedral in Sydney just 10 days after the Bondi terror attack in December. Related Article Antisemitism royal commission ‘I’m sorry’: Uni of Sydney boss apologises to Jewish students over protest camp “I was struck by the absence of security. How this magnificent house of worship had its doors wide open, and people from all walks of life were able to just walk off the street with a knapsack on their back and come inside and pray and feel like nothing would go wrong,” Wolff said. “Would that ever be a possibility [at my synagogue]? Where there would be no armed guards, no bollards, no ongoing security screenings for every single person to be able to walk through?” Wolff said the threat began with words, and ended with violence. He drew attention to the language heard at campus protests.



“I often hear people say, ‘I’m not anti-Jewish. I’m simply anti-Zionist’, and in the same breath they deny the Jewish people’s spiritual, historical and indigenous connection to their ancestral land. “I mean, to me, it’s almost like saying, ‘I’m not racist against Aboriginals; Aboriginal Australians, I absolutely love you. I just simply don’t believe that you have any cultural or historical connection to this land,’” he said. “For many Jews, Zionism is not an abstract political ideology. It is the belief that the Jewish people, like every other people, have the right and self-determination to their ancestral homeland.” Adass Israel members Benjamin Klein (left) and Izzy Nussbacher outside the ruins of their synagogue last August. Simon Schluter The assertion of indigenous connection to Israel is politically controversial – pro-Palestinian protesters, and much of the political left, assert that the Zionist movement which began in the late 19th century and culminated in the Jewish state of Israel was a colonial project.



The commission heard from witnesses on Monday who spoke of the increased reliance on community security groups, or CSGs – organisations of volunteers set up to protect Jewish people and institutions against threats and attacks – at Jewish schools and synagogues across Australia following October 7, 2023. Benjamin Klein, who appeared on Tuesday as a lived experience witness on behalf of the Adass Israel synagogue in the inner Melbourne suburb of Ripponlea, said he knew of two people from his son’s school who had “picked themselves up and moved to Israel” amid rising antisemitism. “Those stories never used to happen. People … were proud to live in Melbourne. They were part of the Australian community. But now there’s good Aussie people … moving,” Klein told the commission. “It’s weird because, if you think about it, Israel is not necessarily a safe place … It’s quite a scary place. But they’re still picking themselves up from Melbourne and moving to Israel.” “Why are rational, successful accountants, lawyers, doctors [doing this?] … And the answer is they just don’t feel safe.”



The Ripponlea synagogue was largely destroyed after it was firebombed on December 6, 2024. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Gateway triples new WA gold discovery strike to 2.5km
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Gateway triples new WA gold discovery strike to 2.5km Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Penny Taylor July 21, 2026 — 3:56pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Gateway Mining may have unearthed a game-changing gold discovery at its Cowza prospect, part of the company’s Yandal gold project in Western Australia, after step-out drilling tripled the continuous high-grade strike from 800 metres to 2.5 kilometres. The latest results also confirmed high-grade gold in fresh rock for the first time, further strengthening the exploration model. Aircore drilling at Gateway Mining’s Cowza gold discovery within the Yandal gold project, Western Australia’s prolific Yandal Greenstone Belt. Every step-out drill line completed since Cowza was unveiled in June has intersected the same gold system, providing growing confidence the find is evolving into a large, continuous gold-bearing structure. The prospect is hosted within a major shear zone marking the contact between mafic and intermediate volcanic rocks. This geological setting has consistently delivered new discoveries across Gateway’s Yandal project. It forms part of a much larger 4.5km-long structurally complex corridor that has been strongly demagnetised.



‘With evidence of a substantial, continuous gold-bearing structure the RC rig may well be focused on Cowza for the foreseeable future.’ Gateway Mining chief executive officer Richard Pugh Gateway believes the same hydrothermal fluids responsible for the widespread demagnetisation also deposited the gold, pointing to a large and fertile mineralising event. The broader corridor suggests Cowza may be in the early innings of its growth, with significant exploration upside still ahead. The recent aircore drilling blitz returned a series of strong gold intercepts from along the newly extended strike, including a 27-metre interval grading 1.4 grams per tonne (g/t) gold from 84m, a 16-metre interval grading 1.9g/t gold from 88m and another 16-metre interval returning 1.3g/t gold from 68m. The 27-metre intercept came from the first aircore hole to properly test mineralisation in fresh rock and ended in mineralisation, with the final metre grading 3.3g/t gold. The result suggests the drilling was only beginning to intersect the primary gold system before reaching the limits of the aircore drill, confirming the discovery extends into primary mineralisation beneath the weathered profile and materially de-risking the exploration model.



Cowza is rapidly emerging as an important piece of the puzzle for Gateway at Yandal, demonstrating the repeatability of a geological model that has already delivered multiple discoveries across the project. Gateway Mining chief executive officer Richard Pugh said: “With evidence mounting in support of a substantial, continuous, and highly fertile gold-bearing structure that extends well beyond the boundaries of the assays received to date, the RC rig may well be focused on Cowza for the foreseeable future.” The company says it will waste little time putting that strategy into action. While a first reverse circulation (RC) rig continues drilling at Gateway’s Haflinger discovery 25km north of Cowza, a second RC rig is now due to arrive this weekend and immediately begin fresh-rock drilling at the new find. The expanded RC program marks a shift from proving discoveries to mapping the scale of fresh-rock mineralisation. Assays are also expected within a fortnight from the remainder of the recent aircore program testing Cowza’s northern extension, where drilling has already intersected the same shearing, veining and alteration observed in the mineralised holes. Cowza forms part of Gateway’s 1,780-square-kilometre Yandal gold project, which hosts almost 100km of prospective gold trends 85km north-east of Wiluna in the Yandal Greenstone Belt. The belt ranks among Western Australia’s premier gold provinces and hosts several multi-million-ounce gold deposits, including Northern Star Resources’ 7.4-million-ounce Jundee operation.



The discovery is the latest success from Gateway’s proven exploration model, joining Haflinger, Hummer, Celia South and Panikin as the company continues to build a pipeline of discoveries across Yandal. Those discoveries complement an existing 400,400-ounce gold resource, providing a solid foundation. Historically elevated gold prices continue to favour explorers delivering new discoveries and resource growth, particularly in tier-one jurisdictions such as Western Australia. Backed by $15.7M in cash and a further $5.6M in liquid ASX-listed securities at the end of the June quarter, the company appears well funded to accelerate drilling across Cowza and its broader pipeline of Yandal discoveries. Gateway still has another 2km of strike awaiting assays, while a second RC rig is about to step on the accelerator. If the geology continues to stack up, Cowza could quickly emerge as the crown jewel in the company’s Yandal crown. Is your ASX-listed company doing something interesting? World.title: Burnham is a devastatingly good politician. But he needs to heed this Aussie’s advice
World.content:
Analysis WorldEuropeUK politics Burnham is a devastatingly good politician. But he needs to heed this Aussie’s advice David Crowe Updated July 21, 2026 — 3:56pm ,first published 10:08am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

London: The first thing Andy Burnham did upon becoming Britain’s new prime minister was to admit failure. It was an honest and necessary step because Britain has seen an awful lot of failure over the past decade. But it also raised expectations that the new leader could arrest the country’s dismal decline. And, so far, there is no sign he has a solid plan to do so. In his opening remarks in Downing Street, just after his meeting with King Charles, he said this was a moment for “reflection and new resolution” about the future. “It requires my generation of politicians to raise our game,” he said. He admitted that Britain’s leaders had not been good enough, and he added: “We will be.” Andy Burnham speaks outside 10 Downing Street after becoming Britain’s seventh prime minister in a decade. Bloomberg A new leader always tries to break with the past and hold out the promise of a better future, so Burnham mainly stuck to that formula. He did, at least, acknowledge that Britain was suffering from a generational failure. Burnham is a devastatingly good politician. He has walked into 10 Downing Street, the prime minister’s official residence, barely a month after returning to parliament. He trounced the right-wing Reform UK party at a byelection. He was elected to the Labour leadership unopposed. His predecessor, Keir Starmer, resigned because his defeat was obvious.



Related Article Updated

UK politics The big surprise on Andy Burnham’s first day as UK PM? Trump wants to help him This required ruthless political skill. Burnham and his allies worked for at least a year to ensure that every mistake by Starmer – and there were many of them – led to a leadership coup. Now their moment has finally arrived. Do they actually know how to use their power to lift Britain’s fortunes? The Conservative Party leader, Kemi Badenoch, mocks Burnham for promising so much. “I have found Andy to be a nice man,” she said on Monday. “But Britain needs a leader who can take difficult decisions, not a people pleaser.” Nigel Farage, the populist leader of the right-wing Reform UK, has an effective line about Burnham’s attempts to appeal to both left and right. “I have to say I find the whole thing utterly vacuous,” Farage said at a conservative conference last Friday. “He is the great chameleon of British politics, capable of being all things to all people.” Burnham styles himself as a different kind of politician – but will style translate into the substance needed to turn Britain around? Christopher Furlong/Pool Getty via AP



In truth, Reform has no great policy plan. It simply has a powerful complaint. “We are going down the drain,” Farage said. “Britain is broken. We have to wake up to that fact, acknowledge the extent of the illness, and until we do that, you’ll never be able to put the right cures in place.” This message resonates because people can feel the decline around them – in the grim town squares with empty shops, in the number of unemployed young people, in the industries being shut down, in the knife crime on the streets, in the wait for healthcare and in the low economic growth. ‘People believe in a basic bargain. Work hard, play by the rules, get an education, and you and your children can have a better life. Across the developed world, people feel that bargain has been broken.’ Lynton Crosby, political analyst But the sharpest message came from an Australian observer, Lynton Crosby, who entered the debate on Monday with a word of warning. He is a former adviser to Liberal governments in Australia, including to John Howard for many years. As the executive chairman of CT Group, he is also a former adviser to Conservative governments in Britain. “What voters are asking for is not ideology, it is substantive delivery and change,” he wrote in The Times on Monday. Crosby offered a contrary view to the conventional wisdom in London. He said Starmer could have survived and, possibly, won the next election if Labour had held its nerve and worked harder on what voters wanted.



Sunlit uplands? Many Britons are feeling the squeeze after a decade of spiralling inflation and sluggish growth. Bloomberg “The most powerful driver of how people vote is a simple question: What does this mean for me and my life?” he wrote. “People believe in a basic bargain. Work hard, play by the rules, get an education, and you and your children can have a better life, a home of your own, a rising standard of living. Across the developed world, people feel that bargain has been broken. “A prime minister who had grasped that, and governed relentlessly around it, would have had something real to offer. The path was there for Starmer to take. Starmer cut a diminished figure just two years on from winning the election that returned Labour to power after 14 years. Getty Images



“Instead, Labour lost its nerve. Rather than hold to a steady, long-term course, the party let itself be governed by polling rather than addressing the underlying values and concerns the polling was being driven by; reacting to every fluctuation instead of doing the patient work of government.” Crosby warned Labour, and Burnham, that changing the leader would solve nothing if the party did not understand the national problems it needed to fix and “hold steady” to some economic foundations. Related Article Analysis

UK politics Is Andy Burnham the man to fight the right? “Burnham is being pulled towards a contradictory program of land taxes, wealth taxes, public ownership of utilities, fiscal discipline and a bigger budget, all at once,” wrote Crosby. “But to govern is to choose. A leader with no rival and no rebellion has the rarest of opportunities in politics: the room to choose one credible plan, govern on it and deliver the growth this country needs. But if he fails to learn the lessons of his predecessors, he will undoubtedly share their fate.”



Burnham may not want to heed the advice from Crosby, but he should. Everyone can see the new prime minister is trying to appeal to both left and right with his vague talk. He is promising to be more caring with welfare, help workers with tax cuts, spend more on services, nationalise industry, stick to the fiscal rules and spend more on defence. The sad fact is that he has very little room to do any of these things. The country’s net public debt is £2.9 trillion ($5.6 trillion), or about 95 per cent of annual economic output. This means the government is spending £110 billion on debt interest this year, which is about 8 per cent of all public spending and among the highest levels in five decades. Britain is not just broken. It’s broke. This is why Burnham is pledging to honour the “fiscal rules” in the budget. He has no other option. His government will be savaged by the bond markets if he and the new chancellor of the exchequer, John Healey, stumble on fiscal policy.

World.title: ‘Get in first’: How alleged ‘old-fashioned’ Sydney street fight turned fatal shooting
World.content:
NationalNSWCourts ‘Get in first’: How alleged ‘old-fashioned’ Sydney street fight turned fatal shooting Amber Schultz July 21, 2026 — 3:55pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A man accused of shooting his opponent in a Sydney street fight over hiring the victim’s wife to work at his inner-west brothel planned to “get in first” and kill him, a court has heard. Ayman Manly, 42, is on trial in the NSW Supreme Court charged with murder over the fatal shooting of Mohammad Chami on March 3, 2022. Ayman Manly has pleaded not guilty to murder. James Brickwood Manly has also been charged with shooting with intent to murder and discharging a firearm with intent to cause grievous bodily harm over the wounding of a second person, known as Witness 1. He has pleaded not guilty to all charges.



Related Article Crime Sydney man charged over ‘brazen’ fatal shooting During closing submissions, Crown prosecutor Eric Balodis SC told the jury Chami arranged the meeting after discovering Manly had employed his wife and began a relationship with her. The court heard the woman denied the pair had a sexual relationship. Chami had a turbulent relationship with the woman, the court was told, marked by domestic violence, infidelity and drug use. The pair split in 2021 after Chami assaulted her and she stabbed him. Chami was jailed over an unrelated incident days later. It’s alleged the woman fled to a friend at Manly’s brothel in Newtown, Mistiques. Manly offered her a place to stay at his Balmain property, and she began working as a receptionist at the venue, where she had previously been employed. When Chami was released from prison, he learnt of the arrangement and messaged Manly to set up a fist fight, the court heard.



“You should have never got her a place to stay … from the second you new [sic] she was my wife,” Chami wrote on March 2, the day before the alleged shooting. “Now straight up we have to have a crack one on one, and then I’ll leave at that.” Manly then called his own wife to tell her about the meetup. “Some f---ing gronk calls me up, wants to fight me,” he said in a phone call played to the court. Chami didn’t show up to the first meeting, with the pair arranging to meet at a semi-industrial cul-de-sac on Fox Street in the suburb of Holroyd the next day. Friends of Chami told the court he believed it would be a fist fight, and that he had left a knife behind before leaving for the meeting. “He said that he was going to go for an old-fashioned bashing,” one woman told the court. She added that she warned Chami “everyone knows that you bring guns to fights”, but Chami insisted it would only be a punch-up.



It’s alleged that just before midnight, Chami arrived on Fox Street with Witness 1. Dressed in socks and slides, Manly emerged from a pedestrian underpass near the Western Motorway with a taller, unidentified man. The pair began a heated exchange, the court heard, before Chami stepped back and raised his arm to punch Manly. Manly shot him five times in the back and buttocks, Balodis said. “Manly has taken the opportunity to get in first with Chami and kill him,” he said. Witness 1 was allegedly shot in the backside as he turned to flee. Chami’s body was found hours later by a passerby. With minimal DNA evidence, the prosecution relied on mobile phone tracking placing Manly at the scene, Witness 1’s testimony, and ballistics trajectory analysis matching the shooter’s height with Manly.



“The accused is a short fella. He did it, he’s guilty,” Balodis said. Defence barrister David Dalton, whose closing argument begins on Wednesday, maintains Manly was not involved. “He wasn’t there. He didn’t shoot anyone,” Dalton told the jury earlier in the trial. The jury is expected to retire to deliberate on Thursday. with AAP Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Beauty billionaires bought Toorak’s most expensive home. Then got help to buy out the neighbours
World.content:
Pharma and beauty billionaires Dennis and Georgina Bastas have been quietly accumulating multimillion-dollar parcels of Toorak’s top real estate with the help of companies linked to the wealthy couple’s associates. The pair already own prized historic mansion Coonac, which they bought for a record $136.1 million in May from businessman Paul Little and his Melbourne University chancellor wife, Jane Hansen. DBG Health chairman and group chief executive Dennis Bastas. Oscar Colman They’ve been given the green light to spend $38.5 million on its renovation, with the Bastases now also seeking permission to spend another $11.6 million on extending the 1867 Italianate mansion. But it can now be revealed the couple also have a foothold on a collection of prestige properties that border the Toorak mansion.



Part of the deal to purchase Coonac, which is on prestigious boulevard Clendon Road, included a 1950s apartment block on the adjacent Stonehaven Court. The two properties share a boundary fence. Since that deal was struck, two other properties in Stonehaven Court – which also border Coonac – have been sold, for $13.1 million and $13.05 million. Corporate records and title documents, seen by this masthead, show an entity called Stonehaven Property Holdings Pty Ltd, which was created in March, is behind the $13.05 million purchase. That corporate vehicle has only one director, Patrick Kypreos, also a director of Arrotex Investments, owned by the Bastases. Arrotex is Australia’s largest generic drug supplier and part of the $5.4 billion rich lister couple’s private business empire DBG Health, which has brands including MCoBeauty and Chemists’ Own. The other property on Stonehaven Court, sold for $13.1 million, is purchased in the name of a company whose sole director and ultimate owner is Kerry Goldfinger.



She is married to Melbourne businessman Eli Goldfinger, the business partner of Kypreos in EGA Corporate Advisers and Accountants. That property’s previous owner was Tania Buckley, the former wife of AFL coach Nathan Buckley. It is a five-bedroom Tudor-style mansion with open fireplaces, an outdoor lounge, and wine storage. The flurry of real estate activity in the area might even present Little, who is the former chairman of the Essendon Football Club, with a further opportunity. Related Article Melbourne luxury property Billionaire spends $136m in cash on Toorak mansion and block next door There remains squeezed into the parcel of prestige real estate a property still owned by Little that backs onto Coonac estate. Little has held the remaining residential block since 2011 and has rented it out ever since.



The Bastases signed on the line to buy Coonac in an off-market deal in February last year. Their purchase of the historic home was settled in May this year. It sits on just over one hectare complete with a pool and cabana, tennis court and sprawling gardens. All up, it means that if the Bastases took over ownership of the Stonehaven Court adjacent homes, the total real estate spend and estimated renovations would amount to an eye-watering $213.25 million. Before the Bastases bought Coonac from the Littles, the title of Australia’s most expensive house was shared jointly at $130 million by two grand Point Piper estates in Sydney’s east – Elaine and Uig Lodge. Coonac is held in the name of Georgina Bastas. The couple’s centrepiece new home was purchased without the need for a mortgage.



In parallel to the nearby real estate dealings, the billionaire couple are seeking approval from local planning authorities to increase the scope of a planned $38.5 million renovation of their historic mansion. Editor's pick United Arab Emirates As my Emirates plane flew into Dubai, missiles started flying again Last month, they lodged an application with Stonnington Council to expand their renovation on the heritage-protected, 1867 Italianate mansion by $11.6 million to a total estimated outlay of $50.1 million. Plans for the expansion have not been made public by the local council. Stonnington Council declined to comment on the Coonac process. Paul Little, Dennis Bastas, Patrick Kypreos and Eli Goldfinger were all contacted but did not respond to requests for comment.
