World.title: Final frontier: Smith and ageing Test team vow to complete unfinished business away from home
World.content:
SportCricketAustralian cricket Final frontier: Smith and ageing Test team vow to complete unfinished business away from home Daniel Brettig July 21, 2026 — 3:54pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Much as the 2005 Ashes defeat kept their legendary forebears together until a blazing 5-0 revenge mission two years later, Steve Smith and his ageing teammates have committed to making collective amends for fumbled trips to India and England in 2023. That much was clear when selection chair George Bailey formally unveiled the squad for two Tests against Bangladesh in Darwin and Mackay next month, with only one player – all-rounder Cameron Green, 27 – under the age of 30. Steve Smith walks off the SCG after a century in the 2025/26 Ashes. Getty Images Games against a Bangladesh side that just lost a Test match by an innings to Zimbabwe would appear the ideal time to choose some more youthful players. But Bailey made it clear that this was more like a roll call of Australia’s frontline men for difficult tours to India (no Australian series wins since 2004), England (none since 2001) and South Africa (none since 2014). This quest is personified by Smith, who clearly wants to cap his international career by breaking the aforementioned droughts, including by continuing to substitute for captain Pat Cummins whenever required. Shane Warne, Glenn McGrath and company were similarly motivated.



“I can’t foresee that changing in the short-term,” Bailey said of Smith’s deputy role. “In my conversations with him over the last few months, I don’t think I’ve seen him as excited or invigorated around the opportunities and challenges, in particular, this Test team have over the next period of time. “For a number of those guys that have played a lot of Test cricket and are at certain stages of their career, you look at some of the series that are coming up and what the opportunities are for this Test team to achieve. It probably comes as no surprise as to how excited and focused they are. Editor's pick Australian cricket Why Australia’s next Test opponents are in crisis mode “So, yeah, I’ve actually been really quite excited by how pumped Steve is, how much thought and time he’s putting into to what’s coming up. I fully expect him to be a major part of it and looking forward to seeing how those really big, key series [provide] a chance to really lay down a marker across a number of different conditions as well. That’s exciting for everyone, but in particular for him.” As was often said in 2023, Australia’s high-performing Test side cannot be considered great without overseas series wins in India and England. South Africa, too, is the source of much intrigue given the ugly events of the previous Test tour there in 2018.



Four years ago, Australia had genuine opportunities to beat India away before losing the series 2-1, and should have skipped away to a 3-0 margin over England after as many Tests, only to finish 2-2. David Warner and Usman Khawaja have since retired, but Smith, Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood, Nathan Lyon and Scott Boland will all look at this cycle as the final chance to redress things. “There’ll be moments out of those series where they look back and wish that things could have gone differently,” Bailey said. “But there are great things that they would have learnt out of that. “They’re constantly trying to get better, and they’re constantly asking questions, particularly around some of those places that do provide different challenges around how they can be better and how they can make the entire team better the next time that we get that opportunity.” Scott Boland received his baggy green cap from Josh Hazlewood before the third Test against England at the MCG in 2021. Getty Images Boland’s durability has seen him step up for both Hazlewood and Cummins in recent times, and Bailey made it clear that he had now made a case to be one of the first three quick bowlers chosen.



“Scotty would never say it, but he’s mounting a strong case that when you use the words ‘the Big Three’ that he could be one of those,” Bailey said. Editor's pick Analysis

Australian cricket How an allegation of an affair between teammates rocked Australian cricket For now, the selectors have a full complement of their first-choice bowlers available, but Bailey also acknowledged how important all-rounders Beau Webster and Green would be in sharing the load. “The fact they both can bowl will be important at different times across the next 18 months,” Bailey said of the pair. Australia may make some left-field selection choices around Test assignments, with white-ball series against South Africa, Zimbabwe and even England likely to see numerous multi-format players rested, while other younger squad members may be sent to India to play for Australia A ahead of next year’s five Tests.



“It will be about identifying some periods between Test series and white-ball series over the next 18 to 24 months, where you can maybe invest a bit back into the body and mind to stay fresh,” Bailey said. “I don’t think the 11 will be the same across each of the next 21 Tests and there will be changes, and for some of them our hand will be forced.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: Lifelong KPMG veteran’s appointment as CEO draws pointed response
World.content:
Updated BusinessCompaniesConsulting Lifelong KPMG veteran’s appointment as CEO draws pointed response Colin Kruger Updated July 21, 2026 — 3:52pm ,first published 10:34am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

KPMG has picked a decades-long veteran to run the embattled consultancy as it prepares to cut hundreds of jobs to counteract the loss of business from the whistleblower scandal and tough market conditions. The consultancy’s chief financial officer, John Sams, began as chief executive officer on Tuesday after rising through KPMG’s ranks in Australia and overseas since 2003. “I do not underestimate the task ahead but commit to our clients and people that I am prepared to be courageous, take the tough decisions and lead the changes we need to set us on the right path,” says new KPMG CEO John Sams. KPMG’s decision to appoint a chief executive who has spent his entire career with the firm drew a pointed response from the senator who exposed the whistleblower scandal, with Labor’s Deborah O’Neill noting his tenure in senior roles at the firm. “Mr Sams’ appointment is the elevation of yet another member of the firm’s leadership which oversaw the series of botched investigations and non-action,” O’Neill said.



There is no suggestion Sams was personally involved in any misconduct, but he has served as chief financial officer of KPMG since October last year. During that period, numerous senior executives at the firm resigned amid its stumbling response to revelations that some of KPMG’s most senior staff allegedly accessed confidential client information to win new customers. KPMG chairman Michael Ebeid said Sams would lead the firm’s efforts to fix its integrity issues. “John has a clear mandate from the board: to strengthen leadership and culture, improve confidence with our people, clients, regulators, government and the parliament, and focus KPMG on the areas where it can make the greatest contribution to our clients, people and stakeholders,” Ebeid said. Sams reiterated the firm’s mistakes in a statement. “The firm fell short of the standards rightly expected of us, and the accountability for these failures will continue to be implemented,” he said. “We have serious work to do on our culture, our leadership and our governance and it will take resolve and endurance.” Among the first tasks on his list are likely to be job cuts. The firm has not denied reports of redundancies, but the process will not begin in earnest until after Sams is established in his new role.



Related Article Updated

Consulting New KPMG chair under fire over ‘false’ whistleblower claims Earlier this month, a KPMG spokesman said it continues to evaluate a range of options to ensure the firm remains well positioned for the challenges ahead. “We are reviewing our operating model, cost base and workforce needs,” the spokesman said. “No decisions have been made regarding any specific measures or any potential impact on roles. We recognise that discussions of this nature can create uncertainty, and as decisions are made, we will communicate with our people first and in a respectful way.” All four of the major consulting giants have been cutting staff in response to a weaker economic environment and falling revenue from federal government business, which has been the single biggest customer for these firms and especially KPMG. Sams joined the UK arm of KPMG in 2003 as a graduate and moved to Australia in 2006. He recently led its commercial advisory and transactions business as lead partner.





The allegations were first raised to the firm in 2024 but did not become public until O’Neill aired them in March this year. “I note reports of concerns within KPMG about the role Mr Ebeid has played in advancing the path of Mr Sams to CEO,” O’Neill said. “Given there has been no formal agreement by partners to allow Mr Ebeid, who is not a partner of KPMG, to assume the role of Chair of the Board.” The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. World.title: Outback priest allegedly plied young boys with alcohol, abused them at Catholic Church-owned properties
World.content:
Breaking NationalWACourts Outback priest allegedly plied young boys with alcohol, abused them at Catholic Church-owned properties Hannah Murphy July 21, 2026 — 4:10pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

One of the nation’s highest-ranking Catholics allegedly plied young Aboriginal boys with alcohol, made them strip off and sexually abused them at Catholic Church-owned properties across outback Western Australia, a court has heard. Christopher Alan Saunders, 76, appeared in WA’s District Court on Wednesday, for the first day of his trial on 26 sexual abuse charges against three young Aboriginal men, ranging from indecent assault to sexual penetration without consent. Former Bishop of Broome, Christopher Saunders. The incidents were alleged to have taken place between 2008 and 2017, when Saunders was the Bishop of Broome, in WA’s Kimberley region. Saunders has pleaded not guilty to all charges, and has long maintained his innocence. The 76-year-old was dressed in an all-black suit on the first day of his trial, with a white vicar collar. He had a crucifix brooch on the lapel of his suit.



Originally from Victoria, Saunders was first ordained as a priest in 1976 and moved to Western Australia’s far northern outback where he worked for the Diocese of Broome. On Tuesday, the court was told Saunders was known for his work in remote Aboriginal communities and was named as the Bishop of Broome in 1995. He had been in the role for two decades when allegations about his conduct began to swirl and police launched an investigation. The subsequent charges made Saunders one of Australia’s most senior Catholic clerics to be charged with sexual abuse, second to only late Cardinal George Pell, who was ultimately acquitted by the High Court of Australia. In court on Wednesday, state prosecutor Adam Ebell revealed for the first time the specifics of Saunders’ charges, alleging he had a sexual interest in young Aboriginal men. “The accused had a propensity to act on that sexual interest when the opportunity presented itself,” he told the court.



“And that opportunity did present itself.” Related Article Updated

Catholic church WA bishop charged with historical sex crimes, held in custody overnight Saunders allegedly hosted alcohol-fuelled parties during his time as a priest at his properties around the Kimberley, the court was told, often enforcing a strict dress code where he would mandate that young Aboriginal men had to strip their shirts off to attend. He provided cigarettes and food – all allegedly paid for by the Catholic Church. Alcohol, strictly regulated in the Kimberley due to its festering impact on communities, was often also served on the church’s dime.



Ebell told the court that, at these parties, Saunders would use boxing and wrestling as a way to excuse physical contact with the men. All three complainants are Aboriginal men, now in their early 30s. The first complainant was 16 years old when he was first introduced to the bishop during a visit with other boys to his home – known in Broome as the Bishop’s House – on Robinson Street. Ebell told the court the boy was with a group of other young men when he attended the house for a party, and the bishop was known by the group as “Brother B”. He sat around drinking and smoking with the group when Saunders reached out and is alleged to have told the boy he knew his father, who had since died.



“This meant a lot to him,” Ebell told the court. The boy was a devout Catholic and originally from the remote northern community of Kalumburu. Some of the abuse allegedly suffered by the young man was at Kalumburu mission on the far north coast. Australia's North West Kalumburu is a deeply religious community and is inaccessible during the wet season due to flooding, meaning the bishop frequently used the church-funded plane to get in and out of the region. It was also for this reason, Ebell told the court, that the boy entirely trusted Saunders, and saw him as a figure of authority.



The court was told the boy subsequently became a frequent visitor to Saunders’ properties across the Kimberley, and the bishop allegedly began to groom him by buying him clothes, food and cigarettes. Over time, Saunders allegedly began to sexually assault the boy at properties owned by the Catholic Church, including his home, at a Kununurra hotel room, on the Kalumburu Mission and at “Bethlehem Retreat” on Riddell Beach. The alleged behaviour was ongoing for the boy between the ages of 15 and 16, only ending when he turned 19. Ebell told the court that, over time, the young man would tell Saunders to stop and push him away, but Saunders would persist.



The defence will give their openings later on Tuesday. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Queensland university shortchanges staff $1.3m in wages
World.content:
NationalQueenslandUniversity Queensland university shortchanges staff $1.3m in wages Catherine Strohfeldt July 21, 2026 — 4:05pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A Queensland university has shortchanged current and former employees by almost $1.3 million, blaming widespread issues in its payment systems. The Fair Work Ombudsman identified 1038 staff members who were shortchanged by CQ University, including academic and professional staff, vocational education and training educators, and student residential advisers. Errors were found in base salary rates, overtime, minimum shift times for casual employees, promotion and progression entitlements for academic staff, and leave entitlements and loading, including for public holidays. CQ University has campuses in Brisbane (pictured), Bundaberg, and Townsville, with its largest in Rockhampton. Catherine Strohfeldt The largest amount missing from any one employee’s pay cheque was $63,350, excluding interest and superannuation.



CQU blamed an incorrect configuration of its payroll system, alongside staff errors, turnovers, and an over-reliance on manual processes. Related Article University Queensland university finalises nearly $2m to underpaid staff While the university had campuses across Queensland and Australia – including Rockhampton, Brisbane, Townsville, and Sydney – most underpaid staff were located at its Rockhampton North campus, a Fair Work Ombudsman spokesperson told this masthead. National Tertiary Education Union Queensland branch secretary Michael McNally said the errors leading to the underpayments were “completely foreseeable”. “The university had every opportunity – from members, as individuals in the union, raising issues about payments to casual staff – to actually invest in the systems that they needed to to pay these people properly,” he said.



“It certainly looks like they’re putting some effort in now ... but they should have been doing that from the start.” McNally said many universities would fix underpayments on a case-by-case basis, but said in most instances, it was evidence of a systemic problem. “We have counted up the underpayments [since 2020], and in Queensland, it’s running at $29.4 million, with about 26,000 staff affected,” he said. The university was ordered to pay $30,000 to the Fair Work Ombudsman as an initial fine. This would be followed by a second fine determined by the number of additional underpayments identified by the office of the Ombudsman, up to a maximum penalty of $100,000.



By May this year, CQU had repaid 875 current and former staff and owed the remaining 163 just over $96,000. Vice-Chancellor Professor Nick Klomp said the university was committed to repaying every current and former staff member who was underpaid. Professor Nick Klomp is the vice-chancellor and president of CQ University. “Whilst all underpayments were unintentional, CQ University takes full responsibility,” he said. He pointed to the fact the university had begun repaying staff and reported itself to the Fair Work Ombudsman in 2023, after it “proactively commenced a comprehensive wage integrity review”.



“Since then, we have established a dedicated wage integrity project team to rectify underpayments and strengthen our systems, processes, and staff awareness to prevent this from happening in the future,” Klomp said. The vice-chancellor said an agreement with the Ombudsman would also ensure the university met commitments to independently audit, issue transparent reporting, and continue to improve compliance. Fair Work Ombudsman Anna Booth said the university deserved credit for engaging with her office. World.title: ‘We should never allow this to become normal’: School leaders tell of armed guards and threats
World.content:
NationalAntisemitism royal commission ‘We should never allow this to become normal’: School leaders tell of armed guards and threats Michael Bachelard July 21, 2026 — 3:59pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The head of the Australian Council of Jewish Schools and two prominent school leaders have suggested government should carry more of the cost of protecting Jewish schools and students, not parents. Appearing at the Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion on Tuesday, Stephen Rothman said the council’s position was that “at least the recurrent expenditure on guards and other operational recurrent expenditures should be funded by the federal government”. In a hearing block focused on the security needs of the Jewish community, the leaders of Mount Scopus College and Bialik College in Melbourne told the commission the security bills for their respective campuses had increased in recent years, with about 70 per cent of the cost going to armed guards – an expense non-Jewish schools do not require, they said. Following the Bondi Beach terror attack, Mount Scopus College in Burwood had an increased security presence which included police. Joe Armao The evidence came as three rabbis from three different synagogues – including Adass Israel, which was burned down in 2024 in an alleged terror attack – spoke of the burden of security on Jewish communal life in Australia.



Dan Sztrajt, the principal of Mount Scopus in Burwood, in Melbourne’s east, spoke of his shock when the words “Jew Die” were painted on the school’s gates in 2024. Quickly, he said, he was contacted by parents “who told me personally that they would not be sending their children to school” because the graffiti suggested “the school might be targeted, or that this demonstrates that the school doesn’t have sufficient security”. Related Article Antisemitism royal commission Violence a legitimate tactic in freedom movements, pro-Palestine student leader tells royal commission Sztrajt told Commissioner Virginia Bell that a number of schools, including his own, began employing armed guards in 2015 following an antisemitic attack in Europe, and charged parents a levy to cover the cost. Following the Hamas incursion into Israel on October 7, 2023, and Israel’s subsequent war on Gaza, the cost of maintaining security had escalated dramatically, he said. Last year, Mount Scopus parents paid a levy of $1130 per student – up from $500 in 2022, which still fell short of covering the $3000 per student security cost, Sztrajt said, noting that while state and federal governments contributed funding, it was not available to spend on guards.



“The idea that government grants should not be used towards providing that level of much-needed protection has been problematic,” he said. Tyson Wodak, board president of Bialik College in Hawthorn East, told the commission parents at the school paid a security levy of $840 per student – up 230 per cent in recent years. The college also receives government funding, but like Sztrajt, he said it did not cover the full cost of security. “In my view, a well-functioning society ought to provide security to its people as a core part of its orderly function,” Wodak said. He said his school was one of three in the area, but the only one with such a high level of security.



“The other schools, you can walk in at the weekend and play basketball or do whatever you like. We have high fences. We have security everywhere – it’s a secure environment. I just can’t understand why we live in a country where one aspect of our community is expected to live under heavy security which it has to pay for in large part itself.” Another witness, Rabbi Levi Wolff of the Central Synagogue in Sydney’s Bondi Junction, told the royal commission: “Our children, as all Jewish children in this country, are growing up attending schools where they have armed guards in front of their schools and the houses of worship, and that’s normal. Rabbi Levi Wolff, chief rabbi of the Central Synagogue in Sydney, arrives for Tuesday’s royal commission hearing in Melbourne. AAP “That’s normal. But that is not normal, and we should never allow this to become Australia’s normal. “And when any Australian feels that they must hide who they are … by covering their kippah with a cap, or ensuring that they have an armed guard in front of their homes of worship, something has gone wrong for all Australians, not just for the Jewish community.”



Wolff spoke of being struck by the difference when standing outside St Mary’s Catholic Cathedral in Sydney just 10 days after the Bondi terror attack in December. Related Article Antisemitism royal commission ‘I’m sorry’: Uni of Sydney boss apologises to Jewish students over protest camp “I was struck by the absence of security. How this magnificent house of worship had its doors wide open, and people from all walks of life were able to just walk off the street with a knapsack on their back and come inside and pray and feel like nothing would go wrong,” Wolff said. “Would that ever be a possibility [at my synagogue]? Where there would be no armed guards, no bollards, no ongoing security screenings for every single person to be able to walk through?” Wolff said the threat began with words, and ended with violence. He drew attention to the language heard at campus protests.



“I often hear people say, ‘I’m not anti-Jewish. I’m simply anti-Zionist’, and in the same breath they deny the Jewish people’s spiritual, historical and indigenous connection to their ancestral land. “I mean, to me, it’s almost like saying, ‘I’m not racist against Aboriginals; Aboriginal Australians, I absolutely love you. I just simply don’t believe that you have any cultural or historical connection to this land,’” he said. “For many Jews, Zionism is not an abstract political ideology. It is the belief that the Jewish people, like every other people, have the right and self-determination to their ancestral homeland.” Adass Israel members Benjamin Klein (left) and Izzy Nussbacher outside the ruins of their synagogue last August. Simon Schluter The assertion of indigenous connection to Israel is politically controversial – pro-Palestinian protesters, and much of the political left, assert that the Zionist movement which began in the late 19th century and culminated in the Jewish state of Israel was a colonial project.



The commission heard from witnesses on Monday who spoke of the increased reliance on community security groups, or CSGs – organisations of volunteers set up to protect Jewish people and institutions against threats and attacks – at Jewish schools and synagogues across Australia following October 7, 2023. Benjamin Klein, who appeared on Tuesday as a lived experience witness on behalf of the Adass Israel synagogue in the inner Melbourne suburb of Ripponlea, said he knew of two people from his son’s school who had “picked themselves up and moved to Israel” amid rising antisemitism. “Those stories never used to happen. People … were proud to live in Melbourne. They were part of the Australian community. But now there’s good Aussie people … moving,” Klein told the commission. “It’s weird because, if you think about it, Israel is not necessarily a safe place … It’s quite a scary place. But they’re still picking themselves up from Melbourne and moving to Israel.” “Why are rational, successful accountants, lawyers, doctors [doing this?] … And the answer is they just don’t feel safe.”



The Ripponlea synagogue was largely destroyed after it was firebombed on December 6, 2024. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Gateway triples new WA gold discovery strike to 2.5km
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Gateway triples new WA gold discovery strike to 2.5km Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Penny Taylor July 21, 2026 — 3:56pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Gateway Mining may have unearthed a game-changing gold discovery at its Cowza prospect, part of the company’s Yandal gold project in Western Australia, after step-out drilling tripled the continuous high-grade strike from 800 metres to 2.5 kilometres. The latest results also confirmed high-grade gold in fresh rock for the first time, further strengthening the exploration model. Aircore drilling at Gateway Mining’s Cowza gold discovery within the Yandal gold project, Western Australia’s prolific Yandal Greenstone Belt. Every step-out drill line completed since Cowza was unveiled in June has intersected the same gold system, providing growing confidence the find is evolving into a large, continuous gold-bearing structure. The prospect is hosted within a major shear zone marking the contact between mafic and intermediate volcanic rocks. This geological setting has consistently delivered new discoveries across Gateway’s Yandal project. It forms part of a much larger 4.5km-long structurally complex corridor that has been strongly demagnetised.



‘With evidence of a substantial, continuous gold-bearing structure the RC rig may well be focused on Cowza for the foreseeable future.’ Gateway Mining chief executive officer Richard Pugh Gateway believes the same hydrothermal fluids responsible for the widespread demagnetisation also deposited the gold, pointing to a large and fertile mineralising event. The broader corridor suggests Cowza may be in the early innings of its growth, with significant exploration upside still ahead. The recent aircore drilling blitz returned a series of strong gold intercepts from along the newly extended strike, including a 27-metre interval grading 1.4 grams per tonne (g/t) gold from 84m, a 16-metre interval grading 1.9g/t gold from 88m and another 16-metre interval returning 1.3g/t gold from 68m. The 27-metre intercept came from the first aircore hole to properly test mineralisation in fresh rock and ended in mineralisation, with the final metre grading 3.3g/t gold. The result suggests the drilling was only beginning to intersect the primary gold system before reaching the limits of the aircore drill, confirming the discovery extends into primary mineralisation beneath the weathered profile and materially de-risking the exploration model.



Cowza is rapidly emerging as an important piece of the puzzle for Gateway at Yandal, demonstrating the repeatability of a geological model that has already delivered multiple discoveries across the project. Gateway Mining chief executive officer Richard Pugh said: “With evidence mounting in support of a substantial, continuous, and highly fertile gold-bearing structure that extends well beyond the boundaries of the assays received to date, the RC rig may well be focused on Cowza for the foreseeable future.” The company says it will waste little time putting that strategy into action. While a first reverse circulation (RC) rig continues drilling at Gateway’s Haflinger discovery 25km north of Cowza, a second RC rig is now due to arrive this weekend and immediately begin fresh-rock drilling at the new find. The expanded RC program marks a shift from proving discoveries to mapping the scale of fresh-rock mineralisation. Assays are also expected within a fortnight from the remainder of the recent aircore program testing Cowza’s northern extension, where drilling has already intersected the same shearing, veining and alteration observed in the mineralised holes. Cowza forms part of Gateway’s 1,780-square-kilometre Yandal gold project, which hosts almost 100km of prospective gold trends 85km north-east of Wiluna in the Yandal Greenstone Belt. The belt ranks among Western Australia’s premier gold provinces and hosts several multi-million-ounce gold deposits, including Northern Star Resources’ 7.4-million-ounce Jundee operation.



The discovery is the latest success from Gateway’s proven exploration model, joining Haflinger, Hummer, Celia South and Panikin as the company continues to build a pipeline of discoveries across Yandal. Those discoveries complement an existing 400,400-ounce gold resource, providing a solid foundation. Historically elevated gold prices continue to favour explorers delivering new discoveries and resource growth, particularly in tier-one jurisdictions such as Western Australia. Backed by $15.7M in cash and a further $5.6M in liquid ASX-listed securities at the end of the June quarter, the company appears well funded to accelerate drilling across Cowza and its broader pipeline of Yandal discoveries. Gateway still has another 2km of strike awaiting assays, while a second RC rig is about to step on the accelerator. If the geology continues to stack up, Cowza could quickly emerge as the crown jewel in the company’s Yandal crown. Is your ASX-listed company doing something interesting? World.title: Burnham is a devastatingly good politician. But he needs to heed this Aussie’s advice
World.content:
Analysis WorldEuropeUK politics Burnham is a devastatingly good politician. But he needs to heed this Aussie’s advice David Crowe Updated July 21, 2026 — 3:56pm ,first published 10:08am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

London: The first thing Andy Burnham did upon becoming Britain’s new prime minister was to admit failure. It was an honest and necessary step because Britain has seen an awful lot of failure over the past decade. But it also raised expectations that the new leader could arrest the country’s dismal decline. And, so far, there is no sign he has a solid plan to do so. In his opening remarks in Downing Street, just after his meeting with King Charles, he said this was a moment for “reflection and new resolution” about the future. “It requires my generation of politicians to raise our game,” he said. He admitted that Britain’s leaders had not been good enough, and he added: “We will be.” Andy Burnham speaks outside 10 Downing Street after becoming Britain’s seventh prime minister in a decade. Bloomberg A new leader always tries to break with the past and hold out the promise of a better future, so Burnham mainly stuck to that formula. He did, at least, acknowledge that Britain was suffering from a generational failure. Burnham is a devastatingly good politician. He has walked into 10 Downing Street, the prime minister’s official residence, barely a month after returning to parliament. He trounced the right-wing Reform UK party at a byelection. He was elected to the Labour leadership unopposed. His predecessor, Keir Starmer, resigned because his defeat was obvious.



Related Article Updated

UK politics The big surprise on Andy Burnham’s first day as UK PM? Trump wants to help him This required ruthless political skill. Burnham and his allies worked for at least a year to ensure that every mistake by Starmer – and there were many of them – led to a leadership coup. Now their moment has finally arrived. Do they actually know how to use their power to lift Britain’s fortunes? The Conservative Party leader, Kemi Badenoch, mocks Burnham for promising so much. “I have found Andy to be a nice man,” she said on Monday. “But Britain needs a leader who can take difficult decisions, not a people pleaser.” Nigel Farage, the populist leader of the right-wing Reform UK, has an effective line about Burnham’s attempts to appeal to both left and right. “I have to say I find the whole thing utterly vacuous,” Farage said at a conservative conference last Friday. “He is the great chameleon of British politics, capable of being all things to all people.” Burnham styles himself as a different kind of politician – but will style translate into the substance needed to turn Britain around? Christopher Furlong/Pool Getty via AP



In truth, Reform has no great policy plan. It simply has a powerful complaint. “We are going down the drain,” Farage said. “Britain is broken. We have to wake up to that fact, acknowledge the extent of the illness, and until we do that, you’ll never be able to put the right cures in place.” This message resonates because people can feel the decline around them – in the grim town squares with empty shops, in the number of unemployed young people, in the industries being shut down, in the knife crime on the streets, in the wait for healthcare and in the low economic growth. ‘People believe in a basic bargain. Work hard, play by the rules, get an education, and you and your children can have a better life. Across the developed world, people feel that bargain has been broken.’ Lynton Crosby, political analyst But the sharpest message came from an Australian observer, Lynton Crosby, who entered the debate on Monday with a word of warning. He is a former adviser to Liberal governments in Australia, including to John Howard for many years. As the executive chairman of CT Group, he is also a former adviser to Conservative governments in Britain. “What voters are asking for is not ideology, it is substantive delivery and change,” he wrote in The Times on Monday. Crosby offered a contrary view to the conventional wisdom in London. He said Starmer could have survived and, possibly, won the next election if Labour had held its nerve and worked harder on what voters wanted.



Sunlit uplands? Many Britons are feeling the squeeze after a decade of spiralling inflation and sluggish growth. Bloomberg “The most powerful driver of how people vote is a simple question: What does this mean for me and my life?” he wrote. “People believe in a basic bargain. Work hard, play by the rules, get an education, and you and your children can have a better life, a home of your own, a rising standard of living. Across the developed world, people feel that bargain has been broken. “A prime minister who had grasped that, and governed relentlessly around it, would have had something real to offer. The path was there for Starmer to take. Starmer cut a diminished figure just two years on from winning the election that returned Labour to power after 14 years. Getty Images



“Instead, Labour lost its nerve. Rather than hold to a steady, long-term course, the party let itself be governed by polling rather than addressing the underlying values and concerns the polling was being driven by; reacting to every fluctuation instead of doing the patient work of government.” Crosby warned Labour, and Burnham, that changing the leader would solve nothing if the party did not understand the national problems it needed to fix and “hold steady” to some economic foundations. Related Article Analysis

UK politics Is Andy Burnham the man to fight the right? “Burnham is being pulled towards a contradictory program of land taxes, wealth taxes, public ownership of utilities, fiscal discipline and a bigger budget, all at once,” wrote Crosby. “But to govern is to choose. A leader with no rival and no rebellion has the rarest of opportunities in politics: the room to choose one credible plan, govern on it and deliver the growth this country needs. But if he fails to learn the lessons of his predecessors, he will undoubtedly share their fate.”



Burnham may not want to heed the advice from Crosby, but he should. Everyone can see the new prime minister is trying to appeal to both left and right with his vague talk. He is promising to be more caring with welfare, help workers with tax cuts, spend more on services, nationalise industry, stick to the fiscal rules and spend more on defence. The sad fact is that he has very little room to do any of these things. The country’s net public debt is £2.9 trillion ($5.6 trillion), or about 95 per cent of annual economic output. This means the government is spending £110 billion on debt interest this year, which is about 8 per cent of all public spending and among the highest levels in five decades. Britain is not just broken. It’s broke. This is why Burnham is pledging to honour the “fiscal rules” in the budget. He has no other option. His government will be savaged by the bond markets if he and the new chancellor of the exchequer, John Healey, stumble on fiscal policy.

World.title: ‘Get in first’: How alleged ‘old-fashioned’ Sydney street fight turned fatal shooting
World.content:
NationalNSWCourts ‘Get in first’: How alleged ‘old-fashioned’ Sydney street fight turned fatal shooting Amber Schultz July 21, 2026 — 3:55pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A man accused of shooting his opponent in a Sydney street fight over hiring the victim’s wife to work at his inner-west brothel planned to “get in first” and kill him, a court has heard. Ayman Manly, 42, is on trial in the NSW Supreme Court charged with murder over the fatal shooting of Mohammad Chami on March 3, 2022. Ayman Manly has pleaded not guilty to murder. James Brickwood Manly has also been charged with shooting with intent to murder and discharging a firearm with intent to cause grievous bodily harm over the wounding of a second person, known as Witness 1. He has pleaded not guilty to all charges.



Related Article Crime Sydney man charged over ‘brazen’ fatal shooting During closing submissions, Crown prosecutor Eric Balodis SC told the jury Chami arranged the meeting after discovering Manly had employed his wife and began a relationship with her. The court heard the woman denied the pair had a sexual relationship. Chami had a turbulent relationship with the woman, the court was told, marked by domestic violence, infidelity and drug use. The pair split in 2021 after Chami assaulted her and she stabbed him. Chami was jailed over an unrelated incident days later. It’s alleged the woman fled to a friend at Manly’s brothel in Newtown, Mistiques. Manly offered her a place to stay at his Balmain property, and she began working as a receptionist at the venue, where she had previously been employed. When Chami was released from prison, he learnt of the arrangement and messaged Manly to set up a fist fight, the court heard.



“You should have never got her a place to stay … from the second you new [sic] she was my wife,” Chami wrote on March 2, the day before the alleged shooting. “Now straight up we have to have a crack one on one, and then I’ll leave at that.” Manly then called his own wife to tell her about the meetup. “Some f---ing gronk calls me up, wants to fight me,” he said in a phone call played to the court. Chami didn’t show up to the first meeting, with the pair arranging to meet at a semi-industrial cul-de-sac on Fox Street in the suburb of Holroyd the next day. Friends of Chami told the court he believed it would be a fist fight, and that he had left a knife behind before leaving for the meeting. “He said that he was going to go for an old-fashioned bashing,” one woman told the court. She added that she warned Chami “everyone knows that you bring guns to fights”, but Chami insisted it would only be a punch-up.



It’s alleged that just before midnight, Chami arrived on Fox Street with Witness 1. Dressed in socks and slides, Manly emerged from a pedestrian underpass near the Western Motorway with a taller, unidentified man. The pair began a heated exchange, the court heard, before Chami stepped back and raised his arm to punch Manly. Manly shot him five times in the back and buttocks, Balodis said. “Manly has taken the opportunity to get in first with Chami and kill him,” he said. Witness 1 was allegedly shot in the backside as he turned to flee. Chami’s body was found hours later by a passerby. With minimal DNA evidence, the prosecution relied on mobile phone tracking placing Manly at the scene, Witness 1’s testimony, and ballistics trajectory analysis matching the shooter’s height with Manly.



“The accused is a short fella. He did it, he’s guilty,” Balodis said. Defence barrister David Dalton, whose closing argument begins on Wednesday, maintains Manly was not involved. “He wasn’t there. He didn’t shoot anyone,” Dalton told the jury earlier in the trial. The jury is expected to retire to deliberate on Thursday. with AAP Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Beauty billionaires bought Toorak’s most expensive home. Then got help to buy out the neighbours
World.content:
Pharma and beauty billionaires Dennis and Georgina Bastas have been quietly accumulating multimillion-dollar parcels of Toorak’s top real estate with the help of companies linked to the wealthy couple’s associates. The pair already own prized historic mansion Coonac, which they bought for a record $136.1 million in May from businessman Paul Little and his Melbourne University chancellor wife, Jane Hansen. DBG Health chairman and group chief executive Dennis Bastas. Oscar Colman They’ve been given the green light to spend $38.5 million on its renovation, with the Bastases now also seeking permission to spend another $11.6 million on extending the 1867 Italianate mansion. But it can now be revealed the couple also have a foothold on a collection of prestige properties that border the Toorak mansion.



Part of the deal to purchase Coonac, which is on prestigious boulevard Clendon Road, included a 1950s apartment block on the adjacent Stonehaven Court. The two properties share a boundary fence. Since that deal was struck, two other properties in Stonehaven Court – which also border Coonac – have been sold, for $13.1 million and $13.05 million. Corporate records and title documents, seen by this masthead, show an entity called Stonehaven Property Holdings Pty Ltd, which was created in March, is behind the $13.05 million purchase. That corporate vehicle has only one director, Patrick Kypreos, also a director of Arrotex Investments, owned by the Bastases. Arrotex is Australia’s largest generic drug supplier and part of the $5.4 billion rich lister couple’s private business empire DBG Health, which has brands including MCoBeauty and Chemists’ Own. The other property on Stonehaven Court, sold for $13.1 million, is purchased in the name of a company whose sole director and ultimate owner is Kerry Goldfinger.



She is married to Melbourne businessman Eli Goldfinger, the business partner of Kypreos in EGA Corporate Advisers and Accountants. That property’s previous owner was Tania Buckley, the former wife of AFL coach Nathan Buckley. It is a five-bedroom Tudor-style mansion with open fireplaces, an outdoor lounge, and wine storage. The flurry of real estate activity in the area might even present Little, who is the former chairman of the Essendon Football Club, with a further opportunity. Related Article Melbourne luxury property Billionaire spends $136m in cash on Toorak mansion and block next door There remains squeezed into the parcel of prestige real estate a property still owned by Little that backs onto Coonac estate. Little has held the remaining residential block since 2011 and has rented it out ever since.



The Bastases signed on the line to buy Coonac in an off-market deal in February last year. Their purchase of the historic home was settled in May this year. It sits on just over one hectare complete with a pool and cabana, tennis court and sprawling gardens. All up, it means that if the Bastases took over ownership of the Stonehaven Court adjacent homes, the total real estate spend and estimated renovations would amount to an eye-watering $213.25 million. Before the Bastases bought Coonac from the Littles, the title of Australia’s most expensive house was shared jointly at $130 million by two grand Point Piper estates in Sydney’s east – Elaine and Uig Lodge. Coonac is held in the name of Georgina Bastas. The couple’s centrepiece new home was purchased without the need for a mortgage.



In parallel to the nearby real estate dealings, the billionaire couple are seeking approval from local planning authorities to increase the scope of a planned $38.5 million renovation of their historic mansion. Editor's pick United Arab Emirates As my Emirates plane flew into Dubai, missiles started flying again Last month, they lodged an application with Stonnington Council to expand their renovation on the heritage-protected, 1867 Italianate mansion by $11.6 million to a total estimated outlay of $50.1 million. Plans for the expansion have not been made public by the local council. Stonnington Council declined to comment on the Coonac process. Paul Little, Dennis Bastas, Patrick Kypreos and Eli Goldfinger were all contacted but did not respond to requests for comment. World.title: Final frontier: Smith and ageing Test team vow to complete unfinished business away from home
World.content:
SportCricketAustralian cricket Final frontier: Smith and ageing Test team vow to complete unfinished business away from home Daniel Brettig July 21, 2026 — 3:54pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Much as the 2005 Ashes defeat kept their legendary forebears together until a blazing 5-0 revenge mission two years later, Steve Smith and his ageing teammates have committed to making collective amends for fumbled trips to India and England in 2023. That much was clear when selection chair George Bailey formally unveiled the squad for two Tests against Bangladesh in Darwin and Mackay next month, with only one player – all-rounder Cameron Green, 27 – under the age of 30. Steve Smith walks off the SCG after a century in the 2025/26 Ashes. Getty Images Games against a Bangladesh side that just lost a Test match by an innings to Zimbabwe would appear the ideal time to choose some more youthful players. But Bailey made it clear that this was more like a roll call of Australia’s frontline men for difficult tours to India (no Australian series wins since 2004), England (none since 2001) and South Africa (none since 2014). This quest is personified by Smith, who clearly wants to cap his international career by breaking the aforementioned droughts, including by continuing to substitute for captain Pat Cummins whenever required. Shane Warne, Glenn McGrath and company were similarly motivated.



“I can’t foresee that changing in the short-term,” Bailey said of Smith’s deputy role. “In my conversations with him over the last few months, I don’t think I’ve seen him as excited or invigorated around the opportunities and challenges, in particular, this Test team have over the next period of time. “For a number of those guys that have played a lot of Test cricket and are at certain stages of their career, you look at some of the series that are coming up and what the opportunities are for this Test team to achieve. It probably comes as no surprise as to how excited and focused they are. Editor's pick Australian cricket Why Australia’s next Test opponents are in crisis mode “So, yeah, I’ve actually been really quite excited by how pumped Steve is, how much thought and time he’s putting into to what’s coming up. I fully expect him to be a major part of it and looking forward to seeing how those really big, key series [provide] a chance to really lay down a marker across a number of different conditions as well. That’s exciting for everyone, but in particular for him.” As was often said in 2023, Australia’s high-performing Test side cannot be considered great without overseas series wins in India and England. South Africa, too, is the source of much intrigue given the ugly events of the previous Test tour there in 2018.



Four years ago, Australia had genuine opportunities to beat India away before losing the series 2-1, and should have skipped away to a 3-0 margin over England after as many Tests, only to finish 2-2. David Warner and Usman Khawaja have since retired, but Smith, Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood, Nathan Lyon and Scott Boland will all look at this cycle as the final chance to redress things. “There’ll be moments out of those series where they look back and wish that things could have gone differently,” Bailey said. “But there are great things that they would have learnt out of that. “They’re constantly trying to get better, and they’re constantly asking questions, particularly around some of those places that do provide different challenges around how they can be better and how they can make the entire team better the next time that we get that opportunity.” Scott Boland received his baggy green cap from Josh Hazlewood before the third Test against England at the MCG in 2021. Getty Images Boland’s durability has seen him step up for both Hazlewood and Cummins in recent times, and Bailey made it clear that he had now made a case to be one of the first three quick bowlers chosen.



“Scotty would never say it, but he’s mounting a strong case that when you use the words ‘the Big Three’ that he could be one of those,” Bailey said. Editor's pick Analysis

Australian cricket How an allegation of an affair between teammates rocked Australian cricket For now, the selectors have a full complement of their first-choice bowlers available, but Bailey also acknowledged how important all-rounders Beau Webster and Green would be in sharing the load. “The fact they both can bowl will be important at different times across the next 18 months,” Bailey said of the pair. Australia may make some left-field selection choices around Test assignments, with white-ball series against South Africa, Zimbabwe and even England likely to see numerous multi-format players rested, while other younger squad members may be sent to India to play for Australia A ahead of next year’s five Tests.



“It will be about identifying some periods between Test series and white-ball series over the next 18 to 24 months, where you can maybe invest a bit back into the body and mind to stay fresh,” Bailey said. “I don’t think the 11 will be the same across each of the next 21 Tests and there will be changes, and for some of them our hand will be forced.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: Health NZ spend on locum doctors hits a new high, at $220 million
World.content:
The amount of money spent on temporary doctors to plug gaps in the health system has hit a new high, topping $200 million for the third year in a row.

Health NZ says it's working hard to recruit permanent specialists and has even cut the budget for locums for the next financial year.

But, others in the health sector say more drastic action is needed to bring the spend under control and incentivise doctors to stay on our shores.

Locums have a place

Dr James Irwin recently resigned as the last full-time permanent gastro specialist at Palmerston North Hospital, a service now staffed by locums and fill-ins from other districts.

He's seen the positive and negative side of using locums.

"In a a department, where you've got a full department and then someone is sick or goes away for a period of time, getting a locum is great because it helps fill holes and helps get work done.

"You have an expectation that you're going to have a full department going forward to deal with all of the long-term stuff and all of the departmental planning, and so forth."

Dr James Irwin. RNZ / Jimmy Ellingham

Reliance on them, however, was less satisfactory when it became more of a medium-term arrangement, or longer.

"As a longer-term employee you're then the one that's dealing with all of the chronic disease management and planning for the department."

This happened to Irwin.

In the 2025-26 financial year, Health NZ spent about $220m on locums, up from about $208m in 2024-25 and $209m in 2023-24. The bill was $168m in 2022-23, Health NZ's first year of operation.

Irwin said constantly changing faces had an effect on continuity of care for patients too.

"It's a consequence of the transactional model of healthcare.

"If you employ a locum and pay them money to do something for six weeks, they come and do that, but they're not going to want to take on additional responsibility that continues after they finish," Irwin said.

"You need to be employing people in a situation where it's clear that they're going to be providing long-term care. That requires a long-tern appointment."

He said that's why permanent appointments were needed.

Budget trimmed after spend increases

Health NZ national director of people, culture, health and safety, Robyn Shearer, said the organisation was recruiting overseas and working with medical schools to get more doctors long term.

"It's a global challenge. It is hard to get all the doctors we need," she said.

"Locums play a really important role for us in maintaining continuity of care and staffing, particularly in specialities and regions which are harder for us to staff.

"They're an important part of how we fill and manage short-term gaps in our rosters and provide cover for our permanent doctors, in particular, to take a break."

New Zealand was competing against other countries for specialists, so Health NZ worked hard to promote the country as a great destination.

"We are in a competitive market, there's no doubt about it, and we have to be prudent financially," Shearer said.

"There is always a balance around what we offer, but we do look at, certainly, what New Zealand has to offer, and you'll have probably seen we've had an influx of doctors in the South Island from America who are promoting New Zealand as a great place to work and live."

She said health authorities had always used locums, but more were required as the demand for health services increased, putting pressure on the workforce.

However, Health NZ was looking to bring the cost under control, cutting the budget for the 2026-27 year to $179m.

"We are deliberately looking to have a decrease in our spend. What we are supporting districts and regions with is how we can given them information so they have more awareness of locum use and spend."

Shearer said Health NZ regions could look at alternatives, drive recruitment and look at "alternate workforce ways of working" such as using nurse practitioners.

Minister orders reliance to end

Executive director of senior doctors' union, the Association of Salaried Medical Specialists, Sarah Dalton, said locums did quality work, but permanent staff provided better value.

"When you're relying on locums to help run a service, anything from the complete collapse of the gastroenterology service in Palmerston North through to another service in another part of the country that needs locums on a regular basis to fill gaps in rosters, it is a cost to patients and to colleagues."

Association of Salaried Medical Specialists' Sarah Dalton. RNZ / Jimmy Ellingham

Patient Voice Aotearoa's Malcolm Mulholland had another idea to try to hold on to doctors, rather than use more expensive locums.

"I do not for the life of me know what Health NZ aren't coming up with a better plan - something along the lines of getting our best and brightest when they graduate from med school and bonding them in hard-to-staff areas.

"[Health NZ] could say as part of that bonding, 'We're also going to take care of your student loan.'

"To my mind it would still be a cheaper option than looking to employ locums left, right and centre."

Simeon Brown. RNZ / Louis Dunham

Health minister Simeon Brown has written to Health NZ's chairperson, saying he expects the organisation to move away from depending on locums.

"As a priority I expect you to monitor and prioritise shifting away from dependence on locums to recruiting permanent senior medical officers to vacancies - with an initial focus on regions that have high dependency on locums," he wrote.

The minister's office told RNZ locums would always play a role, as the minister's priority was to make sure patients received the care they needed, when and where they needed it.

World.title: Nicola Willis blames 'Trump spike' for high inflation
World.content:
The Finance Minister says US President Donald Trump is to blame for New Zealand's rising inflation.

StatsNZ figures released on Tuesday showed annual inflation lifted to 4.1 percent, the highest level in more than two years as fuel prices surged due to the US-Iran war.

Nicola Willis said the figures reflected the international oil shock, which the government could not control.

"What they show was the Trump spike in inflation, driven by higher petrol and diesel prices," she said.

"New Zealanders have already experienced this at the pump, and we know that it's been a very difficult period for many."

Willis said without higher fuel prices, inflation would have been within the target band, at 2.9 percent.

"That is an encouraging sign that the underlying factors driving inflation are being better controlled by our government," she said.

However, it was not only fuel prices driving inflation. There were also annual jumps in electricity prices (12 percent) and rates (9 percent).

Willis said the government was doing everything it could to keep costs down for New Zealanders, including introducing rates caps.

"We do not accept that the level of rate increases that New Zealanders have had to put up with in recent years is acceptable, and we are acting to prevent that happening in future," she said.

On electricity, Willis said the government was consenting more renewable generation, which would bring down households' prices in future.

Labour finance spokesperson Barbara Edmonds blasted Willis for pinning high inflation on uncontrollable factors.

"She just continues to blame everybody else but take no responsibility for some of those other underlying costs, such as government costs, that has increased by 21 percent over the last two years," Edmonds said.

"GP fees have also gone up by over 20 percent. Those are all factors that she could have looked at in the last two years but decided to pass those costs on to everyday New Zealanders."

Edmonds said she was holding Willis to the same standard as Willis held former Labour finance minister Grant Robertson to.

"Which is, you can't just blame everything on overseas factors, you've got to take some work yourself."

Power rises

Meanwhile, an economist is raising questions about the lack of savings being passed on to households by power companies.

The latest figures showed power prices are up 12 percent annually and in the last nine months electricity prices increased at the fastest rate since 1989.

Tim Hazeldine from the University of Auckland told Checkpoint that New Zealand produced most of its own electricity.

He said much of that was hydropower, which was relatively cheap.

But Hazeldine said wholesale electricity was largely priced on the cost of thermal generation, which was more expensive.

"Everybody has to pay the higher price and the electricity retailers pocket a big, windfall gain on that and that is worth a bit more government attention."

World.title: Wellington bike shop owner recovers $10,000 worth of goods using GPS trackers
World.content:
A Wellington bike shop owner has recovered more than $10,000 worth of goods by using GPS trackers in his bikes.

Switched on Bikes was broken into early on Saturday morning, where a rental e-scooter and e-mountain bike were stolen.

Owner Ryan O'Connell said a notification from his alarm system woke him up.

Checking the security cameras in the store from his phone, he said he saw someone rolling out an e-scooter through the smashed-open front door.

"So I quickly called the police and then they responded really quickly. And I also let them know that we had follow GPS trackers installed on the scooter," he said.

O'Connell stayed on the line to update the police on the goods' location in real time.

Police said the alleged offender left the scene in a vehicle with the goods, which they found within 20 minutes on Vivian Street.

But the driver fled when asked to stop.

"I just kind of ran downstairs, got my laptop out and logged into my phone and started providing those locations. But you just want to be able to do everything really quickly," O'Connell said.

Police said they used road spikes to stop the car near the Basin Reserve and arrest a 35-year-old man just before 5am.

Within an hour of the burglary, police reunited O'Connell with the e-scooter and e-bike.

"I was just really happy that everything worked out and we were able to get the items back as quickly as we did," he said.

He told RNZ the incident showed him how well his security system worked,

"We had an alarm system and we had CCTV and we had a security company that helped out.

"I think it's a good validation of all of the systems that we have in place to either prevent or to respond to things like this," he said.

He said it was satisfying being able to help police.

World.title: Rural communities rally to help flood-hit farmers rebuild damaged fences
World.content:
Rural communities are rallying to fundraise and support storm-affected farmers get damaged fences up again.

Earlier this month, South Islanders bore the brunt of a low-pressure weather system that brought heavy rain, flooding and snow in its northbound path from Otago to Waitaki, North Canterbury and Kaikōura.

On Monday, Marlborough-based Repost Fence Posts sent a delivery of thousands of free fence posts to farmers in need around neighbouring Kaikōura.

Co-owner Greg Coppell said storm damage varied, but it was widespread across the large catchment.

He hoped the 3500 fence posts that would create around 24 kilometres of fence line would help farms get up and running again.

"That's landed now and it's already going out the gate there at Kaikōura. So that was pretty exciting to get that bit done."

He said it was about getting livestock secured behind wires, off roads and away from rivers.

"It's a start, but there's a fair bit to go yet," he said.

Greg Coppell is co-owner of Marlborough-based Repost Fence Posts. Cosmo Kentish-Barnes

The storm arrived in the lower North Island affecting Wairarapa farmers, many of whom were already struggling with wet conditions.

Coppell said it was planning a second unit to go to Wairarapa, but still had some fundraising to go to cover freight costs.

"We've got about another $2500-$3000 to go, and we'll get another unit to Wairarapa to help support those guys there."

In contact with councils, fence posts would go to the farmers most in need, Coppell said.

He added that farmers' storm recoveries could go on for years.

Rural influencer, farm chef and author Philippa Cameron of Otematata rallied her 70,000 or so followers across her What's for Smoko social media platforms to help Repost fundraise for the two deliveries.

Repost Fence Posts thanks donors who supported its drive to help flood-affected farmers. SUPPLIED/REPOST NZ

Having raised just under $8000 as of Monday, Cameron said storms affected farmers and rural communities, so it was important to help out.

"It will affect the feed going into the end of winter and into spring based on if there are fence lines down," she said.

"Being able to get those fences up quicker means that stock will be in the right places."

Cameron said donations would directly help these affected farmers.

"It's the power of a community, and I suppose that's the great thing about living rurally is that we know the power of a community," she said.

"So to be able to share that with the wider New Zealand, then that's cool too."

World.title: Waikato prison inmates were readily accessing contraband, report finds
World.content:
Waikato prisoners accessing contraband, prison overpopulated Checkpoint Download MP3 7m

Low staff morale, no onsite drug testing for years, contraband readily available, and filthy uninhabitable parts of the jail.

They are some of the serious concerns identified at the Spring Hill Correctional Facility in north Waikato in the Office of the Inspectorate's May 2025 inspection report which was released today.

It also highlights issues with staff absences and inexperience, long lockdowns for inmates, inadequate meals, clothing and bedding.

It found some prisoners had only one set of clothing, were cold due to a lack of bedding, and were often given sandwiches for lunch with just margarine.

The prison was over capacity for its original design as an end destination site for 650 prisoners. It had essentially became a remand site, housing over 800 prisoners at the time of inspection. The report found this change in population proving a challenge for the site's infrastructure and staff alike.

Parts of the prison were determined not fit for purpose, with pigeons causing health risks and making some areas unfit for living. Facilities in unit kitchenettes and day rooms varied, with many items broken or missing.

It said many prisoners reported feeling safe on site, but a significant number did not. Bullying and standovers were considered to be a part of prison life.

The use of force was not always being recorded and the report said in several cases staff should have made more of an attempt to deescalate before using force.

"Overall, while we found some areas of positive practice, we had serious concerns with conditions in some areas of the prison, and with certain practices and processes," said Chief Inspector Janis Adair.

This included hearing about and observing several "concerning security issues". She said staff and prisoners told them contraband was readily available, and there had been no drug testing at the site for five years.

Spring Hill opened in 2007 as an end destination site for 650 sentenced prisoners. But Adair said over the past 10 years, it had become a remand site, with 76 percent of prisoners on remand at the time of the inspection.

This change in population, she said, was proving a challenge for the site's infrastructure and staff alike.

The inspection found custodial staffing levels were at 94 percent, but that morale was low amongst custodial staff and unplanned absences, like sick leave, were common and left units short staffed.

Adair said 38 percent of custodial staff also had less than two years of experience working in a New Zealand prison and many senior and principal corrections officers lacked experience in their roles.

"The lack of availability of custodial staff and the unsuitable infrastructure had significant impacts across the prison."

She said morale was high in the health team, but many felt unsupported by custodial staff, and some did not always feel safe as custodial staff would sometimes leave them unsupervised with prisoners.

Corrections custodial services commissioner Sean Mason said it was positive to see many of the areas identified for improvement in the report aligned with work Corrections had already addressed or that was underway since the inspection was carried out more than a year ago.

"Many prisoners go to extreme lengths to get contraband into prisons and Corrections is constantly working to stay one step ahead in contraband prevention."

At Spring Hill, Mason said the intelligence team had developed a contraband dashboard which provided staff with information on trends, patterns and emerging risks.

Drug testing was reintroduced in November 2025 after it was suspended during the Covid-19 pandemic, when all non-essential prison activities were paused to reduce operational risks and support public health requirements and when staffing pressures were at their tightest.

"Throughout the period when drug testing was suspended, the site maintained a strong focus on identifying and managing drug-related risks.

"The current testing activity, combined with ongoing searching routines, intelligence-led monitoring, the vigilance of dog handlers, comprehensive screening of all mail and parcels, and continual assessment of operational and intelligence information, aims to ensure that drug-related risks are being actively identified, tracked, and managed across the site."

Mason also said following an extensive nationwide recruitment drive, there was now an additional 45 custodial staff working at the site, and this had reduced the day-to-day impact on the prison when staff called in sick.

World.title: Coroner told about LynnMall terrorist's time in prison's extreme risk unit
World.content:
The Coroners Court has heard about conditions inside the extreme risk unit where LynnMall attacker Ahamed Samsudeen was housed.

Samsudeen was shot dead by police, ending his stabbing spree at a West Auckland mall five years ago.

A coroner's inquest is under way into his death, with parts two and three looking into the time leading up to the attack and Samsudeen's path to violent extremism.

Just seven weeks before the 2021 attack that resulted in six people stabbed and another injured, Ahamed Samsudeen was released from his second stint in prison.

He was first behind bars in 2017, bailed a year later, and back in prison by August 2018.

During this time, Samsudeen was moved from Mt Eden Prison to Auckland's Paremoremo maximum security prison.

While there, he spent time in the prison's extreme risk unit, kept away from other prisoners.

The coroner heard from the unit's principal Corrections officer at the time, who cannot be named.

He was asked by the lawyer representing Samsudeen's family, Fletcher Pilditch KC, about what a day in the unit looked like.

"His yard time, so therefore the time that he spent outside, that was outside of his cell but in his personal yard?" Pilditch asked.

"Correct," the officer said.

"And at all other times he would be in his cell?" - That was also correct.

The officer told Pilditch that Samsudeen and others would be served breakfast at eight in the morning, eaten in their cells on their own.

How much time they spent out of the cell would depend on what appointments the inmate had, as well as their yard time, he said.

Counsel assisting the coroner, Rebekah Jordan, asked the officer how Samsudeen would spend time inside his cell.

"He has a TV in his cell, he has reading material, he would use his cell-attached yard, pray, that sort of thing," he said.

Samsudeen was allowed two hours of yard time a day, one in the morning and another in the afternoon, the officer said.

He also had library books and a Quran to read, as well as his own legal documents.

She quoted evidence given earlier in the inquest from another prisoner in a cell near to Samsudeen, who's identity was also suppressed.

" 'The daily comments and abuse from staff and inmates did not help, we would be locked in this environment for 22 to 24 hours a day, so there was no escape from it. Staff would condone or ignore this behaviour from other prisoners'," she said.

"It's not uncommon for prisoners to abuse each other," the officer said.

The officer said this kind of abuse would be addressed.

"If Mr Samsudeen for example was shouting abuse, you'd encourage him to cut it out, there's not much more you can do."

He did not respond to comments about abuse from staff.

Jordan asked the officer about the prison programmes that would have been available for Samsudeen.

"He assessed in June 2020 as not being suitable to participate in group programmes due to his influence capability - I just wanted to explore with you, what does that mean?" she asked.

"Attempting to spread his ideology, for example," the officer said.

World.title: Thousands sign petition seeking Keytruda funding for early-stage breast cancer
World.content:
A petition asking for cancer drug Keytruda to be funded for early-stage breast cancer has received more than 17,000 signatures.

A group of survivors, those currently in treatment, and their supporters gathered on the steps of Parliament on Tuesday morning to meet a handful of politicians and call for change.

Catherine Cooke, the author of the petition, said in total it had received 17,096 signatures.

As well as feeling gratitude for her own remission, she said she carried the guilt of surviving while others did not get access to the same treatment.

But even though she had qualified for access, her treatment had not been funded. Cooke said she had suffered a $750,000 loss when she sold her business to pay for Keytruda.

Currently, the drug - also known as pembrolizumab - is funded for late-stage cancer diagnoses, meaning people in the early stages are missing out, or forking out tens of thousands of dollars.

Triple negative breast cancer is a sub-type of breast cancer which lacks the receptors for hormones or HER2 protein found in other breast cancers, affecting about 10 percent of New Zealand woman diagnosed.

It is more common in younger women - that is, under the age of 44 - and tends to be more aggressive than other sub-types.

[https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/health/583019/i-want-to-sit-down-with-her-cancer-patient-demands-meeting-with-nicola-willis

Keytruda] is funded for early stage triple negative breast cancer in more than 40 countries, including Australia, the UK and Canada.

A group gathered at Parliament on Tuesday to support the petition and meet with politicians. RNZ / Kate Green

Cooke's petition asks to expand the eligibility criteria to those with an early diagnosis, which she said would be a more effective treatment and save the health system money in the long term.

It is currently on Pharmac's options for investment list, which contains more than 100 drugs it would like to fund if it had the money available.

"There's no winners," Cooke said. "I mean, yes, I'm alive and I'm grateful. I'm grateful for the people that supported me, but at the end of the day, equity must be for everybody and not just for those that can't afford to crowdfund or can't afford it."

Among those who had come down to support the petition, Annette Wikeepa and Angela Davies knew better than most the difference funded treatment could make.

Back in 2007, Wikeepa was among a group who took a case to the High Court to get Herceptin funded for HER2-positive breast cancer, helping about 600 women each year.

Davies was one of them, diagnosed at the age of 47 in 2023. She received a year of chemotherapy and Herceptin, followed by a year on Kadcyla.

Because of Wikeepa's work, funding the treatment was "one thing I didn't have to worry about", she said. "Knowing that Annette was here today, I had to come."

Davies, who had Wikeepa herself, was 48 at diagnosis - now, she is nearing 70.

She paid $80,000 for her treatment, and then raised $100,000 to take their case to court almost 20 years ago.

Davies was very grateful for that work.

"If it had have been a conversation about finances, I certainly wouldn't have been able to complete my treatment," she said. "It just wouldn't have been possible."

Annette Wikeepa, left, a breast cancer survivor who was among those who fought for funded treatment in court nearly two decades ago, and Angela Davies, right, who recently benefited from that work. RNZ / Kate Green

Cooke is set to present her petition to the Health Select Committee at Parliament on Wednesday.

Todd Stephenson, ACT health spokesperson, told RNZ he had been following Cooke's campaign for several months, calling her a "fierce advocate".

His party had been very supportive of reforms at Pharmac to change the culture and the way it approaches funding decisions, he said, but he acknowledged there was "more work to be done there".

He said there was work going on to improve Pharmac's ability to advocate, and better improve its budget bids.

World.title: Parliament's week: Government and (unusually), non-government bills
World.content:
MPs are back in Wellington to debate legislation and this week - for the first time in two months - this includes bills not proposed by the government.

The non-government bills will get four and a half hours on Wednesday evening. The other 13 or so hours of legislative debate will focus on turning government policy into law.

The government 'half' - Tuesday and Thursday

This week follows the new normal of including an extra morning sitting. This week it is the Thursday select committee meetings that will be replaced with debate in the House. The Thursday subject committees are: Economic Development, Science & Innovation; Foreign Affairs; Defence & Trade; Environment; Primary Production; Regulations Review; Transport and Infrastructure; and Justice.

The government focus is on just four policy bills, and these will be debated across Tuesday evening and all day Thursday. The hope is that three of the four may complete two stages of debate. Whether that occurs will depend on how much energy the Opposition puts into carefully and slowly considering them in their Committee of the whole House (CwH) stages.

* Arms Bill - Second Reading (2R), and (CwH)

* Employment Leave Bill - 2R and CwH

* Infrastructure Funding and Financing Amendment Bill - CwH

* English Language Bill - 2R and CwH

The Arms Bill slightly walks back a little of the toughened regulation of weapons that occurred after the 2019 mosque attacks. Major changes include removing the arms regulator role from the police, introducing new licence types for museum employees, and new rules for who can use restricted types of weapons for pest control.
