Opposition parties are concerned about the loss of police intelligence capacity from the body that will determine arms licences, and some potential loopholes in weapon rules. In the select committee report, Labour argued that the "fit and proper person" test should explicitly include online connection to groups that "promote violence, hatred, or extremism".

The Employment Leave Bill would replace the Holidays Act 2003, which has long caused confusion. There is wide agreement that it could be improved, but less agreement over whether this bill will fix the issue. This is a tough area to get right when it must cover full time, part-time, variable hours, shifts, contracts, and casual workers. The Select Committee report on the bill is here.

The Infrastructure Funding and Financing Amendment Bill is written to ease the use of Special Purpose Vehicles, entities created to fund and build infrastructure at a remove from a Local Council's balance sheets; and to repay their financing by charging levies to those benefited by the infrastructure, for up to 50 years. The ongoing liability for levies would be added to a property's LIM. This bill has reached the CwH stage, but the earlier Select Committee report can be read here.

The English Language bill is what American political commentators would call a messaging bill. It doesn't change anything, but it satisfies the feelings or desires of a voting bloc. Once you remove the legal niceties and formatting requirements it is just eight words long. It says "English is an official language of New Zealand." Legal scholars will tell you that this is already the case - the fact that this bill is written in English and that this is legally acceptable is a clue.

The eight word-long bill generated 1601 submissions to the Justice Committee. The committee report reads as slightly apologetic. It points out that the government was required to pass this bill as a result of its coalition agreement with New Zealand First. It says: "We note that English currently has official language status and will continue to have official language status even if the bill is not enacted or if the enacted bill is later repealed. …We consider that the bill would not change the status of the English language, nor its use."

The non-government 'half' - Members' Wednesday

Member's days are typically scheduled every other sitting week at Parliament, but recently government urgency has overridden that norm. The most recent Members' day was two months ago, on 20 May.

This week all but one of the member's bills up for debate are new, and the debate on each will be whether or not to allow them a first reading and progression to a Select Committee. The odd bill out is the Life Jackets for Children and Young Persons Bill which is returning from select committee.

The Concealment of Location of Victim Remains Bill is from National MP Tom Rutherford. It allows for the denial of parole to any prisoner who refuses to disclose the location of a victim's remains.

The Life Jackets for Children and Young Persons Bill is from National MP Shane Reti. For any recreational vessel under six metres, it requires that every person on board under 15 years of age must be wearing a life jacket.

The Criminal Records (Clean Slate) (Additional Eligibility) Amendment Bill is from Labour MP Tangi Utikere. The bill would expand the clean slate scheme to include two new categories of offenders providing they have not re-offended for 10 years. The two categories are those who have had custodial sentences of a year or less, and those who have had a mandatory disqualification from driving for repeat offences.

The Crimes (Virginity Testing Practices) Amendment Bill is from Labour MP Priyanca Radhakrishnan. Its General Policy Statement is short enough to reproduce in full.

"Virginity testing refers to the inspection of female genitalia for the purpose of ascertaining history of vaginal intercourse. It is an unscientific, unreliable, and medically unnecessary practice that violates human rights and is associated with adverse outcomes for physical, psychological, and social wellbeing. Women and girls are often coerced or forced into this honour-based abuse against their will. This Bill seeks to protect vulnerable women and girls by amending the Crimes Act 1961 and introducing new offences that criminalise virginity testing and the related practice of hymenoplasty."

The Local Government (Management of Local Authorities) Amendment Bill is from the National MP Stuart Smith. It would make it clear that while the council executives direct the staff, they are in turn subject to the direction and oversight of the mayor and council.

The Crown Minerals (Prohibition on Mining on Conservation Land) Amendment Bill does what it says on the tin. This is a Green Party bill (MP Lan Pham), and is unlikely to progress as it is contrary to a current government bill.

World.title: Vaughters says night tests would have saved cycling '25 years of drama'
World.content:
Former professional cyclist and Cannondale-EF team boss Jonathan Vaughters has weighed in on the row over pre-dawn doping tests at the Tour de France, arguing such controls ​could have exposed cycling's blood-doping era decades earlier had they existed at the time.

Riders including race leader Tadej Pogačar and Jonas Vingegaard were woken in the early hours of Sunday for unannounced doping checks ahead of ​the 15th stage, prompting ‌complaints that the disruption to sleep was unfair and potentially dangerous.

Vaughters, who rode professionally through the late 1990s and early 2000s, defended the practice.

"2am testing is one of the very effective ways ‌to prevent peptide (EPO, hGH) and testosterone micro dosing," Vaughters wrote on social media.

"If ⁠UCI [Union Cycliste Inter]ationale) had tested us in 2001 at 2am? We'd all have ‌been suspended and saved the sport ​25 years of drama."

His comments ‌carry particular weight given his own history with doping.

Jonathan Vaughters (right) was teammates with Lance Armstrong (left) on the US Postal team. (Getty Images: Graham Watson)

Vaughters was a teammate of Lance Armstrong on the US Postal Service team and later admitted using performance-enhancing drugs, including EPO, during his career.

When Lance met Oprah Lance Armstrong had successfully doped for years. But when the evidence backed him into a corner, he took control of the narrative and confessed live on Oprah's couch, martyring himself to cycling's EPO era.

He subsequently testified in the US Anti-Doping Agency's (USADA) investigation into ​Armstrong, ‌who was stripped of his seven Tour titles in 2012 after the agency concluded he ran what it called the most sophisticated doping program the sport had seen.

Vaughters ⁠went on to found the team now ‌known as Cannondale-EF, positioning it as ‌an advocate for clean racing.

His remarks come as riders pushed back on the timing of ‌Sunday's tests.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Vingegaard, tested at 2 am, said the visit cost him about 40 minutes of sleep before a mountain stage on which he later ‌crashed ​and broke his collarbone.

Pogačar, ⁠tested at 5 am, said he managed only four hours of sleep. Stage winner Remco Evenepoel called the practice "inhuman".

The International Testing Agency, which oversees doping controls for the UCI, said it was "conscious that night-time testing may be disruptive ⁠to riders' rest and recovery" but that effective testing must, "in limited and justified circumstances," occur outside daytime hours.

Micro-dosing of substances ‌such as EPO ‌and human growth hormone, which can clear the body within ​hours, has long concerned anti-doping authorities, who say predictable daytime-only testing makes such practices easier to evade.

Reuters

World.title: Weatherald retains Australian Test spot despite middling Ashes returns
World.content:
Opening batsman Jake Weatherald has retained his spot in Australia's Test squad for the looming series against Bangladesh.

Despite a middling Ashes campaign last summer, Weatherald is among a 13-man squad bolstered by the return of a trio of big guns.

Captain Pat Cummins, paceman Josh Hazlewood and spinner Nathan Lyon all return after recovering from injury.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"They have worked extremely hard, individually and with the [fitness] teams, over the past few months to return from their respective injuries," Australia's chairman of selectors George Bailey said.

"While this is a 13-player squad, we have players prepared and available should any adjustments be required in the lead-up to these matches.

"The volume of cricket and schedule across the next 12 months are likely to present further opportunities across all formats for many players."

Missing from Australia's squad for the final Test against England last January are Usman Khawaja (retired), Michael Neser, Todd Murphy and Brendan Doggett.

The Australians host Bangladesh in Darwin from August 13-17 and Mackay from August 22-26, the start of a gruelling 12 months featuring 20 Test matches.

Weatherald will resume his opening batting partnership with Travis Head after playing all five Tests last summer against England.

The Darwin-born left-hander made only 201 runs at an average of 22.33 but has been given another chance to enhance his Test credentials.

AAP

World.title: Buckley opts out of Dons, Blues coaching races after Tasmania snub
World.content:
A disappointed Nathan Buckley is ruling out bidding for other vacant AFL head coaching jobs after being overlooked by the Tasmania Devils.

While Buckley, who openly coveted the Tasmanian post that went to Ken Hinkley, says he wants to be a head coach again, he is unlikely to pitch for the vacant positions at Essendon and Carlton.

"I haven't really reflected on where those roles sit, and I don't think I would enter those processes," Buckley told Fox Footy on Monday night.

Loading...

Buckley said his most likely outcome next year was to remain at Geelong, where he is an assistant to Chris Scott.

"I am absolutely focused on the next six to 10 weeks with Geelong and how that plays out," he said.

"I will take some time to reassess what is after that."

Buckley was committed to winning the Devils job that instead was given to former Port Adelaide boss Hinkley.

"I went home, kicked the dog, threw the toys out of the cot … because I was really keen on it," he said.

"If you're going to go for a job, you have got to decide if you're absolutely all in on it — and I was.

"And I absolutely respect the process that the Devils have run, and I respect their decision with Ken as well. I am glad they have found their man, and they're really clear that Kenny is the guy for them."

However, the former Collingwood boss said the Devils' decision was a personal "fork in the road".

"I was really deliberate in getting back into Geelong, and that was as much to give myself the very best chance to be ready to go for the Tasmania role," he said.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"Now that is off the table, so I will be absolutely committed to what is going on at Geelong. I have got an option for next year there and that is probably the most likely outcome.

"There are no guarantees in this, and you have got to put yourself out there, and you have got to have a crack.

"So there's disappointment."

Asked if he remained steadfast in wanting to be a head coach again, Buckley replied: "Yeah. I determined that about 12 months ago.

"That is what I believe I am capable of doing. It's what I want to do."

AAP

World.title: Millions greet Spain's WC heroes as FIFA probes ugly post-match fights
World.content:
Spain's World Cup-winning team has been met with an estimated two million fans at a raucous championship parade through the streets of Madrid.

The 26 players and their coaching staff met with the country's royals, and then with Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, after arriving in the Spanish capital a day after beating Argentina 1-0 in the final in New Jersey.

"Thank you to the coaches and players for the style of play, the effort and the victory," Sánchez said. "We have truly enjoyed watching you play."

Spain's World Cup win a reminder collective spirit trumps solo stars As some of football's biggest names lit up the World Cup, Spain flew under the radar all the way to hoisting the trophy on its final day.

The squad then boarded an open-top bus for a raucous parade through central Madrid. "Stars shine together" was written on the bus, which also carried photos of the footballers.

Players — carrying the World Cup trophy and wearing shirts with the words Somos Campeones (We Are Champions) — danced and interacted with the fans along the route.

"It's been an emotional and proud experience to represent a wonderful country with such passionate and devoted fans," Spain coach Luis de la Fuente said before the parade started. "We are filled with joy."

The squad travelled down Madrid's historic avenues from near Moncloa Palace, the prime minister's official residence, to Cibeles Square, where authorities told local media that some 120,000 people were on hand for a ceremony.

Players were introduced one by one before entering the stage set up at the square. Each picked the song to be played when they came in. Álex Baena, celebrating his 25th birthday, entered with the World Cup trophy.

Coach De la Fuente was thrust into the air by his players after being introduced. The coach was among those who sang along to the song being played for them.

Striker Borja Iglesias featured as a DJ at one point, with his teammates dancing on the stage.

Singers Aitana, Ana Mena and Lola Índigo were among those entertaining the crowd and the players.

Thousands of Spanish fans gathered around the Cibeles Fountain (Fuente de Cibeles) in Madrid to celebrate their World Cup win. (Ruben Albarran/Anadolu via Getty Images)

The ceremony ended with the whole Spain squad lifting the trophy again, just like at the awards ceremony on Sunday, but now in front of the local crowd.

Groups of fans had begun securing their spots near Cibeles late Monday morning local time ahead of the team's arrival, bringing umbrellas to protect against the sun and temperatures of up to 35 degrees Celsius.

The square is where previous Spain teams and their supporters have typically gathered to celebrate. It is also the traditional celebration spot for Real Madrid when it wins titles.

FIFA launches investigation into ugly post-game fracas

Argentina's Leandro Paredes was given a red card after fighting Spain's Gavi following the final whistle. (Getty Images: Marvin Ibo Guengoer - GES Sportfoto/Getty Images)

FIFA opened an investigation Monday after Spain's celebrations on beating Argentina in the World Cup final took an ugly turn when players briefly clashed on the field.

Video replays showed several players involved in a scuffle, including Argentina midfielder Leandro Paredes.

He appeared to shove Spain's Eric Garcia by the throat. When Spain substitute Gavi jumped in to intervene, Paredes pushed him to the ground.

Spain captain Rodri also seemed to be hit in the stomach by Argentina defender Nahuel Molina as he ran past to join teammates celebrating the title win.

Molina later crowded Rodri, who was the target of a verbal confrontation by his former Manchester City teammate Nicolas Otamendi.

Argentina coach Lionel Scaloni and other players rushed in to de-escalate the situation.

FIFA said in a statement its "disciplinary committee has appointed a Disciplinary and Ethics Prosecutor to investigate potential breaches of the [FIFA disciplinary code] with regard to the post-match incidents".

The brief statement gave no timetable for an investigation and did not name Paredes, who was not shown a red card after the game yet could face a suspension.

Spain needed extra time to win Sunday's final 1-0 after Argentina was reduced to 10 men. Enzo Fernandez was sent off with a second yellow card in stoppage time at the end of 90 minutes.

The Argentina players stood facing their fans, with their backs to the podium, when Spain's squad lifted the trophy. It was an unusual show of disrespect to the new champions, who had given their opponents a guard of honour to collect their medals.

AP

World.title: Aussie world champs name new rugby sevens coach for LA Olympics
World.content:
Reg Tayler has been named head coach of the world champion Australian women's rugby sevens team, as the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics loom on the horizon.

The decision completes a succession plan following Tim Walsh's departure from the position after Australia clinched the World Championship in France last month.

Tayler was an assistant coach to Walsh, who has since become Rugby Australia's (RA) director of women's high performance.

New Australia coach Reg Tayler (right) pictured with Tim Walsh. (Rugby Australia)

Tayler will guide Australia through its two-year build-up to the Olympics.

"The squad is determined for continued success through to the Olympics in Los Angeles," Tayler said in an RA statement.

Rugby Australia setting high standards Only three years out from hosting the Women's Rugby World Cup, Australia makes a key appointment it hopes will help deliver success on the international stage.

"Our players are professional and dedicated to achieving a gold medal, and I am confident we will have the squad capable of that in 2028."

Tayler, who joined the Australian sevens program last year, has big shoes to fill.

Walsh not only led Australia to its recent World Championship victory but was also in charge when it won the inaugural Olympic gold in women's rugby sevens at the 2016 Rio de Janeiro Games.

It is the only time Australia has won Olympic gold in the sport.

Australia won the first women's Olympic rugby sevens gold on offer in 2016. (Getty Images/World Rugby: Dan Mullan)

Walsh, who coached Australia across two stints, will still have input through his newly created role as part of RA's strategy to align the sevens and Wallaroos programs.

He is confident Tayler will leave his mark as head coach, describing the appointment as a "seamless acquisition" for the squad.

"Reg is highly knowledgeable of the World Series circuit and has worked with many of our players coming through the pathways system," Walsh said.

"He's not going in cold, he completely understands the game and his expertise is going to be fully utilised by the program.

"It's a privilege and honour to retain Reg."

Tayler has previously coached the Australia A women's sevens team.

He also spent time working with Ireland's women's and men's squads between 2023-25.

Australia claimed the World Championship with victories in the final two legs of the series in Valladolid and Bordeaux.

World.title: Football world 'devastated' by death of English icon Keegan
World.content:
Former England captain and manager Kevin Keegan has died aged 75.

Keegan's family and Newcastle United revealed in January that the two-time European Footballer of the Year was undergoing cancer treatment, without disclosing details of his illness. His death was confirmed by Newcastle overnight.

Last month, Keegan, who was nicknamed "King Kev" and "Mighty Mouse" and was one of the most influential figures of his generation in English football, revealed he had stage four cancer.

Fans lay flowers at St James' Park, Newcastle United's home ground, in memory of Keegan after his death. (Getty Images: Owen Humphreys)

"We are devastated to learn of the passing of Kevin Keegan, one of the most iconic, influential and deeply loved figures in our club's history," Newcastle said in a statement.

"As a player, he brought world-class talent, ambition and belief to St. James' Park, helping to transform perceptions of what Newcastle United could be.

"As a manager, he ignited our city. Kevin gave supporters hope and pride, and led a team whose style, spirit and passion captured the imagination of football fans around the world. He was so much more than an entertainer."

Glittering career as player and manager

Keegan became one of English football's biggest superstars in his time with Liverpool from 1971-77. (Getty Images: Harry Ormesher)

Keegan began his career at Scunthorpe United before joining Liverpool in 1971.

He made 323 appearances for Liverpool in all competitions, scoring 100 goals over six seasons. He won three First Division titles, the FA Cup, two UEFA Cups and the 1977 European Cup during a glittering spell at Anfield.

After moving to Hamburg, Keegan was named European Footballer of the Year in 1978 and 1979, becoming the only British player to win the Ballon d'Or twice. He later returned to England to play for Southampton and Newcastle before retiring in 1984 at the age of 33.

Keegan scored 21 goals in 63 appearances for England between 1972 and 1982, captaining the side 31 times.

He moved into management at Newcastle in 1992, guiding the club into the Premier League and transforming it into one of England's most entertaining sides.

Keegan's team came agonisingly close to winning the 1995-96 Premier League title before they were overtaken by Manchester United.

Although the title race did not go Keegan's way, his rant aimed at United manager Sir Alex Ferguson in the heat of the race went down in football folklore.

After leaving St James' Park in January 1997, he had a brief spell at Fulham before taking charge of England in 1999 following Glenn Hoddle's departure.

He resigned after Euro 2000 and a defeat by Germany at Wembley Stadium, famously saying he was "not good enough" to do the job, at a media conference. He won seven of his 18 matches in charge.

Keegan later managed Manchester City before leaving the club in March 2005 and initially announcing his retirement from football. He made an emotional return to Newcastle in 2008, though his second spell at the club lasted only eight months.

A lasting legacy

A statement from Keegan's family, quoted by British media, said on Monday: "It is with immense sadness that we announce that Kevin Keegan has passed away at the age of 75.

"The former England player and manager had been battling cancer and was surrounded by his wife and daughters in his final moments."

Tributes poured in for Keegan, with Liverpool saying in a statement: "Our 'Mighty Mouse', his legacy at Liverpool will be forever etched in history."

England Football wrote on X: "We are incredibly saddened by the news that Kevin Keegan OBE has passed away," while former Newcastle striker Alan Shearer wrote: "My Hero. My manager. My friend. Sleep easy Boss".

Reuters

World.title: PM backs bid for future NT AFL team, no promises on funding
World.content:
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has backed the prospect of an AFL team in the Northern Territory, but has stayed tight-lipped on whether his government would help fund it to get off the ground.

With a 20th AFL licence up for grabs, the NT has been touted as one of the top options to take it home, with Western Australia and the ACT also billed as possible contenders.

It comes as Tasmania prepares to enter the AFL with the Devils in 2028, bringing the competition a step closer to becoming truly representative of each state and territory.

This year's Tiwi Islands grand final marks the first time a sitting PM has ever attended the iconic match. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

Despite being known as a breeding ground for some of the competition's most exciting talent, from regions like Gove and the Tiwi Islands, the NT has never had a top-tier team.

Mr Albanese visited the Tiwi Islands on Sunday, the first time a prime minister has travelled to the islands north of Darwin in more than 25 years, where he voiced his support for an NT team.

"I'd love to see a team here in the territory, as I'm sure all Territorians would," he said.

"It's a while off, [but] we'll continue to talk and engage with the AFL as well."

Anthony Albanese met with local players at the Tiwi Islands grand final on the weekend. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

Mr Albanese was asked whether the Commonwealth would help finance an AFL team in the NT as it has done to help create an NRL team in Papua New Guinea.

"I don't run the AFL, so I'll wait, and certainly any submissions from the AFL [for funding] would be welcome," he said.

"We'll engage constructively with the AFL as well.

" The Northern Territory has a great history of producing great footballers. "

'We have the raw talent'

Reacting to the prime minister's comments, Northern Land Council (NLC) chair Matt Ryan said an AFL team would bring huge social benefits to the jurisdiction.

'Work to do': AFL targets Indigenous player boost The AFL is considering a range of measures to boost the number of Indigenous players in the league following a significant decline in recent seasons.

"We have the raw talent, and I think we can do it," he said.

"I would push that 100 per cent."

When asked if the NLC would be prepared to consider helping with funding the establishment of a team, alongside possible federal financial support, Mr Ryan said, "I think we should all chip in".

"It's our team and I think we should sponsor or support them," he said.

Mr Ryan said he believed the establishment of an NT team would help offset the falling number of Indigenous players in the league.

Tiwi Islands women's footy player Mara Munkara, who played in the weekend's grand final, said an NT team would "mean a lot to the Tiwi people".

"It could bring excitement, everyone happy, everyone around Northern Territory," she said.

Mara Munkara says an NT AFL team would bring a lot of excitement to the Territory. (ABC News Pete Garnish)

A task force has been formed in the NT to try to build the case a local team to be created.

A business case published in 2024 included the recommendation for the federal government to fund construction of a new stadium in Darwin's CBD, to help bolster the jurisdiction's chances for a team.

The AFL has been contacted for comment.

World.title: Ex-league star Dureau dies at 39 after long cancer battle
World.content:
Former Newcastle Knights NRL halfback Scott Dureau, who became a Super League star with the Catalans Dragons, has died after a battle with cancer. He was 39.

Dureau fought cancer for the past 13 years and passed away on Saturday.

In a statement, Once a Knight Old Boys, the organisation that represents former players, said Dureau had earned enormous respect throughout the game.

"There are players whose careers are remembered because of what they achieved on the field. There are others who are remembered because of the people they were," the statement read.

"Scott Dureau will be remembered for both."

Loading Instagram content

He left a lasting impression on many in rugby league, but former teammates said it was the way he lived his life away from the field that would leave the greatest impression on those who knew him.

"Even as he fought for his own future, he continued helping young people build theirs," the Once a Knights Old Boys statement read.

After retiring from playing in 2015, Dureau returned to Newcastle in coaching and development roles, helping to guide the next generation of players.

Despite his challenges over the past 13 years, Dureau will be remembered for his positivity.

Scott Dureau spoke to the ABC's 7.30 TV program in 2019 about his fight with aggressive cancer. (ABC TV: 7.30 Report)

"Even when confronted with the most devastating news imaginable, his instinct was to focus on what he could still do rather than what had been taken away from him," the old boys statement read.

The Calatan Dragons also issued a heartfelt statement.

"A former iconic player of the club, he had been courageously battling the illness for several years," the Dragons' statement said.

"Beyond the exceptional player that he was, Scott was a man cherished by all those who had the privilege of knowing him.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"His talent and numerous achievements on the field, but above all his humility and kindness, will forever be etched in our memories.

"In these painful moments, president Bernard Guasch and the entire club extend their most sincere condolences to his wife Libby, his two daughters Imogen and Everly, his family, and all his loved ones."

Dureau played 42 games over four seasons with Newcastle before teaming with French club the Catalans Dragons for four years, chalking up 97 appearances.

He was named in the British Super League's "Dream Team" in 2011 and 2012 and won the Albert Goldthorpe Medal, the competition's equivalent of the NRL's Dally M medal, in the second of those seasons.

Dureau had been battling cancer for more than decade, having retired from playing after a tumour was removed from behind an eye.

ABC/AAP

Tech.title: Here are the 30,000 songs Sony is suing Udio’s AI music generator over
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Sony Music Entertainment has filed another lawsuit against Udio, accusing the AI music generator of infringing the copyright of more than 30,000 of its songs, ranging from Elvis Presley’s Hound Dog to Beyoncé’s Say My Name, and Harry Styles’ As It Was. The lawsuit, filed in a New York court on Monday, claims that this list represents “only a small portion of Plaintiffs’ works that Udio infringed,” as reported earlier by Music Business Worldwide.

In 2024, Sony, along with Universal Music Group and Warner Records, filed a lawsuit against Udio and the AI music-maker Suno. After gaining access to Udio’s training data through discovery, Sony claims it identified additional songs using an “audio fingerprinting” technique. Sony filed a request to add more than 30,000 songs that Udio allegedly “copied and ingested into its generative AI models,” but a judge later rejected the company’s motion, leaving the scope of the original lawsuit at 333 works.

Sony has now made the more than 30,000 songs the subject of its new lawsuit, which the company says it could expand. It claims Udio “admitted that its generative AI models were ‘constructed by showing the program a vast amount of different kinds of sound recordings,’” including from YouTube. UMG and Warner Music Group have since settled with Udio and are now partnering with the company as the music industry embraces AI.

You can read the full list of songs Sony is suing Udio over in this filing. The company is asking to block Udio from infringing its works, as well as for up to $150,000 per work infringed.

Tech.title: The FCC is planning to retroactively ban disguised DJI gadgets
Tech.content:
is a senior editor and founding member of The Verge who covers gadgets, games, and toys. He spent 15 years editing the likes of CNET, Gizmodo, and Engadget.

Last October, we told you how the FCC had given itself the power to retroactively ban gadgets that have already received its approval to be imported and sold in the United States. Now, the FCC’s getting ready to wield that power for the first time, by cracking down on the “DJI front companies” suspected of sneaking the Chinese company’s tech past its foreign drone ban.

For example, we highlighted a deal on Xtra’s version of the DJI Osmo Pocket 3 just two weeks ago, a product that already got FCC approval before the drone ban ever came down, and a proudct which Amazon offers with next-day shipping. If the FCC’s retroactive ban goes into effect, that product should disappear from all major online retailers and Xtra’s own website, and the company may even need to write off however many cameras are still sitting in US warehouses like Amazon’s.

The Xtra Muse and the DJI Osmo Pocket 3 — too close to even call it a “clone.“ Photo by Sean Hollister / The Verge

The ban wouldn’t affect gadgets that have already been purchased, and it wouldn’t happen immediately. The FCC’s currently taking public comments for 30 days first. While the FCC has “tentatively” concluded that these companies are selling equipment that should be banned over national security fears, it claims it’ll listen to “specific evidence” otherwise.

But that should maybe be taken with a grain of salt: the FCC largely ignored public comments about net neutrality and lied about a cyberattack. It’s also worth pointing out that the US government has never provided specific public evidence that foreign drones pose a national security threat to begin with, or why other products like cameras should be caught up in that ban. If you want to comment anyhow, you can do so with an “Express Filing” here.

In the meantime, the FCC says it has “temporarily deferred the grantee codes of these companies,” a phrase that it does not define. (A former FCC official tells The Verge he’s never heard that phrase before; we’re asking the FCC if that means these companies can’t get future gadgets authorized for import and sale.)

The specific companies that the FCC is targeting include Cogito Tech, Fixaxo Technology, Lyno Dynamics, Skyhigh Tech, Spatial Hover, SZ Knowact and WaveGo Tech (both of whom are behind Skyrover), and Xtra Technology, none of which responded to the FCC’s requests for information. It also includes agricultural drone brand XAG, which did reportedly reply to the FCC once, but not with the information that the FCC asked for.

All save XAG were brought to the FCC’s attention by Konrad Iturbe, who figured out how to track the “FCC front companies” last year. The FCC also cites our story about Xtra.

Today, the FCC is also announcing that it’s parting ways with one of the Chinese test labs that helped some of these products make it to market: SGS-CSTC Shenzhen. While SGS-CSTC did reply to the FCC to claim it’s not controlled by the Chinese government, as the China-owned CSTC only has 15 percent ownership of the lab, US law currently considers another entity to have control if it has 10 percent or more or a company — at least when it comes to authorizing radios for use in the US.

On July 10th, the FCC said it might take even more actions against the eight “DJI front companies” if they didn’t reply by today, July 20th. We’ll let you know what we hear.

Tech.title: The Odyssey turned me into an IMAX believer
Tech.content:
After seeing Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey for the first time early last week, I came away impressed, but somewhat conflicted about two of the film’s more fantastical set pieces. While those scenes were beautifully crafted and tremendously acted, there was something a little bit off about the way they hit my eye. I spent days wondering what, exactly, wasn’t quite working for me during that first theatrical viewing, and I thought that might have just been splitting hairs. But it wasn’t until I saw the movie again over the weekend — this time in IMAX — that the issue became crystal clear.

Though I’d heard all of the buzz about The Odyssey being the first feature shot entirely with 70mm film IMAX cameras, I thought a lot of it was clever marketing hype meant to activate Nolan’s cinephile fan base. I hadn’t considered how watching the film in larger format would make for a markedly different viewing experience. But The Odyssey really is a movie that needs to be seen in IMAX if you want to get a true sense of the story Nolan is telling.

Spoiler warning: This story contains spoilers for The Odyssey (which, to be fair, is an adaptation of Homer’s almost 3,000-year-old epic poem).

There are many scenes throughout The Odyssey that look perfectly fine when the film is displayed in the 35mm format. Majestic, wide shots of Odysseus (Matt Damon) and his men at sea make you appreciate the Mediterranean’s expansiveness, and you can feel the soldiers’ claustrophobic tension as they hide within the Trojan horse. Even though you can see that the film is cropped, Odysseus’ disastrous encounter with the Laestrygonians gives you a sense of how gigantic they are compared to the wandering Ithacans. But The Odyssey’s scenes involving some of the story’s more gargantuan monsters take on a different gravity when they’re displayed in IMAX because of how much more visual information there is to take in.

When I saw The Odyssey in 35mm — which is projected in a widescreen, 2.39:1 aspect ratio — I knew that the Cyclops Polyphemus (Bill Irwin) towered over the humans who marched into his cave searching for food. But when I saw a standard IMAX screening of the film — whose 1.90:1 aspect ratio is smaller than the 70mm’s 1.43:1 ratio — I had a much clearer understanding of the creature’s stature and the subtle nuances baked into Irwin’s physical performance. Because the IMAX screening projected a taller image, I was able to spend more time taking in details that were easy to miss the first time around, like the way Polyphemus has to hunch in order to keep his head from hitting the cave’s ceiling.

The substantive difference between the two screenings became exceedingly obvious once I saw the Cyclops chasing Odysseus and his men down a mountain for a second time. In 70mm, you can see more of the monster’s upper body as it lumbers through trees in a fitful rage, which brings an added sense of danger and urgency to the chase scene. I had a similar experience seeing the soldiers rowing past a whirlpool not knowing that they were drifting directly into the sea monster Scylla’s reach. The 35mm screening shows you that Scylla’s humongous, but the IMAX screening’s added real estate makes it easier to understand how she’s able to snatch her victims up before any of them realize that she’s lurking in the cliffs above them.

By shooting The Odyssey completely in 70mm, Nolan crafted a film whose size and visual detail could make it feel immersive in ways that most modern features aren’t. But he also chose a format that makes it difficult for most theatergoers to see the movie in its most impressive form. Because there are only about 40 theaters globally (25 in the US) that are able to screen 70mm IMAX films, the vast majority of people will probably never get a chance to take The Odyssey in as Nolan intended. This and the fact that standard IMAX screenings are more expensive than standard movies have prompted some to accuse the director of being anti-art and contributing to the culture of obsessive format purism.

One could also argue that Nolan is using The Odyssey to show IMAX and theater owners that there is a genuine public demand for films shot in 70mm. The current shortage of 70mm screenings of The Odyssey is due to the fact that IMAX hasn’t been able to produce new projectors. Speaking to Variety, IMAX CEO Richard Gelfond explained that the company has largely been focused on retrofitting old projectors, but there aren’t many movie exhibitors willing to take on the construction costs it would take to build the 1.43:1 screens necessary to display 70mm films. If IMAX and various theater chains were willing to pony up the cash for projector part development and venue expansion, 70mm screenings could become more common. But for the time being, the industry seems comfortable using the format’s scarcity as an effective marketing tool.

That marketing strategy has worked for The Odyssey — a highly anticipated project from one of the world’s most revered filmmakers. But Nolan’s star power clearly has a lot to do with the movie’s box office success. There aren’t that many other directors who could get people journeying across the country just to see one of their features. It also helps that the movie is actually worth seeing, especially in IMAX.

Tech.title: SpaceX in your index fund, explained
Tech.content:
is a reporter who writes about tech, money, and human behavior. She joined The Verge in 2014 as science editor. Previously, she was a reporter at Bloomberg.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Index funds are touted as one of the safest ways to invest. Rather than picking and choosing individual stocks, index funds let you bet on the market as a whole. So what happens when a company like SpaceX — a giant gamble, and, in my opinion, terribly overpriced — is fast-tracked into the Nasdaq-100? Does it suddenly threaten the stability of index funds based on the Nasdaq-100? Can a $1.77 trillion IPO crater the retirement funds of regular people who would ordinarily have no interest in investing in Elon Musk’s meme stock?

The answer has less to do with SpaceX and more to do with index funds — how they work, their history, and why they’ve been treated as one of the least risky ways to interact with the stock market. So I talked to Burton Malkiel, one of the people most responsible for the rise of the index fund.

“If I were buying individual stocks, I would think twice about buying SpaceX, which is tremendously overhyped,” he tells me. But SpaceX isn’t a reason to avoid index funds, he says. To explain why, here’s a dive into index funds, how SpaceX interacts with them, and how it all might play out.

What is an index fund?

An index fund is an investment vehicle that seeks to match a specific market benchmark, such as the S&P 500 or the Nasdaq-100. It was popularized in part by Malkiel’s 1973 book A Random Walk Down Wall Street. The “random walk” of the book’s title means that the past prices of a stock don’t predict the future, and because it is hard to predict the future, it is very difficult to beat the overall market returns over a long period of time. For that reason, most of us might as well just invest in the overall market and trust it will increase in value as a whole. “A very small minority of stocks are responsible for the whole return, and experts can’t pick them any better than the index as a whole,” Malkiel told me.

The strategy of index fund investment has been endorsed by Warren Buffett, who has suggested that the average investor is best served by putting 90 percent of their money in “a very low-cost S&P 500 index fund.”

And they are very popular! In 2024, the assets under management in passive investing, such as index funds, outpaced that of active funds, according to Elise Ryan of State Street Investment Management.

Why are people worried about SpaceX specifically?

Shortly before SpaceX went public, the Nasdaq changed its rules for the Nasdaq-100, so that a newly public company that’s large enough can join the benchmark on its 15th day of trading. That rule change was requested by SpaceX, Reuters reported.

When SpaceX joined the Nasdaq-100, on July 7th, index funds had to buy in. Interestingly, at close on July 6th, the stock was down. There’s some structural reason for that — namely, that everyone knew the index funds would have to buy in, and so banks and hedge funds most likely did some fun trades. Index rebalancing funds made out like bandits. Finance is fascinating and full of monsters.

There’s reason to believe that the index fund buying is part of the reason SpaceX had its initial IPO pop, according to research from Harvard Business School. What’s more, SpaceX is the initial entry into indexes for a number of expected mega-IPOs. Anthropic and OpenAI are expected to make their debuts later this year.

What does the index fund inclusion mean for SpaceX?

Some degree of price stability. New IPOs often fluctuate wildly. For instance, Facebook’s shares dropped 25 percent the Monday after its 2012 IPO, tripping breakers to halt trades.

Beyond the fluctuations from the market itself, a lot of people will soon be able to sell SpaceX shares that aren’t yet on the market. SpaceX employees are subjected to “lockup periods,” where they can’t immediately cash out and sell their stock following the IPO. Those periods are going to expire, and doubtless some people will want to sell shares. The index funds are likely to “help absorb some of the selling,” thus keeping the price from dipping too low, according to The Wall Street Journal.

How important is SpaceX in these index funds?

The company has a market cap of more than $1.5 trillion as of this writing, which is obviously enormous. But the IPO sold less than 5 percent of the company’s shares. Because of the way the Nasdaq adjusts its index, SpaceX will be treated like a much smaller company.

But remember, next month more SpaceX shares will be released from lockup. People with 180-day lockups can sell more shares than were initially sold in the IPO after SpaceX publishes its second quarter financial results, notes Bloomberg’s Matt Levine. Those results are expected in mid-August. That will make it more important in those index funds — though whether the price will fluctuate much is anyone’s guess, as short sellers are also anticipating the lockup releases. These market mechanics may explain some of the stock’s short-term price fluctuation, even though the company hasn’t had much major news occur.

SpaceX may take up more room in index funds as more shares are sold. But it might not, as selling usually drives down the price.

Why are people mad about SpaceX in index funds?

Musk has the majority of the voting rights for SpaceX. In other companies, shareholders can theoretically influence outcomes through shareholder proposals. With SpaceX that isn’t true. Other companies can be sued by shareholders for bad behavior, but SpaceX has limited shareholders’ litigation rights. One way to avoid a company that has made these choices is to sell the stock — but the inclusion in index funds means that’s harder.

But wait. I don’t vote on the corporate governance for companies in my index funds. Why does corporate governance matter to me?

You don’t, but the big indexers do. That means a lot of power is concentrated in just a few hands. It’s one of the worries people have about index funds. There are some other criticisms of index funds, too — that they buy high and sell low when they rebalance, for instance — and some investors believe they distort the market, making big companies even bigger. That’s why some analysts have called index funds “worse than Marxism.” Coming from capitalists, that’s a pretty big insult.

But still — if you believe those big indexers are sophisticated investors who are working on your behalf, you want them to make choices in corporate governance. To, for instance, vote against acquisitions that might be bad for shareholders, or install problematic members of the board of directors.

It seems like if you add up all these mega-IPOs along with the existing tech companies, there’s a lot of AI concentration in the index funds. Should I worry about that, in case AI is a bubble that pops?

Even before SpaceX entered the Nasdaq-100, most of its biggest companies were already AI-heavy — like Nvidia, Apple, Microsoft, Amazon, Google parent Alphabet, Broadcom, and Meta.

One of the biggest criticisms Malkiel hears about index funds is that the market is extremely concentrated, so that 10 companies are worth more than 30 percent of it. But he doesn’t view that as an argument against index funds. “The market’s always been concentrated,” he says.

“We’ve overhyped every technological change in history,” Malkiel adds. Railroads were overhyped, and so was the internet in the ’90s, and doubtless we are overhyping AI right now. That’s not a reason to be scared of index funds. “You’ve got to remember that it’s a very small minority of stocks that are responsible for all the return in the market,” Malkiel says. “That’s why you shouldn’t be terribly worried.”

What else are people worried about?

SpaceX isn’t getting fast-tracked by the S&P 500, another major index with its own governance rules. That may create significant differences in returns between index funds tracking the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq-100. (I, for one, look forward to seeing how that plays out.)

I suspect that most of the growth in SpaceX’s value has already been realized — which is why we have a megacap IPO in the first place, so that all the private investors can cash out — but as with Tesla, SpaceX is a meme stock with a sizable interest from retail investors. That decouples its performance from its fundamentals, effectively making it difficult to predict how the stock will actually do.

Does SpaceX’s size and inclusion suggest people should simply buy SpaceX stock directly?

No, says Malkiel. “If I were buying individual stocks, I would think twice about buying SpaceX, which is tremendously overhyped,” he tells me. But people wouldn’t be better off by avoiding an index fund in order to avoid SpaceX.

Over time, the market has produced a return of about 10 percent a year. But the majority of companies aren’t responsible for that return, Malkiel says. Only 4 percent of stocks give that rate of return, and everything else underperforms. If you own an index fund, you will definitely own a bunch of the stocks that lose money, but you’ll also own that crucial 4 percent. “We know experts can’t determine which ones are going to be good,” he says. “The point is, we don’t know which ones are going to be the best and which ones are going to fail.”

Besides, if you have an index fund with SpaceX in it, and SpaceX loses value, the fund rebalances with fewer SpaceX shares, since SpaceX is proportionately less of the overall market. Lots of companies, including those that are in index funds, go bankrupt every year. The focus isn’t on losses — it’s about gains.

Are there other SpaceX schemes I should be aware of?

SpaceX president Gwynne Shotwell donated shares of the company to Trump Accounts, which are investment accounts for children. The president said the donation was worth $325 million. That is perhaps more alarming than the index funds, because it ties SpaceX very closely to political power.

Let’s say I want to avoid owning SpaceX shares at all. How can I do that?

Besides preferentially investing in the S&P 500 index funds, you might also choose to invest in environmental, social, and governance funds. They generally have higher fees than index funds and don’t perform as well, but if not having SpaceX in your portfolio is a high priority, that might be a way to avoid it — since Musk’s control of SpaceX means the company flunks the “G” part of the requirement. (It may also flunk the “E” part, environment, thanks to the pollution from rockets and AI.) Different ESG funds have different criteria, but someone trying to avoid SpaceX because of Musk might end up with Tesla in their ESG fund — for its electric vehicles, Malkiel says.

Tech.title: Get Borderlands 3, Risk of Rain 2 and 13 other great PC games for $15
Tech.content:
Brad Bourque is a tech journalist and commerce writer based out of Portland, Oregon. He’s contributed to sites like Digital Trends, Business Insider, and WIRED.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

The aptly-named “2K Megahits 2026 Bundle” from Humble includes 15 Steam games for $15. It’s a smattering of the publisher 2K’s biggest games of the 2010s, including BioShock Infinite, Risk of Rain 2, Borderlands 3, and XCOM: Enemy Unknown. The bundle will be available until August 7th, though the bundle page notes that keys for some games are already starting to run low. All of the games work on Windows, while some support MacOS and SteamOS.

One of my personal favorite games, Risk of Rain 2, is included in the bundle. In the third-person roguelike, you’ll face off against increasingly difficult waves of enemies, fighting to stay alive as long as you can and collecting power-ups and useful perks before extracting to the next zone to do it all again. It’s just challenging enough to make victory satisfying, and fun to play alone or with friends. You also get 2012’s XCOM: Enemy Unknown, a legendary turn-based strategy game that’s usually $15 on its own, to give you a sense of the bundle’s value.

The bundle also notably includes three games from the Borderlands universe. Borderlands 3 Special Edition is a traditional looter-shooter FPS, Tiny Tina’s Wonderlands adds RPG elements like an overworld map and spellcasting, and Tales from the Borderlands is an interactive episodic visual novel from Telltale Games. You’ll also get a variety of shooters, including BioShock Infinite, Duke Nukem 3D, Bulletstorm, plus Hidden and Dangerous from the turn of the millenium.

Part of the proceeds from the bundle benefit Covenant House, an organization that benefits young people facing homelessness, as well as the publisher and Humble. You can adjust how you pledge is split between the beneficiaries by clicking the button that says “adjust donation” under the checkout button.

You can find the full list of games in the bundle below:

Mafia II: Definitive Edition

The Quarry

Tribes of Midgard Deluxe Edition

Homeworld Remastered Collection

Hidden and Dangerous Bundle
